[2516] Development is enhanced by the collaborative and incremental defence contribution to the developmental agenda

[2517] Objectives

[2518] Government has set the following objectives as the broad path for growth and development that will accelerate economic growth, reduce poverty and include the marginalised in the mainstream economy: a

[2519] The growth of the economy as the central and main intervention

[2520] b. Decisive State intervention to promote involvement of the marginalised in economic activity

[2521] c. Targeted intervention in the second economy to ensure socio-economic inclusion and increase social cohesion

[2522] The challenges faced by Government to meet these objectives include: a. Intensification of the work of Government to meet these objectives

[2523] The massive infrastructure outlay required to reduce the cost of doing business

[2524] The requirement to develop capital goods and supplier industries

[2525] An industrial programme to meet significant domestic demand, increase exports and create jobs

[2526] e. Development programmes to meet skills requirements in the economy and increase domestic employment

[2527] NATIONAL DEVELOPMENT AND THE DEFENCE FORCE The primary functions of any defence force are deterrence, defence and the protection of key national interests; a defence force is not a social agency, nor a prime economic investment

[2528] But due to the nature of the defence force it can, without detriment to its primary functions: a. Serve a valuable social role, particularly in a diverse society; b

[2529] Provide an economic boost to targeted areas of the country; and c. Leverage the establishment and development of some sectors of industry

[2530] A defence force can, thus, be an important agent of national development, which has been and continues to be demonstrated in several countries, outstanding examples being Brazil and Pakistan

[2531] In general, a defence force contributes to development by creating the peace and stability conditions whereby growth and development may take place

[2532] This it achieves by addressing the military dimensions of conflict and insecurity and by maintaining peace and stability

[2533] As a major national asset, the defence force may also be tasked to contribute more directly to national developmental ends in collaboration with all other departments and agencies, through the use of its collateral utility without detriment to its primary role or resource allocation

[2534] The broad defence contribution to national development may include the following aspects: Youth Development

[2535] Millions of young South Africans in the age bracket 15 to 25 years lack employment, skills, discipline and educational opportunities

[2536] This provides Government with a huge developmental challenge

[2537] The collateral utility of the Defence Force can be used to improve the employability of South African youth by means of skills development and community service through targeted interventions

[2538] These interventions will not constitute military training and will therefore not contribute to the militarisation of the youth

[2539] The focus of these interventions will be citizenship, discipline, teamwork and self-actualisation with the national youth development programme and any other tailored youth programmes

[2540] Should specific funding become available, the Defence Force will be able to expand the youth leadership and character-building programme in partnership with government and other entities

[2541] “Patriotism is not the exclusive domain of the military, but the Defence Force remains and provides a perfect template and platform from which to begin to address patriotism in South Africa.”

[2542] Spatial Dispersion of Defence Infrastructure

[2543] Military bases in outlying areas provide employment and improve the economic profile of rural communities

[2544] Defence will seek to enhance its rural dispersion and will promote employment from the local communities

[2545] Defence Force bases in rural areas will also prioritise procurement from local business and industry

[2546] c. Reserve Utilisation

[2547] The utilisation of Reserves from rural communities augments the income streams of poorer households

[2548] Reserves with specialised skills and experience can also be utilised to assist in development projects

[2549] The expansion of the Reserve system in rural areas will consequently be prioritised

[2550] Defence is committed to the continuous 100% filling of all funded vacant posts and an increased utilisation of its Reserves

[2551] Entry level recruitment to the Defence Force will be done through advertisements in the local and national media, and contact sessions at schools and tertiary education institutions, followed by country-wide selection boards

[2552] Community Services

[2553] The Defence Force can be tasked to render specific community services in areas where other authorities are unable to render the required support

[2554] Defence Force facilities may be utilised for the education, training and development of local communities

[2555] Such initiatives will be executed in collaboration with the relevant authorities and stakeholders

[2556] f. Critical Infrastructure Interventions

[2557] As a principle defence will not generally compete with the private sector in the provision of infrastructure

[2558] However, the collateral capability of defence may be tasked to enhance critical infrastructure in rural and inaccessible areas

[2559] These actions will allow for the sourcing of labour from remote communities and will assist in skills development and upliftment in such communities

[2560] “The Army must always be available to assist and support government action in the planning, provision and maintenance of infrastructure

[2561] The infrastructure planning and development must first and foremost serve the needs of the Army for its rapid mobility, operations and maintenance of that Army

[2562] The infrastructure planning and provision must go beyond the horizon of that Army to ensure sustainability and future requirements of that Army as it develops further

[2563] It will always be possible to have trickling down effects and for civilians and sundry to benefit from this infrastructure development. Inherent Potential The inherent potential of the Defence Force to support national development can be realised almost automatically as a direct result of its normal peacetime activities, although some minor steering can enhance this effect without detriment to its primary functions and with appropriate additional resources and time to establish capabilities to this effect

[2564] The Defence Force’s potential in this respect can be realised without detriment to its primary functions, and with appropriate additional resources and time to establish necessary capabilities

[2565] The Social Role – Developing the Person

[2566] Military service, even quite brief periods, can play an important and valuable role in: a. Maturing and socialising young adults; b

[2567] Providing a stable environment in which to enhance the education of young people from disadvantaged backgrounds; c. Developing in young people from different communities and social sectors a national consciousness and cohesion; and d. Enhancing and deepening the integration of minority groups in the wider community

[2568] The Socio-Economic Role – Supporting Local Communities

[2569] There is considerable potential for the Defence Force to support socio-economic development in, particularly, rural communities and towns

[2570] This arises from the fact that any military unit: a. Will inject resources into the surrounding community, through: i. Its personnel spending their salaries locally; ii

[2571] Local purchases (eg food, fuel, cleaning materials, stationery

[2572] Procuring certain services locally (eg glazier, plumber); iv

[2573] Hiring locally to fill certain civilian posts within the unit; and v. Recruiting from among the local population

[2574] Can provide assistance from certain units in emergencies – medical, firefighting, support to police, repair of critical machinery (eg emergency vehicles, generators, pumps

[2575] c. Can enhance or provide certain community health services

[2576] The Defence Force has an inherent ability to support economic activity within the country, arising from its need: a. To procure normal consumables, both locally and at the national level (for its reserve stocks), which can be procured from the business community; b

[2577] For uniforms and general field equipment, which can be manufactured by the business community; c

[2578] To purchase some commercial-standard equipment and vehicles that can be supplied and supported by the business community; d. To procure certain commercially available services (construction, civil engineering) that can be cost-effectively contracted to the business community; and e. To acquire locally produced and integrated defence systems and high-end technology

[2579] Finally the Defence Force has an inherent ability to support development of the industrial sector, arising from its requirement for: a

[2580] The maintenance, repair, overhaul, modernisation and upgrading of military equipment, which will not always justify in-house capability, thus creating commercial opportunity; b

[2581] The manufacture of equipment required on a scale that justifies local manufacture, as well as the manufacture of munitions and spares; and c

[2582] The development of optimised equipment

[2583] Science, Engineering and Technology

[2584] The Defence Force’s requirements can also stimulate the national science, engineering and technology base in a range of technical fields, which will: a. Spin-off into other sectors of industry, thereby broadening the country’s industrial base; and b

[2585] Attract young people to engineering, science and technology, thereby expanding and deepening the country’s technical skills base

[2586] Potential for Directed Development Support

[2587] In addition to its inherent potential, and given appropriate additional funding and time to ramp up and improve specific capabilities, the Defence Force also has the potential to, without detriment to its primary function, carry out a range of directed activities in support of national development

[2588] It can also support the civil authorities and police in dealing with natural and man-made disasters

[2589] Short term and medium-term service systems can be structured to include further education or training that prepares the member for a career outside the military

[2663] South Africa’s defence spending has fluctuated considerably over the past century

[2664] After the spikes of the First World War and the Second World War, when spending reached a high of more than 17% of GDP, spending declined sharply to around 1% of GDP until the 1970s, when it increased to between 2% and 3% of GDP, rising sharply to almost 5% in the late 1970s (Figure

[2665] The defence budget grew almost tenfold in nominal terms between 1975 and 1989, from R1 billion (Bn) to R9.4 Bn

[2666] In constant dollar value, however, the increase was modest, growing from US$3 bn per year in the early 1980s to US$3.43 bn per year in the last half of that decade, based on 1988 prices

[2667] Defence spending averaged 16.4% of government spending in the 1980s; it ranged from a high of 22.7% in 1982 to a low of 13.7% in 1987, but rose again to 15.7% of government spending in

[2668] In 1989, South Africa ranked 13th in total world-wide military expenditure, 44th in world military spending as a percentage of gross national product and 63rd in world military spending as a percentage of total government spending

[2669] South Africa also ranked 49th in the size of its armed forces, but only 103rd in terms of the size of armed forces in relation to population

[2670] By the mid-1990s, South African defence spending had been reduced to less than 3% of gross domestic product and less than 10% of total government spending

[2671] Military salaries by that time consumed more than half of defence spending

[2672] Spending on armaments and equipment declined from 44% of defence spending in the 1980s to 28% in

[2674] IMPACT ON DEFENCE CAPABILITIES Between 1995 and the approval of the Defence Review in 1998, the defence budget was cut by 11.1% (R1,4 bn) in nominal terms, with the concurrent mismatch arising between policy intent and execution

[2675] The defence budget further decreased from 1.54% of GDP in 2004/05 and has levelled out in recent years at around 1.2% to 1.1% of GDP

[2676] The 1998 Defence Review force design was consequently neither affordable nor sustainable, especially following the defence budget cuts in the late 1990s

[2677] South Africa at present spends less than 1.2% of GDP on defence, translating to less than five cents out of every rand of total budget being expended on defence

[2678] The Defence Force is effectively nearly 24% underfunded (in respect of its current size and shape

[2679] While South Africa is not perceived to be a global military force, it can be considered a regional military power in the context of Southern Africa

[2680] It furthermore has major international commitments to Africa in the form of peace support operations, most notably in Darfur and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), and has also recently begun military operations to support Mozambique in fighting piracy off its coast

[2681] In addition to the enduring deployments in support of the United Nations (UN) and African Union (AU), various deployments of a shorter duration are also being executed

[2682] Internally, the Defence Force has redeployed back to the country’s borders, further increasing the Defence Force’s operational tempo

[2683] Domestic and international commitments are thus currently at a level far beyond the policy predictions of the late 1990s

[2696] The integration of the Strategic Defence Packages has proven to be far more costly than was originally planned

[2697] The introduction of recently acquired modern defence equipment has resulted in an unprecedented increase in their operating cost

[2698] In most instances: a. In order to reduce initial cost, lifecycle logistic support was not fully provided for during acquisition and it was envisaged that this would be covered in the operating budget of the combat services

[2699] The current operating budget has proven insufficient to cover higher than planned fuel costs, inservice training, maintenance, repair and support to modern defence systems

[2700] The introduction of new defence systems required that they were extensively operated to prove doctrine, resulting in unanticipated costs

[2701] The on-going support needed to optimise these new defence systems, develop doctrine, tactics and battlehandling and ensure interoperability with other higher-order defence capabilities is placing excessive demand on the defence science, engineering and technology system

[2702] The current defence research and development budget had never planned to support these through lifecycle activities and argues for a separate in-service science, engineering and technology system and budget

[2703] Defence prime mission equipment is thus unsustainable within the current budget allocation and standards of proficiency are ever-decreasing, due partly to both limited funds for force preparation and the poor serviceability of certain major prime mission equipment

[2704] The major defence programmes (landward defence, air defence, maritime defence, military health support and command and control systems) therefore have definable risks and shortcomings, exacerbated by the escalation in fuel and medical prices, increased maintenance costs and the high tempo of operations which have to be supported along extended logistic lines

[2705] The South African military is consequently too poorly equipped and funded to execute the widening spectrum of tasks to the desired level

[2706] The increase in defence commitments from 1999 onwards, the introduction of new weapon systems and the lack of any significant adjustment to the defence allocation have rendered the Defence Force unsustainable and only partially compliant with the constitutional imperative to defend and protect South Africa and its people

[2707] It is severely stretched and many of its core military capacities require an intervention to make them sustainable

[2708] Internationally it is well understood that systems need to be managed over the intended life of that system

[2709] Generally it is accepted that the acquisition costs of a military system will reflect approximately 10-20% of the total lifecycle costs of that system

[2710] It therefore stands to reason that between 80-90% of the lifecycle costs will have to be provided over the life of that particular system (Figure

[2711] In essence this means that for a system with a 30-year lifespan, 2.67% of the total lifecycle costs will have to be made available every year, for 30 years

[2712] By example, it means that for a vessel with an acquisition cost (20%) of R2,5 bn, the lifecycle costs (80%) will approximate R10 bn

[2713] Annually, over a period of 30 years, the system owner will have to ensure that it allocates R333 mil to that system for lifecycle management (constant Rand value

[2714] This reality must influence the acquisition of new systems

[2715] IMPACT ON READINESS The Minister, the Military Command and the Defence Secretariat have consequently raised their concerns on the persistent defence underfunding and have consistently articulated the consequences, as set out below

[2716] The Services are integrated systems that can be defined as “an organised, purposeful structure regarded as a whole and consisting of interrelated and interdependent elements (components, entities, factors, members, parts, etc

[2717] These elements continually influence one another (directly or indirectly) to maintain their activity and the existence of the system, in order to achieve the goal of the system”

[2718] The Defence Force is a ‘system of systems’ and as such the various components are integrally reliant on one another

[2719] “These are perhaps the most significant statements in the document, and the most serious

[2720] If the authorities are not shaken by these, they do not have a good understanding of what national priorities should be

[2721] These very explicit warning signs should convince every sensible leader or politician of the need for an increase in the Defence Budget.”

[2722] Karel Nel – Private Submission Kruger, A., Peace Mission Programme ISS, 07 April

[2723] The SA Army faces block obsolescence of its prime mission equipment and much of its support capabilities

[2724] This is directly attributable to the SA Army not having benefitted from a Strategic Defence Package capital renewal programme as did the SA Air Force and the SA Navy

[2725] The lack of an adequate operating budget has further resulted in the serviceability of equipment remaining in service to steadily decline as major repair and maintenance programmes have been pushed back in order to reallocate the majority of its operating budget to personnel related expenditures

[2726] As a result of the above constraints the SA Army is no longer in a position to conduct major combat operations, nor fully roll out the forces needed to safeguard South Africa’s borders within the required timeframes

[2727] The SA Army is further finding it increasingly difficult to sustain the deployment of its soldiers in the various peace missions across the continent

[2728] The SA Air Force remains critically underfunded

[2729] This has a direct impact upon its ability to maintain combat readiness across the full spectrum of operational tasks expected of it

[2730] The air combat and air combat support capability is severely constrained due to an inadequate flying-hours budget

[2731] This has resulted in insufficient pilots being trained to fly the newly acquired fighter aircraft and combat support helicopters; those that have been trained are not being afforded the opportunity to fly the requisite hours for maintaining combat proficiency

[2732] From a combat readiness perspective these capabilities, therefore, remain largely grounded

[2733] Such aircraft as can be accounted for in an operation will also be restricted in their combat radius due to the loss of the in-flight refuelling capability

[2734] The medium and light fixed-wing transport aircraft are all reaching the end of their operational life

[2735] Increased upgrade, repair and maintenance cycles have resulted in a reduction of their operational availability

[2736] Currently the fleet is unable to meet the lift requirements for supporting the external operations and any surge in this requirement will result in an even greater reliance on contracted airlift services

[2737] The current medium rotary wing transport capability falls far short of the operational requirement

[2738] The absence of airborne early air warning sensors has resulted in a situation where only limited aerial domain awareness exists over large parts of South Africa’s airspace today

[2739] The conduct of intelligence-driven operations aimed at safeguarding South Africa’s territorial integrity and protecting its borderlines is thus severely restricted

[2740] The SA Navy experiences severe pressure on its operating budget

[2741] This has primarily been brought about by increased sustainment costs resulting from the increased operational tempo of its frigates as well as the need to keep the obsolete offshore patrol vessels operating until their eventual replacement

[2742] The situation is further exacerbated by increased personnel spending, necessitating the reallocation of critical maintenance and repair funds

[2743] This has resulted in a situation where the SA Navy’s vessels can no longer be made combat-ready to execute the full range of missions they were designed for

[2744] In particular it is the primary war-fighting capabilities that have been severely affected

[2745] The absence of dedicated static and airborne maritime sensors has resulted in a situation where virtually no maritime domain awareness exists around South Africa’s coasts today

[2746] The conduct of intelligence-driven operations aimed at safeguarding South Africa’s territorial integrity and protecting resources in its Exclusive Economic Zone is thus severely restricted

[2749] The cost of medicine, medical equipment and contractual obligations places enormous strain on the military health budget, exacerbated by increased personnel spending

[2751] The quality of medical care delivered to serving members of the Defence Force is consequently less than acceptable

[2752] Shortfalls in professional medical expertise severely limit operational medical support

[2753] Medical support can currently only be sustained at less than a conventional brigade through the deployment of a medical battalion group minus

[2754] Similarly, chemical and biological defence capabilities have become aged and obsolete and the professional medical institutes are struggling to provide specialised medical and research services

[2756] However, these hospitals must be recapitalised, new Military Base Hospitals built, pharmaceutical stocks replenished and a specialised Medical Base Depot established to store pharmaceuticals, including those required for national reserve stock

[2788] d. Defence retains people who no longer fit their post-profile or who cannot be economically employed

[2789] e. Recent service improvements for defence personnel were introduced without commensurate budget augmentation from the National Treasury. f

[2790] The defence budget was augmented each year accordingly for the Strategic Defence Packages

[2791] The tapering off of these additional capital funds means that in recent years the ratio of personnel, operating and capital has distorted the defence budget

[2792] The expanding defence personnel budget impacts negatively on the defence operating budget, resulting in an underinvestment in the levels of maintenance and repair, training and force preparation required to meet South Africa’s defence commitments

[2793] However, this apparently inflated personnel budget is not necessarily an indication of inflated staffing, but of an insufficient operating and capital budget to support the activities of the Defence Force

[2794] Similarly, capital spending has declined to close on 10% of the allocation, impacting negatively on the consequential renewal of prime mission equipment, constant reprioritising of the capital budget, and delayed decision-making on defence acquisitions

[2795] The acquisition of new armament has been sub-optimal due to a number of interrelated factors impacting upon the process

[2797] as reflected in the Strategic Capital Acquisition Master Plan (SCAMP) within the MTEF timeframe

[2799] It has further resulted in acquisition priorities being shifted frequently and in critical needs being only partially satisfied

[2800] In the second place the acquisition process itself is very slow due to the cumbersome regulatory checks and balances that have been built into it

[2801] This results in, inter alia, equipment only becoming available long after the requirement was registered, by Figure 9-6: Personnel, Operating and Capital as Portions of the Defence Budget SOUTH AFRICAN DEFENCE REVIEW 2015 9-8 THE DEFENCE STRATEGIC TRAJECTORY which time the requirement has invariably changed, giving rise to a new requirement or a modification(s) to the requirement being initiated

[2831] Restoring the Defence Capability

[2832] The persistent disconnect between the defence mandate, South Africa’s growing defence commitments and the resource allocation has eroded defence capabilities to the point where the Defence Force is unable to fully fulfil its constitutional responsibility to defend and protect South Africa and its people, and is hard pressed even to maintain its current modest level of commitments

[2833] The current Defence Force baseline is: A personnel complement of approximately 97 000 employees inclusive of Regulars, Reserves and Defence Civilians

[2834] Approximately 67 combat units, including Army, Air Force, Navy, Special Forces and Military Health units

[2835] c. Funding of about R40 billion in 2013 Rand value, equating to 1.1% of GDP and 3.8% of government expenditure (GE

[2836] SOUTH AFRICAN DEFENCE REVIEW 2015 THE DEFENCE STRATEGIC TRAJECTORY The Defence Force is in a critical state of decline which is characterised by: force imbalance; unaffordability of its main operating systems; inability to meet current standing defence commitments; and the lack of critical mobility

[2837] Left unchecked, and at present funding levels, this decline will severely compromise and further fragment South Africa’s defence capability

[2838] South Africa’s defence ambition is driven by its strategic posture, the role that it wishes to play both regionally and continentally and the consequent level of defence commitments made

[2839] There must be either a greater budget allocation, or a significantly scaled-down level of ambition and commitment which is aligned to the current budget allocation

[2840] In short, there are two strategic options available for Government: budget must be determined by policy or budget must drive policy

[2841] The reality will most probably lie somewhere in between

[2842] Nonetheless, the fundamental principle remains that the force design must match the level of commitment, without compromising the necessary ratio between personnel, operations and capital, and the balance between Regulars and Reserves

[2843] A balance of expenditure must be achieved, as currently there is a severely disjointed and institutionally crippling relationship between spending on personnel, capital and operating

[2844] Even with an immediate intervention, it could take at least five years to arrest the decline and another five years to develop a limited and sustainable defence capability

[2845] The longer the neglect is perpetuated, the greater the effort, time and cost that would be necessary to arrest the decline and restore the minimum capabilities required to safeguard South Africa’s borders, protect its maritime trade routes, conduct peace missions and humanitarian interventions, safeguard South Africa and its people and defend and protect the country against external aggression

[2846] SOUTH AFRICAN DEFENCE REVIEW 2015 THE DEFENCE STRATEGIC TRAJECTORY THE REQUIRED DEFENCE CAPABILITY South Africa requires a relevant, balanced and sustainable defence force to fulfil its constitutional mandate

[2847] This constitutional mandate can be distilled into four strategic goals: defend and protect South Africa; safeguard South Africa; promote regional peace and stability; and contribute to developmental and other ordered tasks

[2848] The future force design will pursue a balance of capabilities that adhere to the strategic concepts of rapid reaction operations for interventions, expeditionary operations to project forces for protracted periods, complex war fighting within the human and physical dimensions of the battle space, interoperability of command and control capabilities, and concurrency of operations in multiple theatres and joint, inter-agency, interdepartmental and multinational (JI2M) operations

[2849] The defence capability must be robust and flexible and able to project and sustain joint landward, air, maritime, Special Force and military health operations over extended distances for protracted periods on the continent

[2850] The military operating attributes of: command and control; movement and manoeuvre; firepower; intelligence; protection and survivability; and sustainment must be embedded in all capabilities

[2851] Joint Command and Control

[2852] South Africa requires a joint command and control capability to ensure joint action with respect to land, air, sea, information and space, and which must be capable of integrating with multinational, interdepartmental and inter-agency components to achieve synergy

[2853] Joint command and control must be enabled through a comprehensive situational awareness capability that provides integrated information acquired through liaison with allied and friendly forces and governments, local human intelligence, and static and mobile sensors for enhanced military decision-making

[2854] This must be pursued at the strategic, operational and tactical levels

[2855] South Africa’s contribution to the prevention and resolution of conflict will be enhanced through an integration of its diplomatic, military and other efforts in a complementary manner, and in instances supported by appropriate military capabilities that strengthen South Africa’s capacity to influence international developments

[2856] This requires a defence diplomacy capability, whose strategy and main effort focuses on those national priorities where defence diplomacy engagements will add the most value

[2857] Defence diplomacy efforts will further centre on fostering long-standing relationships with key African states and other strategic partners

[2858] South Africa’s increasingly complex and unstable security environment dictates an increasing reliance on Special Forces in defence operations, indicating an expansion of the current Special Forces capability in the landward, airborne and amphibious operational domains

[2859] Special Forces capabilities must be suited to: strategic reconnaissance; ordered strategic special tasks; deep reconnaissance in support of the combat services; and the execution of Special Forces-unique operations including, hostage rescue, and urban and anti-terror operations

[2860] Figure 9-8: Defence Goals and Tasks SOUTH AFRICAN DEFENCE REVIEW 2015 9-11 THE DEFENCE STRATEGIC TRAJECTORY areas for specific preventative and intervention operations

[2861] Such Special Operations Forces must be able to conduct joint and supported airborne, air-landed and sealanded assault operations, with air- and sea-deployable firepower, protection and manoeuvre

[2862] Special Forces and Special Operations Forces will be supported by joint defence capabilities, and will normally be followed on by more robust combat forces, specifically tailored to the mission

[2863] The larger portion of South Africa’s landward defence capability must be configured and maintained as a projectable, multi-roled medium-combat capability with enhanced firepower, manoeuvre and protection making it suitable for a range of contingencies

[2864] Such medium forces would be the bulk of South Africa’s contribution to enduring multinational operations; own safeguarding operations and other directed tasks

[2865] These medium-combat forces will be self-supporting, having embedded armour, artillery, engineer, communications, intelligence, logistics, medical support and other requirements

[2866] This medium capability may be further augmented by heavy-combat capabilities

[2867] These forces also have the contingent liability to support civil authority and the Police Service, and protect critical infrastructure if so required

[2868] Heavy-Combat Forces

[2869] The configuration and maintenance of a heavy-combat capability are required to deter South Africa’s potential adversaries and conduct landward operations in high-threat situations

[2870] Maintained at a core-growth level within a self-supporting armour brigade, it will comprise: armour, mechanised infantry, artillery, combat engineering, communications, intelligence, logistics, medical support and other requirements

[2871] Although relatively small, this heavy-combat capability must be able to augment the combat requirements of other multi-roled medium and special operations capabilities, specifically where the threat situation dictates enhanced protection, firepower and manoeuvre

[2872] This core must be sufficient to expand in response to changes in the strategic environment

[2873] Figure 9-11: Army Operations Capability SOUTH AFRICAN DEFENCE REVIEW 2015 9-12 THE DEFENCE STRATEGIC TRAJECTORY Maritime Operations

[2874] South Africa has a maritime-dependent economy and significant maritime interests which it must defend and protect through the configuration and maintenance of a versatile littoral maritime capability, a credible deep-ocean capability and effective maritime domain awareness

[2875] This maritime capability must be able to provide an enduring presence in South Africa’s areas of maritime interest

[2876] This will be pursued through a maritime defence concept involving deterrence and powerful intervention through surface, sub-surface and air capabilities

[2877] This will be pursued in concentric layers that are focused on South Africa’s ports, territorial waters, trade routes and marine resources

[2878] In support of the landward strategy, the maritime capability must be able to conduct riverine and inland water operations and augment firepower when so required

[2879] It must also be capable of strategic reach and joint rapid response across the spectrum of conflict, supporting the sustainment of protracted joint operations over long distances

[2880] Figure 9-12: Naval Operations Capability SOUTH AFRICAN DEFENCE REVIEW 2015 9-13 THE DEFENCE STRATEGIC TRAJECTORY Air Operations

[2881] South Africa requires a responsive and agile air defence capability to defend and protect the integrity of South Africa’s airspace through the application of air power, and to support the landward and maritime strategies

[2882] The air defence capability must provide deterrence and powerful intervention during joint operations, specifically through comprehensive air domain awareness, air combat, combat support and air mobility capabilities

[2883] Deployed landward and maritime forces must be supported through appropriate airspace control, reconnaissance, close-air support, augmentation of firepower and inter- and intra-theatre air mobility in complex operational circumstances

[2884] The air defence capability must also be capable of strategic reach and joint rapid response across the spectrum of conflict, supporting the sustainment of protracted joint operations over long distances

[2885] Figure 9-13: Air Operations Capability. Military Health

[2886] South African forces require sustained, layered military health support to protracted operations over long distances

[2887] Such support must ensure both force health protection and force health sustainment

[2888] Future information warfare will be conducted in parallel with more conventional forms of warfare in the maritime, land and air domains

[2889] Defence must develop a comprehensive information warfare capability, tied into other intelligence-related information systems and complementary to its other military capabilities

[2890] Defence must further work closely with other government departments and industry to: a. enhance joint operational capabilities; b. secure vital networks; and c. guide the development of new information warfare technologies, practices and capabilities

[2891] SOUTH AFRICAN DEFENCE REVIEW 2015 THE DEFENCE STRATEGIC TRAJECTORY Defence command and control must be enabled, with a specific focus on both operational command and control and the enablement of administrative information systems

[2892] The information warfare capability must focus on: a. network warfare; b. electronic warfare; c. psychological operations; d. information-based warfare; e. information infrastructure warfare; and f. command and control warfare

[2893] FIVE PLANNING MILESTONES TO RESTORE THE DEFENCE CAPABILITY

[2894] The considerations provided hereunder are intended to provide strategic-level guidance on the necessary planning which should be pursued to rejuvenate the Defence Force

[2895] The detail indicated in each planning milestone will be expanded through a military strategy and force design process to be conducted under the authority of the Chief of the Defence Force

[2896] The Defence Accounting Officer must capture the intent of the above in an Extended Long-Term Defence Development Plan, inclusive of capability development and funding trajectory, and integrate such within the government planning cycle

[2897] The Constitution of the Republic of South Africa establishes the Defence Force; requires it to “be structured and managed as a disciplined military force”; and provides the “primary object” of the defence force as being to “defend and protect the Republic, its territorial integrity and its people in accordance with the Constitution and the principles of international law regulating the use of force”

[2898] An immediate intervention is required to arrest critical areas of decline in the Defence Force and to create a firm foundation against which an appropriate defence capability can be developed to be able to sustain ordered commitments and have the capacity to respond to nascent challenges in the strategic environment

[2899] The restoration of South Africa’s defence capability can be mapped by quantifying five strategic planning baselines as firm foundations to direct the development of the Defence Strategic Trajectory

[2900] The following milestones (Figure 9-15) are posited as the foundation for development of the Extended Long-Term Defence Development Plan (in the order of twenty-five years), namely: Figure 9-15: The Defence Strategic Trajectory SOUTH AFRICAN DEFENCE REVIEW 2015 9-15 THE DEFENCE STRATEGIC TRAJECTORY a. Planning Milestone 1: Arrest the decline in critical capabilities through immediate, directed interventions

[2901] Planning Milestone 2: Rebalance and re-organise the Defence Force as the foundation for future growth

[2902] c. Planning Milestone 3: Create the sustainable Defence Force that can meet current ordered defence commitments

[2903] Planning Milestone 4: Enhance the Defence Force’s capacity to respond to nascent challenges in the strategic environment

[2904] e. Planning Milestone 5: Defend the Republic against insurgency and/or armed conflict to the level of limited war

[2905] It is important to note that Milestone 5 above reflects the constitutional mandate to its fullest possible extent

[2906] However, this Defence Review has carefully considered possible, probable and plausible circumstances in the strategic environment, at both the inter-state and intra-state levels, and thus realistically posits that: a. Milestone 3 must be urgently pursued and achieved in the shortest possible time so as to enable the Defence Force to: sustain its current level of ordered commitments and provide a reasonable interim level of compliance with the requirements of the Constitution

[2907] Milestone 4 must be pursued as the appropriate end-state for the Defence Force so that it: appropriately complies with the requirements of the Constitution; has the capability and capacity to respond to nascent challenges in the strategic environment; and, in so doing, provides significant deterrence against strategic risk

[2908] c. Milestone 5 is not a planning milestone per se, but nonetheless reflects and acknowledges that South Africa must be cognisant of the capability that may be required to counter significant insurgency and/or armed conflict to the level of limited war

[2909] Thus: i. Figure 9-15 indicates a ‘critical decision point’ that would have to be addressed before crossing from Milestone 4 to Milestone 5. ii

[2910] Achieving Milestone 4, however, significantly reduces strategic risk and therefore minimises the likelihood of having to cross the threshold into Milestone

[2911] It is improbable that the Defence Force will be able to migrate from its current state of critical decline to the levels of compliance set out in Milestones 3 and 4 without first implementing specific personnel, logistic, finance and organisational interventions

[2912] e. Milestones 1 and 2 are consequently stipulated as cardinal steps for establishing a necessary firm foundation for attaining Milestones 3 and

[2913] Milestones 1 and 2 can be executed concurrently should the resources therefore be available, thus shortening the timeframe of implementation

[2914] Notwithstanding, the organisational and capability interventions indicated in Milestone 1 cannot be ignored

[2915] To this end the following factors are identified as being critical to the Defence Strategic Trajectory: a

[2916] The President of the Republic of South Africa, as the Head of the Executive and the Commander-in-Chief, champions the Defence Review and directs the Defence Strategic Trajectory

[2917] The Defence Review and the Defence Strategic Trajectory have the support of Cabinet and Parliament

[2918] A strategic communication intervention is developed to pursue a national consensus on Defence

[2919] An appropriate defence funding mechanism is identified and implemented to support the Defence Strategic Trajectory and as such, the Defence Force is appropriately resourced along this trajectory

[2920] The implementation of the Defence Review and the Defence Strategic Trajectory is driven as a strategic priority by the Cabinet Member responsible for defence, the Defence Accounting officer and the Military Command, with specific emphasis being placed on the core deliverables and value propositions within each Milestone

[2921] This should be supported by an appropriate monitoring and evaluation mechanism

[2922] The Defence Review and the Defence Strategic Trajectory form the foundation of the Future Military Strategy and the Extended Long-Term Defence Development Plan, inclusive of the Blue-Print Force Design and Force Structure

[2923] The implementation of the Defence Review and the Defence Strategic Trajectory is directed and cascaded in a coordinated manner by the Defence Accounting Officer and the Military Command at all levels within the defence organisation; this being driven against an interactive and target-driven timeline

[2924] h. Monitoring and evaluation of implementation is instituted at all levels in the defence organisation, with comprehensive reports being tabled with the Executive and the Legislature on a biannual basis

[2925] SOUTH AFRICAN DEFENCE REVIEW 2015 THE DEFENCE STRATEGIC TRAJECTORY PLANNING MILESTONE 1 ‘ARRESTING THE DECLINE’ PRIMARY FOCUS The decline of critical defence capabilities must be arrested through immediate and directed interventions concerning defence capabilities that may be at risk, be unsustainable or be necessary for the meeting of current operational commitments

[2926] The primary focus in Milestone 1 is therefore to initiate the defence trajectory through directed organisational and capability interventions

[2927] Direct Implementation

[2928] The implementation of the Defence Review and the Defence Strategic Trajectory must be directed through comprehensive ministerial instructions and guidelines to the Defence Accounting Officer and the Military Command

[2929] The Defence Accounting Officer, in conjunction with the Military Command, is to develop and promulgate the overarching implementation plan that will direct all defence components according to targets and timelines

[2930] The Military Command must initiate and complete the Military Strategy, Blue-Print Force Design, Force Structure and the Long-Term Defence Capability Development Plan

[2931] A deliberate communication intervention must be pursued to establish a national consensus on defence and comprehensively inform the people of South Africa on defence matters

[2932] d. Particular initiatives to develop a culture of military professionalism at all levels in the Defence Force, with particular focus on the leadership cadre emphasising accountability and merit-based progression

[2933] Areas of Key Leverage for Milestone

[2934] The following areas of key leverage are identified in Milestone 1, and are also the critical success factors for migration to Milestone

[2935] Applying the 40:30:30 principle, the FY2013/14 allocation can only sustain a personnel component of approximately 66 000 Regulars, Reserves and Defence Civilians

[2936] Any personnel expenditure significantly larger than 40% will not provide the financial latitude for the rebalancing of the Defence Force

[2937] Recognising that the achievement of a 40% personnel expenditure will have to be achieved over a period of time, personnel expenditure should not exceed a 45% ceiling by the end of Milestone

[2938] Right-sizing of the personnel component would have to be achieved through a government-level intervention, which may include one or more of the following mechanisms: The reduction of those fulltime employees who are either: no longer able to meet their post profile requirements; who are surplus to the future defence requirement; or who are close to retirement; an external intervention to fund personnel above the 66 000 threshold; a combination of the above; or an alternate mechanism as established by Government

[2939] b. Leverage the capital and operating portions of the defence budget by establishing a mechanism whereby the reimbursement for troop contributions to multinational peace missions accrues back to Defence for utilisation in the capital and operating portion of the budget

[2940] An appropriate defence funding mechanism is identified and implemented to support the Defence Strategic Trajectory, with the following cardinal elements: An Extended Long-Term Defence Development Plan to attain the Defence Strategic Trajectory

[2941] An Extended Long-Term Defence Funding Plan established by National Treasury to support the Defence Strategic Trajectory

[2942] A reflection on the Defence Strategic Trajectory in the National Development Plan

[2943] Re-position the Defence Secretariat in order that the Secretary for Defence, as the primary tool and resource for the Minister to exercise civil control, and thus perform the constitutional imperative to: ‘function under the direction of the cabinet member responsible for Defence’, with the following support being extended to the Minister: i. Enhancing the Minister’s ability to exercise civil control over the defence function

[3008] Figure 9-16: Targets for Milestone 1 Figure 9-17: Defence Capability for Milestone 1 i. Initiate necessary processes to attain the defence capabilities required in Milestone

[3009] In Milestone 1 (Figure 9-16), the Defence Force will broadly: a. Consist of not more than 72 000 employees inclusive of Regulars, Reserves and Defence Civilians (average of 45% personnel expenditure

[3010] This should comprise in the order of: i. 47 000 Regulars. ii. 15 000 Reserves on active service

[3011] iii. 10 000 Defence Civilians, excluding members of the Ministry of Defence and the Defence Secretariat

[3012] b. Consist of approximately 66 combat units, including Army, Air Force, Navy, Special Forces and Military Health units

[3013] c. Have sustainable funding in the order of R43 bn in 2014/15 Rand value, equating to 1.1% of GDP and 3.6% of Government expenditure

[3014] The defence value-proposition for Milestone 1 is posited as: a. Internal Operations

[3015] One sustainable infantry battalion group with associated medical, air and other support, dedicated to cooperate with the Police Service and conduct other routine internal tasks

[3016] b. Border Safeguarding Operations

[3017] The border safeguarding strategy requires: i

[3018] The sustained deployment of five infantry battalions, with appropriate embedded combat support and combat service support capabilities, in a 1-in-3 rotation-cycle, implying a pool of 15 battalions to conduct this task appropriately

[3019] However, in Milestone 1, a reduced capacity of four infantry battalions will be deployed in a border safeguarding role in a 1-in-3 rotation-cycle from a pool of twelve infantry battalions

[3020] In Milestone 1, deployed infantry battalions may not always have the required combat support and combat service support

[3021] The sustained deployment of a two warships, with the required embedded capabilities, on patrol along the east coast and two warships, with the required embedded capabilities, on patrol along the west coast of South Africa

[3022] However, in Milestone 1, the funding constraint implies the limited sustainment of only two warships for maritime patrol along the east and west coasts

[3023] In some instances such vessels may not always have all the required embedded capabilities

[3024] The sustained deployment of two maritime reconnaissance aircraft on patrol along the east and west coasts of South Africa

[3025] However, in Milestone 1, the funding constraint implies the limited ability to sustain a maritime patrol presence along the east and west coasts

[3026] c. Peace Missions

[3027] South Africa’s current commitment to two medium, enduring peace missions can be maintained in Milestone 1 at the level of a battalion in each instance

[3028] In each instance, additional rifle companies and other support may be added during mobilisation for a peace mission operation

[3029] However, as is currently the case, such peace missions are constrained by two main factors: A 1-in-3 rotation-cycle in each deployment area, as opposed to the international norm of a 1-in-4 rotation-cycle

[3030] This has significant implications on morale, health, social and family stability for the soldier

[3031] Aged equipment that is difficult to maintain to the serviceability requirements that the international mandating authority may require in the troop contribution agreement

[3032] Such equipment may also lack the firepower, protection and manoeuvre required for operations in complex and often hostile environments

[3033] d. Intervention Operations

[3034] In Milestone 1, an intervention force comprising a single early-entry combat-group can be deployed to either fulfil South Africa’s continental obligations or to protect vital national interests

[3035] Such an intervention force could be deployed for a limited duration and would be further constrained by the following: i. Limited inter- and intra-theatre air mobility

[3036] Limited air combat support

[3037] The absence of link-up or follow-on forces

[3038] Equipment may lack the firepower, protection and manoeuvre required for operations in complex and often hostile environments

[3039] Regional Assistance Operations

[3040] In Milestone 1, regional assistance, disaster relief and humanitarian aid can be provided, to the extent that limited air and maritime lift allows

[3041] ‘REBALANCE THE DEFENCE FORCE’ Building on the organisational and capability interventions initiated in Milestone 1, the primary focus of Milestone 2 is to reorganise and rebalance the Defence Force as the platform for further growth along the Defence Strategic Trajectory

[3042] Critical to the migration from Milestone 1 to Milestone 2 is that the areas of key leverage identified in Milestone 1 must have been addressed fully, these being: a

[3043] The defence allocation becomes balanced according to the 40:30:30 principle during Milestone

[3044] The current exponential spending on the personnel component is being arrested and normalises at around 40% of the allocation, thus providing financial latitude to address critical operating and capital matters

[3045] The reimbursement for troop contributions to multinational peace missions is accruing back to the operating portion of the defence budget

[3046] An appropriate defence funding mechanism is identified and implemented to support the Defence Strategic Trajectory, supported by an Extended Long-Term Defence Development Plan

[3049] The Defence Secretariat is positioned to provide appropriate support to the Minister

[3051] A comprehensive defence organisational structuring regime exists in law

[3053] Chiefs of Services and Divisions are managing own subordinate structures within the targets and delegations set by the Defence Accounting Officer

[3054] Procurement is delegated to the lowest possible functional level and appropriate procurement capabilities are established across the defence organisation

[3055] The Defence Force has a coherent military command and staff system with commanders at all levels having command over all allocated resources

[3056] Commanders are accountable to the next higher level of command for their actions

[3057] The Defence Force is organised into combat formations that are embedded with all the required operating attributes for joint combat operations

[3058] A unique and dedicated officer recruitment programme exists for both Regulars and Reserves

[3059] Other ranks and civilians are recruited on a decentralised basis

[3060] The pool of professional and specialist military officers, engineers and technical staff is expanding to meet the requirement and experienced personnel are retained

[3061] The number of supernumerary members does not exceed 2% of total

[3062] k. All higher defence training institutions have formal linkages to accredited tertiary academic institutions

[3063] Career planning and merit-based career advancement are instituted for all defence members, coupled to education, training and development achievement

[3064] m. Rank is decoupled from salary for Regulars, Reserves and Defence Civilians

[3065] The military disciplinary system, minor corrective measures system and consequent administrative measures are established and enhance the discipline of the Defence Force

[3066] The integrated defence enterprise information system drives both defence administration and defence command and control

[3067] The defence industry responds in a coordinated manner to the Defence Strategic Trajectory

[3068] The defence acquisition system is responsive to those programmes specified in the long-term defence capability strategy and is able to deliver required defence capabilities within shorter timeframes

[3069] a. Redundant equipment and ammunition have been disposed of

[3070] Defence facilities are developing along a defined development trajectory

[3071] The capability interventions initiated in Milestone 1 are on a steady combat-ready trajectory

[3072] b. Development of a special operations joint rapid response intervention capability with the rejuvenation of airborne and air-landed and sea-landed assault forces and associated equipment

[3073] c. Simultaneous and critical renewal of the medium and light airlift capability, the in-flight refuelling capability, and the military air-ambulance capability, and the enhancement of the medium rotarywing lift capability

[3074] d. Enhancement of air domain awareness including static, mobile and airborne surveillance and tracking systems together with associated interdiction capabilities

[3075] e. Enhancement of maritime domain awareness and the extended maritime protection capability inclusive of patrol vessels, reconnaissance aircraft, unmanned surveillance systems as well as static, ship-borne and airborne surveillance and tracking systems

[3202] PLANNING MILESTONE 5 ‘LIMITED WAR AND INSURGENCY’

[3203] Should the strategic environment deteriorate to the extent that South Africa would have to counter a significant insurgency or repel armed aggression to the extent of a limited war, the entire national effort would focus on the creation of a war force

[3204] It is extremely difficult to predict the nature and requirements of the future war force, as this would be subject to the specific circumstances at that time

[3205] Nonetheless, the solid and firm foundations created from Milestone 1 to Milestone 4 would place the Defence Force in a very sound position for development into a ‘war force’ in a reasonably short time

[3206] DELIVERABLES The development of a war force would assume priority over any other defence commitment

[3207] Forces committed to any standing or contingent defence obligations would be reassigned and redeployed

[3208] The focus of main effort would be the rapid and continued growth of the heavy combat capabilities to that of mission-ready formations, commensurate with the anticipated threat

[3209] The existing capacity of the Defence Force would be expanded, those forces committed to standing defence obligations would be reroled and appropriate additional defence capabilities would be created

[3211] The protection of the rear area and all lines of communication

[3214] Enhanced strategic alliance and strategic partnering

[3215] The positioning of the defence industry in full support of the military requirement

[3220] The Defence Strategic Trajectory is intended to broadly span three cycles of the Medium-Term Strategic Framework

[3221] The following strategic policy options (Figure 9-26) are available for government to pursue the development of South Africa’s defence capability

[3222] Policy Option 1: Maintain the Status Quo Should for whatever reason the Defence Strategic Trajectory not be pursued by way of either agreement on the trajectory or the funding strategy thereto, the Defence Force would have to enter into an urgent redesign process to counter its current state of critical decline and attempt to establish a healthy, though significantly reduced defence capability that would be focused primarily on domestic matters

[3223] Its primarily domestic orientation and reduced capabilities would provide a very limited capability to: defend territorial integrity, ensure national sovereignty and support South Africa’s continental leadership role

[3224] The significantly reduced force design would have to arrest the critical decline in the Defence Force and establish limited capabilities that: a. are lighter and cheaper with a greater tooth to tail ratio; b. reduce the overhead costs of headquarters and command structures to single command corps; c. establish balance within a lighter force; d. reside within relatively unsophisticated main operating systems; e. meet a significantly reduced level of standing domestic and international defence commitments; and f. promote a spatially dispersed footprint

[3225] This significantly redesigned force would have to be modelled according to the following concepts for it to develop utility: a. A lighter, infantry-based landward capability focused primarily on internal operations

[3226] An air defence capability focused primarily on light, tactical mobility

[3227] A littoral maritime defence capability focused primarily on the protection of territorial waters

[3228] A Special Forces capability focused on a limited spectrum of Special Forces operations

[3229] Policy Option 2: Implement the Defence Strategic Trajectory Independently The pursuit of the Defence Strategic Trajectory will, over time, develop a defence capability capable of conducting major combat operations in the defence and protection of South Africa, its national sovereignty and territorial integrity

[3230] The capability created would be commensurate with South Africa’s continental leadership responsibilities, establishing the gravitas required in support of Africa’s peace and security architecture

[3231] The ability to project forces over long distances and sustain them for protracted periods of time will further bolster South Africa’s continental leadership responsibilities and influence, as well as making a significant contribution to the security of South Africa’s vital national interests

[3232] Should government wish to pursue the Defence Strategic Trajectory on a solely national basis, it would take significant time to establish all the necessary competence and capabilities to achieve the degree of defence capability set out in Milestone

[3233] Policy Option 3: Implement the Defence Strategic Trajectory in Partnership Government may consider a course of action that would shorten the duration of the Defence Strategic Trajectory

[3234] In essence, the main point of leverage would be the extent to which government might decide to pursue the Defence Strategic Trajectory with the assistance of either a strategic partner or a number of strategic partners

[3235] Partnering, either with a single strategic partner or with multiple strategic partners in specific capability areas, would accelerate the overall implementation of the Defence Review and the Defence Strategic Trajectory, as well as leverage a number of funding options for the trajectory
