[4283] CAREER-LONG CIVIC EDUCATION Complementary to the above, all defence members must be exposed to a career-long robust civic education programme

[4284] Civic education is regarded as the process in which taught values are translated into lived values

[4285] The aim and purpose of the civic education programme are to instil respect amongst military personnel and civilian members of Defence for the core values of a democratic South Africa through appropriate education and training

[4286] These values derive principally from the Constitution

[4287] They include respect for human rights, the rights and duties of soldiers, the rule of law, international law, non-partisanship, non-discrimination and civil supremacy over the armed forces

[4288] This programme must consist of and cover at least the following aspects: Subjects Covered

[4289] The key features of: the democratic political process; the South African Constitution; the Bill of Rights; civil-military relations in a democracy; International Humanitarian Law (the Law of Armed Conflict); the defence corporate value system and military professionalism in a democracy

[4290] b. Target Group

[4291] The civic education programme will extend to all defence personnel, both for uniformed and civilian members, but will necessarily be tailored according to function and rank

[4292] It must cover all the levels of military professional education and training for officers, WOs and NCOs, as well as for defence civilians

[4293] Applicable subjects must also extend to all levels of combat-mission-readiness training

[4294] c. Contextualisation of Civic Education

[4295] The civic education programme will be integrated into all aspects of education and training rather than being treated as an isolated subject

[4296] It will be applied in the military and defence civilian contexts through lectures, simulated exercises, combat/mission-readiness training exercise scenarios and case studies, as applicable

[4297] The civic education programme does not replace military or civilian disciplinary processes or procedures

[4298] The defence institutional culture will be imbued with respect for human rights and the rule of law only if its members are subject to disciplinary action in the event of transgression

[4299] A revised and cohesive military disciplinary system, a minor corrective measures system and concomitant administrative measures are required to meet the constitutional imperative that “the defence force must be structured and managed as a disciplined military force”

[4300] The current military disciplinary system was developed within the constitutional framework to assert norms applicable to military judicial processes

[4301] The current system of military justice is thus based mainly on the Military Discipline Supplementary Measures Act (Act No 16 of 1999) as read with its Rules of Procedure and the First Schedule of the Defence Act (Act No 44 of

[4302] However, challenges arising from the application of the Military Discipline Supplementary Measures Act and limited training thereon have led to perceptions that military discipline has been compromised and the authority of commanders eroded

[4303] The current system has specifically disempowered commanders by removing the summary discipline system away from the commander to the military courts

[4304] Certain challenges, shortcomings and opportunities for improvement have been identified and are being addressed through the development of a draft Military Discipline Bill (MDB

[4305] MILITARY DISCIPLINE An effective soldier is proud, tough and disciplined, and displays morale, cohesion, trust, shared soldiering values and high standards of military conduct at all times

[4306] Soldiers, in joining the military, agree to accept the lawful direction of those placed in authority over them

[4307] Soldiers train for the application of lethal force under conditions of conflict and in so doing accept the risk of death or serious injury in the execution of orders

[4308] Military discipline is that mental attitude and state of training which renders military obedience instinctive under all conditions and, if necessary, for soldiers to engage in major combat operations to defend and protect South Africa and its people – even to the forfeiture of one’s own life

[4309] It is this function that distinguishes the Defence Force from other government departments and from all other sections of our society

[4310] Sound military discipline is the cornerstone of a professional and functional defence force

[4311] It is founded upon respect for, and loyalty to, properly constituted authority

[4312] It is achieved through rigorous training that develops self-control, character and efficiency

[4313] Such training implies subjection to control exerted for the good of the group

[4314] Justice Kriegler of the South African Constitutional Court clearly spells out the requirement for military discipline in his judgment on the Minister of Defence vs Potsane and Another, and concurred with by Justices Chaskalson, Langa, Ackermann, Madala, Mokgoro, O’Regan, Sachs, Yacoob, Du Plessis and Skweyiya: “The ultimate objective of the military in time of peace is to prepare for war to support the policies of the civil government

[4315] The military organization... requires, as no other system, the highest standard of discipline [which] can be defined as an attitude of respect for authority that is developed by leadership, precept and training

[4316] It is a state of mind which leads to a willingness to obey an order no matter how unpleasant the task to be performed

[4317] This is not the characteristic of the civilian community

[4318] It is the ultimate characteristic of the military organization

[4319] It is the responsibility of those who command to instil discipline in those who they command

[4320] In doing so there must be the correction and the punishment of individuals

[4321] Modern soldiers in a democracy, those contemplated by chapter 11 of the Constitution, are not mindless automatons

[4322] Ideally they are to be thinking men and women imbued with the values of the Constitution; and they are to be disciplined

[4323] Such discipline is built on reciprocal trust between the leader and the led

[4324] The commander needs to know and trust the ability and willingness of the troops to obey

[4325] They in turn should have confidence in the judgment and integrity of the commander to give wise orders

[4326] This willingness to obey orders and the concomitant trust in such orders are essential to effective discipline

[4327] At the same time discipline aims to develop reciprocal trust horizontally, between comrades

[4328] Soldiers are taught and trained to think collectively and act jointly, the cohesive force being military discipline built on trust, obedience, loyalty, esprit de corps and camaraderie

[4329] Discipline requires that breaches be nipped in the bud – demonstrably, appropriately and fairly

[4330] The most common form of disciplinary proceeding against a soldier is a summary and relatively informal appearance before the commanding officer of his or her unit

[4331] This swift and purely internal disciplinary procedure is retained in the Act, which also creates courts of first instance staffed by military judges with more extensive punitive jurisdiction

[4332] For a civilian prosecutor, even one attached to the particular military unit but not forming part of the command structure, to have to take [such] decisions would be unfair to both the prosecutor and the accused

[4333] For such decisions to have to be debated at a more senior level by or with the officials of the NDPP, who have no knowledge of and little feel for the local circumstances would be even more problematic

[4334] In either event the effect on military lines of authority and command would be potentially disastrous

[4335] The effectiveness of a military organisation is inextricably linked to the concepts of command, leadership and discipline

[4336] In essence, military discipline is that state of good military order which should exist in a military command

[4337] A lack of discipline compromises the effectiveness of the Defence Force and renders it unable to perform its constitutional mandate of defending and protecting South Africa and its people

[4338] It is this good order that allows all members of a military command to act together as a cohesive fighting force

[4339] Deviation from this state of good military order is dealt with within uniquely military disciplinary and corrective measures systems

[4340] It is the responsibility of those who command to instil discipline in those who they command

[4341] In doing so there must be the correction and punishment of individuals

[4342] Disciplinary or corrective action may be taken against a defence member who fails to meet or uphold the military standard of conduct

[4343] This is entirely consistent with the military doctrine of ‘mission command’ whereby commanders fully control their resources and are empowered to make command decisions within their areas of direct competence

[4344] The broader concept of military discipline should be distinguished from military disciplinary measures, corrective measures and the prosecution of criminal offences committed by persons subject to the Military Disciplinary Code

[4345] In the first instance, military discipline is not about punishing crime or maintaining and promoting law, order and tranquillity in society, but about ensuring an effective military force capable and ready to protect the territorial integrity of the country and the freedom of its people

[4346] In the second instance, the military disciplinary system exists to uphold good military order and discipline using statutory powers to: Deal with minor infringements summarily and apply minor sanctions through a disciplinary hearing. Address more serious contraventions in a formal manner through a court martial

[4347] Address more serious contraventions in a formal manner through a court martial

[4348] Provide for extra-territorial jurisdiction when defence members subject to the military disciplinary system are deployed outside the borders of the Republic

[4349] In the third instance, minor corrective interventions are measures that the commanding officer may routinely pursue to address shortcomings that may from time to time arise regarding the personal and professional performance of a military member

[4350] Corrective measures are regimental interventions that embed military standards, correct errant behavior or adjust behaviour inconsistent with military norms

[4351] In the fourth instance, military offences must be distinguished from criminal offences

[4352] Certain criminal offences committed by members outside the borders of the Republic during deployments are dealt with by military courts in accordance with the extraterritoriality jurisdictional principle

[4353] There are, however, certain criminal offences which, if committed inside the borders of the Republic, are dealt with by civil courts

[4354] Purpose

[4355] The fundamental purpose of the minor corrective measures system is to: a

[4356] Provide commanders at all levels with a swift and formally regulated way of dealing with minor failings or defaults related to standards and performances

[4357] b. Foster, promote and uphold the requisite discipline and behaviour for the maintenance of operational effectiveness

[4358] Terms and Principles

[4359] The following terms and principles are confirmed: a. Minor Corrective Measures

[4360] i. Officers commanding or superior officers, using their command authority, may implement against any direct subordinate, minor corrective measures to rehabilitate, censure conduct or correct minor professional or personal failings and defaults in order to achieve, restore and maintain operational effectiveness and efficiency

[4361] Specific corrective actions may be applied to contribute towards the achieving and maintaining of operational effectiveness and efficiency

[4362] Corrective measures are inappropriate to address the following: Criminal transgressions

[4363] Habitual repetition of minor transgressions

[4364] The Minor Corrective Process

[4365] The minor corrective process shall involve the following: observation, reporting or informal investigation, recording and carrying out of appropriate action

[4366] The authority for the administration of minor corrective measures is derived from the command authority of commanders at all levels, according to powers appropriate to rank, appointment and utilisation

[4367] Corrective action implies regimental intervention by the command or delegated authority in minor transgressions with the intent to impact with immediate effect on the transgressor's conduct

[4368] Any person subject to the Military Discipline Supplementary Measures Act (Act 16 of 1999) may be subjected to minor corrective measures, whether inside or outside the borders of the Republic

[4369] Officers commanding or superior officers may implement minor corrective measures against any direct subordinate

[4370] Minor Corrective Action

[4371] A minor corrective action must: i. Be formally recorded in writing in the prescribed manner

[4372] Be applied with a sense of immediacy

[4373] Promote or enforce the maintenance of routine discipline within a unit

[4374] Comply with the principles of proportionality and appropriateness with regard to: The transgression or default

[4375] The impact on operational effectiveness

[4376] The adverse impact, or likely impact, on the individual or unit

[4377] The transgressor’s / defaulter’s rank, age or rate of remuneration where relevant

[4378] v. Be carried out under supervision, where appropriate

[4379] A minor corrective action must not: i. Be unreasonable. ii

[4380] Have public humiliation as an objective

[4381] iii. Result in unreasonable or unjustified discrimination

[4382] c. Minor corrective actions may include the following non-punitive regimental measures: i. Special instruction with regard to accepted dress requirements. ii

[4383] Conditioning drills and instructions

[4384] iii. Drill practice

[4385] v. Corrective training

[4386] MILITARY DISCIPLINARY SYSTEM The military disciplinary system serves to empower commanders to effectively enforce military discipline through the medium of military courts

[4387] This will support the command line to uphold the discipline and behaviour required for the maintenance of operational effectiveness

[4388] Terms and Principles

[4389] The following terms and principles are defined: a. Disciplinary Measures

[4390] Disciplinary measures may be taken by the chain of command, using statutory powers, to uphold good order and military discipline

[4391] Disciplinary measures are taken where it is necessary to correct breaches of discipline, punish the individual and/or deter others

[4392] b. Military Justice System

[4393] The line commander may undertake disciplinary measures through statutory powers, to uphold, maintain and enforce good order and military discipline

[4394] Military judicial measures are taken where a statutory military offence has been committed and it is necessary to punish behavioural deviations of individual or group conduct

[4395] Substratum of the Military Disciplinary System

[4396] The substratum embodies the following: a. A military discipline statute

[4397] A code of conduct for uniformed members

[4398] A code on the legal rights of the soldier

[4399] d. Military law training at each level of staff training

[4400] The execution of the provisions of the statute by competent functionaries with a sense of integrity and justice

[4401] The primary role of managing the efficiency of a disciplinary system is led, inter alia, by officers commanding, commanding officers at all levels, unit adjutants, regimental and other sergeant-majors or coxswains and other warrant officers, military police officials, military law practitioners and the military courts

[4402] MILITARY COURTS The Military Discipline Supplementary Measures Act (Act 16 of 1999) establishes the following military courts

[4403] The Commanding Officer’s Disciplinary Hearing

[4404] The Court of a Military Judge

[4405] The Court of a Senior Military Judge

[4406] The Court of Military Appeals

[4407] The Military Discipline Supplementary Measures Act (Act 16 of 1999) creates new terminology which steps away from internationally recognised terminology

[4408] This has been counter-productive and it is recommended that the term ‘courts martial’ is reintroduced into the South African military justice system, with greater participation in the proceedings of military courts by military line-officers albeit in conjunction with legal officers

[4409] COMMANDING OFFICER’S DISCIPLINARY HEARINGS A commanding officer and every officer subordinate in rank to such commanding officer and of a rank not less than field rank, who is authorised thereto in writing by such commanding officer, may conduct a disciplinary hearing of any person subject to the Military Disciplinary Code, other than an officer or warrant officer, who has elected to be heard by a commanding officer, for any military disciplinary offence, and may on conviction sentence the offender to any prescribed punishment

[4410] The penal jurisdiction of a Commanding Officer’s Disciplinary Hearing is as follows

[4411] A fine not exceeding R

[4412] In the case of a private or equivalent rank, confinement to barracks for a period not exceeding 21 days

[4413] In the case of a private or equivalent rank, corrective punishment for a period not exceeding 21 days. d

[4414] Extra non-consecutive duties for a period not exceeding 21 days

[4415] e. A reprimand

[4416] A person subject to the Military Disciplinary Code of a rank not higher than staff sergeant or its equivalent rank may, in respect of a charge relating to a military disciplinary offence on which that person intends to tender a plea of guilty, if he or she elects to be dealt with by a disciplinary hearing, be so heard without legal representation

[4417] Every finding of guilty, any sentence imposed and every order made by a Commanding Officer’s Disciplinary Hearing shall be subject to the process of ‘automatic’ review

[4418] Every sentence shall be reviewed by a review counsel who may uphold the finding and the sentence: provided that, if the review counsel is of the opinion that the finding or sentence should not be upheld or on the request of the Director Military Judicial Reviews, that counsel shall submit the record or the requested record of the proceedings, together with his or her views on the case, to the Director Military Judicial Reviews, who may thereupon, subject to the changes required by the context, exercise in respect of those proceedings, the powers conferred on a Court of Military Appeals, or refer the case to a Court of Military Appeals

[4419] The sanction imposed by the commanding officer presiding at a Commanding Officer’s Disciplinary Hearing is reviewed by a Military Judicial Review Counsel

[4420] Such Review Counsel may review the facts or law of that case or the validity or justice of any finding, sentence or order made there at and may uphold the finding and the sentence

[4421] Should the Review Counsel be of the view that the finding or sentence should not be upheld, he or she may request the Director Military Judicial Reviews to exercise the powers conferred on a Court of Military Appeals

[4422] The Director Military Judicial Reviews may also refer the case to a Court of Military Appeals

[4423] The accused person also has the right to approach the High Court for relief at his or her own cost

[4424] A military court may try any statutory military as well as certain criminal offences

[4425] The punishments which may be imposed by a military court are one or more of: a. imprisonment; b. in the case of an officer: i. cashiering; or ii

[4426] dismissal from the Defence Force; c. in the case of any rank other than that of an officer: i. discharge with ignominy from the Defence Force; or ii

[4427] discharge from the Defence Force; d. in the case of any rank other than that of an officer, detention for a period not exceeding two years; e. in the case of a private or equivalent rank, field punishment for a period not exceeding three months; f. in the case of an officer: i. reduction to any lower commissioned rank; or ii

[4428] reversion from any acting or temporary rank to his or her substantive rank; g. in the case of any rank other than that of an officer: i. reduction to any lower rank, to any non-commissioned rank or to the ranks; or ii. reversion from any acting or temporary rank to his or her substantive rank; h. reduction in seniority in rank; i. a fine not exceeding R6000,00; j. in the case of a private or equivalent rank, confinement to barracks for a period not exceeding 21 days; k. in the case of a private or equivalent rank, corrective punishment for a period not exceeding 21 days; l. in the case of any rank other than that of an officer: i. extra non-consecutive duties for a period not exceeding 21 days; or ii

[4429] Where it is impractical to impose the punishment of detention or confinement to barracks, including where the offender is serving outside the borders of the Republic or on a ship which is at sea, in lieu of that punishment, a military court may sentence the offender to be deprived of his or her pay as prescribed

[4430] In case of a sentence of detention or imprisonment, a military court may order the operation of the whole or any portion of the sentence of detention, or the whole of the sentence of imprisonment to be suspended as it may determine in its order

[4431] The jurisdiction of military courts extends to certain categories of civilian persons as depicted in Section 3 of the Military Discipline Supplementary Measures Act (Act 16 of

[4432] Every acquittal or discharge of an accused shall be final, but every finding of guilty, any sentence imposed and any order made by a military court shall be subject to the process of review by a Military Judicial Review Council or the Court of Military Appeals or on application be dealt with by the Court of Military Appeals

[4433] A Court of Military Appeals shall be the highest military court and a judgement thereof will bind all other military courts

[4434] A Court of Military Appeals shall be both institutionally and judicially independent from executive or command interference

[4435] A Court of Military Appeals shall be competent to exercise full appeal and review in respect of the proceedings of any case or hearing conducted before any military court and may, after due consideration of the record of the proceedings of any case or hearing and of any representations submitted to it or argument heard by it: a. uphold the finding or the finding and the sentence; b. refuse to uphold the finding and set the sentence aside; c. substitute for the finding any valid finding; or d. if it has upheld the finding, or substituted a finding, vary the sentence

[4436] A Court of Military Appeals shall comprise at least a serving Judge or retired Judge of any division of the High Court of South Africa (Chairperson), a serving military law practitioner (Member) with experience exceeding ten years in the administration of military or criminal justice and an officer with experience in exercising command in the field in the conducting of operations (Member

[4437] Independence further requires that the modes of appointment to a Court of Military Appeals and the conditions of service of its members are free from command influence

[4438] REVIEW BY A HIGH COURT Upon sentencing a convicted person, a military court shall inform such person, inter alia, of his or her right to approach the High Court for relief at his or her own cost

[4439] CIVILIAN COURT Members of the Defence Force can be tried in civil courts for common law, statutory and military offences

[4440] They can also be tried in military courts for military offences and for most common law and statutory offences

[4441] There is also protection against double jeopardy between the two court systems

[4442] However, only military courts, and no other South African court, can exercise criminal jurisdiction in respect of offences committed by soldiers outside the borders of South Africa (extra-territorial jurisdiction

[4443] Charnelley notes that “review to the High Court has not been, and should not be, excluded”

[4444] INTEGRATED DEFENCE INFORMATION SYSTEM REQUIREMENT Defence's legacy information systems no longer support defence business efficiently and are becoming unaffordable to operate and sustain

[4445] This results in the majority of available funding being directed to operating and sustaining these legacy systems and therefore insufficient funding being available for renewal and investment

[4446] Defence thus requires the establishment of an integrated management system to drive both defence administration and defence command and control

[4447] To this end an ‘integrated defence enterprise system’ will be established as the backbone information system for end-to-end defence business processes

[4448] The pursuit of an integrated defence enterprise system will be a matter of utmost priority

[4449] It will replace the disjointed legacy defence information systems and will provide automated, realtime, end-to-end defence management - supporting both defence administration (blue network) and military command and control (red network

[4450] The National Treasury programme, the Integrated Resource Management System, will have a major impact on the replacement of the current legacy defence corporate systems and will imply that Defence will have to develop the unique functionalities to conduct those elements of its business which are not included in the integrated financial management system

[4451] The migration to the National Treasury’s Integrated Resource Management System implies that Defence will utilise information systems common to all government departments

[4452] The integrated defence enterprise system and ‘general defence network’ (blue network) will be established as the foundation for all defence business processes and activities, including adding and reusing information functionality as it becomes available

[4453] The integrated defence enterprise system means the complete spectrum of: a. Establishing agile and dynamic policy on systems, software and standards, with cascading directives and delegations

[4454] This must be based on best-practices policy standards across the technology platform and may require Defence to obtain cutting edge decisionsupport services during this process

[4455] Collaboratively building the enterprise system, by establishing in parallel the following dimensions: i. Business processes across the resource areas. ii

[4456] The communication and network infrastructure

[4457] Establishing web-based business systems that enhance functionality and end-to-end values chain in all resource areas

[4458] Establishing resource services processes in all functional areas

[4459] e. Ongoing enhancement of the platform through new business processes, services and functionality

[4460] The enterprise system must integrate and optimise all defence information system requirements and serve as a basis for ensuring standardisation, compatibility, connectivity and interoperability

[4461] Proven systems are in service in some defence forces across the world having already been adapted for unique military use

[4462] An option is to procure such a proven military-off-the-shelf (MOTS) enterprise system where the development and adaptation costs have already been borne by other parties and which has already been tailored for both military use and modern compliance, accounting and reporting standards

[4463] A MOTS enterprise system must be able to interface with government information systems, yet provide modular security for defence information

[4464] The priority milestones, linked to the ICS strategy, in this process will include: a. Migration of defence applications to web-based services

[4465] Such web-based services may be necessity not be connected to the Internet

[4466] Enhanced personal connectivity for defence members

[4467] c. Revolutionised office automation

[4468] d. Institution of information systems training at all levels of the Defence Force

[4469] e. Data clean-up of all legacy functional systems by functional owners

[4470] f. Data integrity determination by functional owners

[4471] g. Staggered migration of personnel, logistic, finance and procurement systems to the defence enterprise resource management system

[4472] h. Archiving of data

[4473] The characteristics of the defence enterprise system will include: a

[4474] The enablement of combat service support through automated, tracked, in-transit visible, real-time information which is integrated with various resource system databases and networks

[4475] The defence enterprise system must be: i

[4476] Driven by core Defence Force doctrine and functional area doctrine

[4477] Granular, secure and accessible

[4478] Compliant with defence regulatory framework standards

[4479] Integrated across all resource areas

[4480] Deployable at all locations of defence activity

[4481] Operational to the lowest functional level in the field, performing over limited bandwidth and non-persistent network infrastructure, or even independently at remote locations

[4482] Figure 13-1: Next Generation Enterprise Architecture

[4483] Complete business-to-business system integration with information at the 5th line of support, industry standard information systems and other defence information management systems

[4484] Enabling of data integrity and clean-up of disparate information

[4485] Enabling of accountability and reporting across all levels and functions

[4486] x. Enabling of organisational auditability and set standards

[4487] Enabling of compliance with standards

[4488] Enabling of aggregated business intelligence

[4489] Contribution to organisational performance management and organisational reporting

[4490] Contribution to early warning and risk aversion

[4491] The defence enterprise system must be able to adapt to rapidly changing business process architecture, data and technology with minimal delay and cost, and without requiring changes in the information system platform and software

[4492] Defence Command and Control The ability to exercise command and control is critical to the effective execution of the defence mission, goals and tasks

[4493] The diversity of military tasks performed by different combat, combat support, combat service support and other support structures requires both single service and joint command and control capabilities

[4494] Military command and control will be driven by the concept of “network enabled command and control” through standardised new-generation digital communication equipment capable of transferring all types of data on the battlefield, thus facilitating network-enabled operations and improved situational awareness

[4495] The command and control network (red network) will be a sub-set of the defence enterprise network (blue network) within the 'next generation technology platform', supported by enhanced granular security

[4496] This network will prioritise quality, integrity and reliability

[4497] PERSONAL MOBILE CONNECTIVITY OF DEFENCE PERSONNEL Portable interconnectivity between defence personnel, independent of the place of work and from remote locations, is crucial for both effective command and control and management in the workplace

[4498] To this end, web-based connectivity between members and employees at appropriate levels in the organisation must be enhanced

[4499] The defence enterprise system must thus provide integrated workplace electronic connectivity enabling real-time communication between members responsible for the command and management of the organisation

[4500] PERFORMANCE MANAGEMENT Defence performance management is defined as that set of management processes, supported by information technology, that help to improve the execution of strategy, day-to-day management and decision-making

[4501] Performance management enables the definition and communication of identified strategies, performance plans, measures and targets that are to be pursued in the improvement of organisational performance

[4502] Figure 13-2 depicts the national planning, budgeting and reporting cycle

[4503] Figure 13-2: Overarching National Planning, Budgeting and Reporting Cycle The performance management process must enhance the formulation of strategic objectives, provide measures for performance and analyse and generate reports on organisational performance as well as align the people and culture towards achieving the set objectives

[4504] Performance reporting, both financial and non-financial, is therefore essential in measuring and quantifying organisational performance and compliance

[4505] The accurate provision of financial information such as budgets, expenditures and revenues remains critical for the determination of the costs and efficiencies of programmes

[4506] On the other hand, the accurate provision of non-financial information such as outcomes and outputs is equally important for assessing the effectiveness and progress of the organisation

[4507] Performance information must be appropriate and promote results-based management, where such results are measured against a determination of risk, success or failure and therefore are drivers to an adjustment to future-oriented strategies

[4508] Measurement of performance therefore ensures, inter alia, that: Civil oversight and control are enhanced

[4509] b. Organisational policy is complied with

[4510] c. Policy, planning, budgeting and reporting are aligned to ensure enhanced efficiency and effectiveness

[4511] Funding equates to measurable results

[4512] e. Information is utilised strategically to improve policy and funding choices

[4513] The defence value-proposition is defined and pursued

[4514] g. Individual employee performance and accountability are enhanced

[4515] h. Organisational and individual focus remains on the defence mandate and policy priorities

[4516] DEFENCE PERFORMANCE MONITORING AND EVALUATION Performance management has numerous facets which are broadly grouped to the following areas: a. Organisational performance

[4517] b. Employee performance

[4518] The selection of a performance management tool is critical and must allow for the full range of assessment, including assessing the organisation against the achievement of its objectives or required outcomes

[4519] The performance management tool must also provide the ability to assess and manage the performance of individual employees against their respective individual performance agreements which must be concomitantly aligned to organisational outcomes

[4520] In so doing, the employees will be aligned to the required outcomes of the organisation

[4521] Each area of performance management is continuously tested and evaluated in accordance with a cycle as depicted in Figure 13-3 below

[4522] Monitoring and evaluation forms part of the overarching performance management process of the organisation as it is inculcated and integral to planning, not an add-on after-thought

[4523] Monitoring and evaluation findings must feed into the next planning process so that new outcomes, outputs and performance baselines and indicators can be set

[4524] Figure 13-4 depicts the monitoring and evaluation process and sub-processes that culminate in the required performance reports which enhance civil control and oversight

[4525] RISK MANAGEMENT Risks to organisational performance are identified during the annual planning phase and are then aligned to performance indicators and targets as set out in the annual performance plan

[4526] These identified risks are generally based on assumptions made during the planning phase

[4527] The application of risk management during planning allows for the development of contingencies and a systematic approach to mitigation of the negative consequences of the materialising risks

[4528] When risks are properly identified, there is a correlation between the deviations from planned performance and the risks that were identified

[4529] Progress on the mitigation of risks is reported on as a mechanism to monitor the minimisation of deviation from planned performance

[4530] DEFENCE ORGANISATIONAL STRUCTURING PRINCIPLES

[4531] The design and structure of the Defence Force must be informed by the defence mandate, mission, goals and tasks, coupled to defence doctrine

[4532] The policy, philosophy, concept and doctrine for defence structure management must thus enable rapid and responsible structure management throughout the defence organisation, including: the establishment, adjustment and alignment of structures under delegation by Service and Division chiefs

[4533] Consequently, the Defence Act (Act No 42 of 2002) must be amended to provide a clear and considered mandate for the management of defence organisational structures

[4534] The following principles must be embedded in the amendment: a

[4535] The Head of Department and Accounting Officer must establish and maintain the defence macro-structure, under approval of the Minister as the Executive Authority

[4536] Such macro-structure will enjoy the force of policy

[4537] The defence macro-structure must be reviewed every five years, or if there are required changes to the Defence Force Establishment Table, or if there is any other amendment the Minister may deem necessary

[4538] The Minister retains the authority to open and close force structure elements and commission and decommission vessels, ships, aircraft, vehicles systems, combat systems and combat-support systems

[4539] The defence macro-structure must include: i

[4540] The mandate of each Service and Division. ii

[4541] The outputs for each Service and Division

[4542] The post-structure threshold for each Service SOUTH AFRICAN DEFENCE REVIEW 2015 DEFENCE MANAGEMENT SYSTEMS and Division, inclusive of the Regular, Reserve and civilian components, and indicating thresholds of both active and non-active posts

[4543] A personnel budget ceiling of each Service and Division, expressed in the Rand value of a particular financial year

[4544] v. As a general principle, at least 30% of active posts on the corporate force structure will be reserved for Reserves to rotate through

[4545] This number may be higher at unit level and lower at headquarters level

[4546] e. Chiefs of Services and Divisions will: i. Receive appropriate delegations to undertake organisational structure management within the context of composite guidelines and restrictions. ii

[4547] Have own inherent capacity to administerate own organisational structures within the context of given delegation, policy, guidelines and restrictions

[4548] Constantly pursue a balance between personnel, operating and capital costs

[4549] Remain aligned with the approved defence macro-structure

[4550] v. Ensure sustainability of prescribed macro-capabilities and achieve set deliverables

[4551] The Head of Department and Accounting Officer must enable the establishment of organisational structuring, internal controls, not limited to: a. Establishing organisational structure management practices, procedures and standards

[4552] Providing functional training on organisational structure management

[4553] Ensuring quality control of defence structures

[4554] Maintaining the necessary ICT system

[4555] DEFENCE FORCE ESTABLISHMENT TABLE

[4556] The role, shape, size and footprint of the Defence Force must be determined as the firm basis for future defence planning and be expressed in a Defence Force Establishment Table

[4557] The Defence Force Establishment Table, informing the defence macro-structure, must provide at least the following information: a. The name, nature and purpose of each force structure element

[4558] An indication of the opening or closing date of the force structure element

[4559] The envisaged readiness level of the force structure element

[4560] The mixture of Regulars, Reserves and defence civilians in the force structure element

[4561] An indication of the prime mission equipment of the force structure element

[4562] The embedded support system within the force structure element

[4563] The Defence Force Establishment Table excludes any temporary task force, temporary headquarters, group element or unit established by the Chief of the Defence Force for military exercises or operations

[4564] The Defence Force Establishment Table must be presented by the Chief of the Defence Force to the Minister on at least a five-yearly basis for approval

[4565] It must be a configured and controlled Defence Force document and must enjoy the force of policy

[4566] The achievement of the Defence Force Establishment Table, however, remains critically dependent on resources

[4567] Thus the Defence Force will continuously mitigate these resource constraints by adjusting the levels of readiness of force structure elements, as well as through a careful mixture of Regulars and Reserves within the ‘one-force’ approach

[4568] Should the allocated or anticipated resources be insufficient to establish and sustain the capabilities required, adjustments to the defence requirement, the defence concept or the resource allocation (or a combination of these) will be required to establish a balance between intent and available resources

[4570] SOUTH AFRICAN DEFENCE REVIEW 2015 DEFENCE RESOURCE SYSTEMS INTRODUCTION

[4571] The rapidly changing strategic environment requires an agile and balanced military force that can execute its function in pursuit of national security in the most efficient and effective way possible, across the defence mission goals and tasks

[4572] Flexibility remains essential

[4573] The defence design, structure, profile and footprint are critical for establishing affordability and therefore sustainability

[4574] The execution of the defence function is achieved through the integration of the force design, the supporting capabilities vested in the force structure, resources and efficient business processes

[4575] This integration is managed by the staff system and enabled by an integrated ICT system and a business process architecture tailored to defence needs and supported in its decision-making by an appropriate defence science, engineering and technology capability

[4576] At the highest level these functions are directed, orchestrated and controlled by the respective Chiefs of Staff Divisions

[4577] Units, across the different levels, must be structured for the required support capabilities necessary for the successful attainment of their respective tasks

[4578] The functional resource areas and the impact of transverse resource systems are depicted in the cross impact matrix below

[4579] OVERARCHING DEFENCE SERVICE SUPPORT DOCTRINE DEFENCE COMBAT SERVICE SUPPORT PRINCIPLES Defence combat service support is an overarching function providing combat services with support across the full spectrum of conflict

[4580] It is the process of supplying combat services with resource support including equipment, facilities, consumables, personnel and finance support for the successful attainment of the defence mission, goals and tasks

[4581] In simple terms, defence combat service support includes health support, personnel resources, logistic resources, financial resources, organisation structure and the ability of the force to continually sustain and restore itself

[4582] Defence combat service support can only be a joint defence endeavour

[4583] This combat service support doctrine is applicable to all support functions and support commands

[4584] Combat service support will be provided within: a. 5th Line Support

[4585] Support from the industrial and commercial base of both national and international partners

[4586] This may include the national and international defence industry and various civilian institutions

[4587] b. 4th Line Support

[4588] Support from the deeper levels in the Defence Force, extending to static bases, mobilisation centres, depots and other static establishments in the rear area

[4589] The delivery of this support is a joint responsibility of both combat services and combat service support, and includes common and unique support

[4590] c. 3rd Line Support

[4591] Support from both static and mobile Defence Force capabilities deployed to shorten the lines of communication to deployed combat forces in the combat zone

[4592] In the SA Army, it would be the responsibility of the combat division to provide 3rd line support

[4593] This may include forward basing, preposition and forward mounting

[4594] nd Line Support

[4595] Intermediate support capability which is provided in the theatre of operations

[4596] In the case of the SA Army, it would be the responsibility of the brigade to provide a second line support

[4597] e. 1st Line Support

[4598] Organisation and organic support at the unit level, provided organisationally at unit level in the theatre of operations

[4599] The unit is required to provide support to its sub-units and lower organisations

[4600] In the case of the SA Army, 1st line support is organisationally provided at the battalion level

[4601] The defence enterprise information system is a critical intervention to drive all combat service support

[4602] Combat service support remains critically reliant on such a transverse system

[4603] The following common principles will guide all components of the defence combat service support system through centralised direction and decentralised execution: a. Functional Authority

[4604] i. Functional control is embedded in the respective staff division, which is responsible to plan, orchestrate, direct and control support through, inter alia, the provision of functional policy, doctrine, functional and competency standards and standardisation, and training curricula. ii

[4605] Functional authorities are responsible for the integration of functional doctrine with Defence Force doctrine, multinational doctrine and practices

[4606] Functional Competency Authorities

[4607] Functional competency authorities are, of necessity, appointed and mandated from both combat services and staff divisions to provide military certification for defence prime mission equipment, support equipment, munitions, personnel selection, and personnel competency certificates

[4608] c. Combat Services

[4609] i. Combat forces will have all necessary inherent support capabilities up to the battalion or equivalent level. ii

[4610] Combat forces are, in turn, sustained by the intermediate and deeper level support structures

[4611] Combat services are responsible for their unique 5th to 1st line support

[4612] d. Common Support

[4613] Transverse support of a common nature, normally of significant quantity, will be provided through the command and staff capabilities of the Chief of the Defence Force

[4614] This may extend to, inter alia: i. Setting of term and transverse procurement contracts. ii

[4615] Management of common commodities and services

[4616] v. Pension management

[4617] Professional development training

[4618] Military tertiary education and development

[4619] DEFENCE SUPPORT AT THE NATIONAL LEVEL The National Executive provides strategic guidance on priorities and national interests

[4620] It further determines the National Defence Policy, and determines the quantity, quality and level of strategic national resources required (e.g.: oil, ammunition, strategic lift

[4621] This sustainment may be coordinated with international partners

[4622] At the national level, sustainment is planned and coordinated interdepartmentally with roleplaying departments responsible for various national strategic resources and industry

[4623] The Defence Force is resourced according to the National Defence Policy

[4624] The Commander-in-Chief, together with the National Executive, consults on and determines the defence budget allocation

[4625] Funds are appropriated by Parliament by means of a vote

[4626] CONCEPTS TO ENHANCE DEFENCE COMBAT SERVICE SUPPORT The Defence Force is responsible, within resource guidelines set by the Executive, to ensure adequate and appropriate combat service support

[4627] The Defence Force is responsible for mobilising and preparing adequate defence personnel and to conclude contracts with the defence industry for product acquisition, services, maintenance, procurement, sustainment, movement and concentration of defence matériel

[4628] The defence combat service support system must have the capability to support and sustain combat forces over protracted periods of time, over extended distances, in diverse and complex theatres and along multiple lines of communication

[4629] Given inherently long supply lines, planning must ensure the physical security of sustainment installations and lines of communication

[4630] Expeditionary Support Deployed forces must have joint and expeditionary sustainment capabilities that support the full spectrum of conflict, consistent with the joint operational concept

[4631] This requires a single, integrated, responsive, end-to-end distribution system, capable of interfacing with inter-agency and multinational capabilities

[4632] Forward Basing, Preposition and Forward Mounting The foundation of the expeditionary sustainment system is the maintenance of strategic, operational and tactical reserve stocks and the prepositioning (forward sustainment) of stock at identified land and sea positions in accordance with the operational requirements that may exist at a particular time

[4633] JIIM Support Defence will support its interdepartmental and inter-agency activities within the framework of the given mission

[4634] a. Within joint forces, the Joint Force HQ will be responsible to sustain its forces with regard to common items

[4635] The Joint Force HQ will also be responsible for equipment that is mission-specific but that is not part of normal service equipment

[4636] Combat services will provide own unique sustainment

[4637] Defence Reserve Stock Levels Defence must prescribe the level of reserve stocks to be maintained to support the spectrum of defence missions, goals and tasks

[4638] These must be able to support rapidly escalating force levels as the core force expands into the surge force

[4639] This includes: a. Strategic Reserve Stocks

[4640] Reserves that are determined by the full spectrum of potential threats to security

[4641] These reserves are maintained to bridge the gap between peace and national defence

[4642] b. Operational Reserve Stocks

[4643] Operational reserves are determined by risks emanating from foreseeable operational contingencies such as imminent military threats, regional disasters, regional instability, crime and domestic instability (health care, disaster relief, air supply, etc

[4644] c. Tactical Reserve Stocks

[4645] Tactical reserves are designed to achieve superiority during military engagements through the employment of operational and combat support units (support echelons, spare bandwidth, deployment in depth, etc

[4646] STRATEGIC RESOURCES ALIGNMENT

[4647] Common approaches and processes are to be used to support both force preparation and force employment so that sustainable combat-ready forces are produced and employed

[4648] This entails the harmonisation of the approaches between the various defence resource systems: a. A single defence plan identifies the resources required to meet defence objectives

[4649] This defence plan ensures alignment between assigned objectives and allocated resources per programme

[4650] The single defence plan forms the basis for the consequent acquisition, utilisation and management of the allocated resources to ensure the successful execution of the defence mandate

[4651] The annual Defence Budget Vote appropriates funds to enable investment in defence resources in accordance with the authorised medium-term defence strategic business plan and programmes

[4652] The Defence Vote allocates funds (spending ceiling) to the main and sub-programmes, enabling the management of resources on inventory as well as the procurement of replacement and/or supplementary resources

[4653] While this single defence plan entails a process of centralised strategic direction and functional authority, the execution of the plan and the subsequent utilisation of the resources will be decentralised to ensure its effective, efficient, and economical management

[4654] The realisation of a credible force design and force structure for the Defence Force is dependent on the appropriate allocation of resources

[4655] d. Support is a command function

[4656] As such, commanders at all levels will be responsible, accountable and empowered to execute the plan through the management of all resources, the fostering of appropriate human skills and appropriate personnel, logistics and financial delegations and authorities

[4657] The effective, efficient and economical utilisation of such critical resources within each resource management system is of paramount importance to meet functional requirements

[4658] All resource systems must provide management information and advice to defence decisions makers

[4659] The information provided in each area must integrate with all other resource areas, using a defence enterprise system

[4660] All commanders and managers must account for their compliance with policy and performance against the defence plan and programmes on a quarterly and annual basis as prescribed in national legislation

[4661] h. Internal controls, risk and performance management must be an integrated aspect of each resource system

[4662] The Chief of the Defence Force must be capacitated by appropriate professional and technical expertise to manage and account for all defence resources allocated

[4663] The main divisions of defence resources are: a. Personnel

[4664] b. Intelligence. c. Operations

[4665] f. Information and Communication Systems (ICS

[4666] Finance. Specialist Staffs

[4667] The defence resource management system will be compliant with all resource administration prescripts in statute and regulation

[4668] The utilisation of defence resources must be audited and reported upon to the National Executive and the Legislature, as may be prescribed in law

[4669] The general principle of transparency is espoused and will be pursued

[4670] Notwithstanding, care will be taken to provide, within the Rules of Parliament, for reporting on confidential aspects of the broader defence function

[4671] DEFENCE ACCOUNTABILITY AND DELEGATION REGIME Defence Accountability Concept The Head of Department and Accounting Officer is accountable for all defence resources

[4672] Linked to the organisational renewal imperative hereunder, the current defence accountability concept must be reassessed, and if necessary, adjusted in order that the Head of Department and Defence Accounting Officer is able to fully meet his or her statutory accountability responsibilities and obligations

[4673] Defence Resource Delegation Regime The current manner whereby responsibility, authority and accountability for resources are delegated from the Accounting Officer, across the entire defence organisation and down to the unit level, compromises military command and control, and specifically the integrity of the line of command

[4674] In accordance with the principles stated earlier in this chapter: a. Due cognisance must be given to the unique nature of the Defence Force relative to the wider public service

[4675] Commanders must have the necessary delegations to execute their assigned mandates, have commensurate responsibility and authority over all resources assigned, and must account for such resources

[4676] In this instance, it is imperative that recognition is given throughout the wider public service that the military organisation is by nature a hierarchical one

[4677] Delegations, and concomitant responsibility, authority and accountability, must formally cascade down the command line, one step at a time, from each level of command to the next level of subordinate

[4678] Without this understanding, commanders cannot account for the performance of a subordinate against a delegation

[4679] It is thus imperative that the Defence Act be urgently amended to provide for a comprehensive defence resource delegation regime in law, whereby powers and duties can be delegated down the command line – one step at a time along that line – with commanders at all levels being responsible and accountable for their resources

[4680] The defence resource delegation regime must be embedded in and be enabled through the fully integrated and defence-wide enterprise system and its associated infrastructure

[4681] Defence Enterprise Information System An integrated defence enterprise information system, linked to the National Treasury’s Integrated Resource Management System, is required as the backbone information system to drive both defence administration and defence command and control

[4682] It must integrate and optimise all other defence information sub-system requirements and serve as a basis for ensuring standardisation, compatibility, connectivity and interoperability

[4683] It will be established as the foundation for all defence business processes and activities

[4735] Definition of Term: Defence Personnel

[4736] a. Defence personnel comprises the Regular component, the Reserve component, the Civilian Component of the Defence Force, the Defence Secretariat and the Ministry of Defence, as well as any member of an Auxiliary Service that may be established in terms of Section 16 of the Defence Act, 2002 (Act 42 of

[4737] This definition recognises that uniformed and civilian personnel are not the same, but acknowledges that Defence Civilians serve a unique organisation that makes unique demands on individuals, which are not experienced by other civilians in the Public Service

[4738] All defence personnel must fall under unified legislation that provides for one service dispensation for all and which is overseen equitably by the Defence Service Commission

[4739] REQUIREMENT Defence personnel are a key resource, the level and quantity of which are determined by the defence mission, goals and tasks, the derived force structure and post establishment table, and an appropriate balance between rank and salary levels

[4740] A single, comprehensive, and rigorous personnel system will be established that can be tailored to requirements and that is capable of delivering support to both internal and external operations from the 5th to the 1st line of support, in accordance with defence combat service support doctrine

[4741] The ‘one-force’ concept seeks to ensure that Defence is supported by the most sustainable, effective, integrated and affordable balance of Regulars, Reserves, Defence Civilians and auxiliaries

[4742] DEFENCE PERSONNEL SYSTEM The defence personnel function consists of core elements: Personnel Strategic Direction and Policy, Personnel Development, Personnel Management and Personnel Transformation

[4743] These core elements are supported by support elements, namely that of Personnel Policies and Processes, Personnel Technology, Personnel Functionaries, Commanders/Managers and the Personnel Budget

[4744] As indicated in the diagram the core elements of the personnel function are interlinked and cannot exist in isolation

[4745] This integrated approach is supported by the indicated support elements to ensure an effective, efficient and economic personnel function for defence

[4746] The defence personnel system will focus on the organisational requirements of defence and will ensure well-managed and -administrated and capable defence personnel through the application of sound defence personnel practices

[4747] It will enable force provisioning, force preparation and force employment through pursuit of the ‘one force’ principle by establishing an appropriate balance between the Regular component, Reserve component, defence civilians and auxiliaries through tailored personnel-feeding systems

[4748] The system must further: a. Support local, distant, dispersed and extended operations

[4749] b. Support participation in international operations

[4750] c. Accord equal priority to all defence strategic goals and strategic tasks

[4751] Comply with the national regulatory framework, government priorities, internal governance and stakeholder requirements

[4752] e. Maximise personnel outputs while minimising costs

[4753] Reduce personnel risk to as low a level as reasonably practicable

[4754] Personnel Management Principles

[4755] The personnel system must be based on the following principles

[4756] It must: a. Comply with the relevant prescribed provisions of the regulatory framework

[4757] b. Pursue the execution of the defence strategy

[4758] c. Reinforce the competent management of personnel as a command responsibility, duly assisted by quality personnel functionaries to provide specialist advice and guidance and the execution of day-to-day personnel functions

[4759] d. Be comparable to military best practices found in defence forces across the world

[4760] Be flexible to meet both defence operational requirements and the needs of individual defence members

[4761] f. Ensure functional alignment with the defence structural design across a four-tier system

[4762] g. Be directed towards the continuous capacity-building and empowerment of all defence members through soundly planned and executed education, training and development opportunities

[4763] h. Place the ‘right person in the right post at the right time’, thereby establishing an optimal organisational fit between people and structures

[4764] i. Possess appropriate technology to facilitate accountable, productive, effective, efficient, economical and transparent personnel management

[4765] j. Recognise and reward appropriate individual and group performance

[4766] k. Apply corrective measures to improve undesired levels of performance

[4767] l. Reflect constitutional values, aspirations and adherence to the principles of equity and equal opportunities, values and diversity, and strive to eradicate all forms of discrimination through: i

[4768] An enabling transformation environment. ii

[4769] Compliance with legislative prescripts and imperatives

[4770] Affirming equity and diversity management and eradicating discrimination

[4771] DEFENCE PERSONNEL BUDGET THRESHOLD

[4772] In order to achieve sustainability of the organisation as a whole, the ‘compensation for employees’ component of the budget will not exceed 40% of the annual allocation to defence

[4773] In most environments, at least 8% of the personnel budget will be ring-fenced and dedicated to the development and utilisation of the Reserve component, but escalating in the contingency of higher levels of operational readiness

[4774] Milestone 4 of the Defence Strategic Trajectory envisages a personnel component of approximately 189000 Regulars, Reserves and defence civilians, of which: a. 90 000 (48%) Regular members

[4775] b. 82 000 (43%) Reserve members

[4776] c. 17 000 (9%) defence civilians

[4777] This figure excludes the civilians employed in the Defence Secretariat and the Ministry of Defence

[4778] Notwithstanding the above, the day-to-day strength of the Defence Force may reflect a Reserve to Regular ratio in favour of the Regulars

[4779] This may especially be true in certain service delivery elements or where specialist mustering and professions are found

[4780] The post structure and personnel budget for any Auxiliary Service will be established by the Minister

[4781] The strategic direction for defence personnel management will be centralised, while the execution of personnel management will be decentralised

[4782] Defence personnel management will be institutionalised as a command function, with full responsibility, accountability and authority fixed by clear delegation to the lowest appropriate level, supported by a comprehensive defence enterprise system

[4783] The Chief of the Defence Force’s personnel staff are responsible to plan, orchestrate, direct and control personnel matters through, inter alia, the provision of personnel policy, doctrine, functional and competency standards and standardisation, and training curricula

[4784] This will be achieved through: a. Establishing an appropriate and relevant personnel regulatory framework

[4785] Integrated planning, consolidated reporting, internal controls and risk management

[4786] Determining personnel output objectives and directing strategic resource allocation

[4787] Positioning the civilian education sector and military education and training institutions to support the development of defence members

[4788] e. Determining strategic, operational and tactical personnel reserves through a risk-based approach to ensure that the demand and supply of defence personnel are affordably reconciled

[4789] Determining employment systems characterising the unique requirements of defence

[4790] Establishing an integrated personnel risk management system and process

[4791] h. Establishing labour and service relations appropriate to the unique attributes of defence

[4792] i. Establishing a grievance system at all levels of the organisation

[4793] Defence will develop and implement its personnel strategy through personnel sub-strategies that specifically address the following: a. Integrated corporate personnel support plans coupled to the medium-term strategic framework and the medium-term expenditure framework

[4794] Rigorous governance, compliance monitoring, risk management and appropriate wellness programmes

[4795] c. Individual and organisational performance management with a jeopardy and reward system in performance monitoring that enhances accountability and responsibility

[4796] d. Updated personnel regulatory framework, policies and personnel delegations in support of all personnel functions

[4797] e. Empowered line managers, commanders and personnel functionaries in all defence subsystems and functions

[4798] Appropriate resilience interventions for defence personnel

[4808] e. Automated personnel reporting

[4817] ACQUISITION OF DEFENCE PERSONNEL Defence will pursue improved marketing, recruitment, selection and appointment processes for all its service systems

[4818] The annual recruitment of personnel will be driven by the approved defence establishment table, personnel turnover tendencies and the specific requirements of corps and musterings

[4819] To prevent excessive growth of the Regular component, annual intakes must be based on the annual attrition rate

[4820] Targeted countrywide recruitment campaigns, designed to meet the rejuvenation requirements of both the Regular and Reserve components, will focus on: a balance between rural and urban areas; top scholars from both secondary and tertiary education institutions; and building awareness amongst youth in specific target areas

[4821] In order to ensure that the personnel quality base is appropriate and meets the profile requirements, recruitment will be executed in a decentralised manner by Combat Services and Staff Divisions

[4822] A pool of professional recruiters will be established per combat service

[4823] In some exceptional instances recruitment may be decentralised to unit level, particularly so in the instance of extremely specialised environments and the Reserve units

[4824] Recruited members will adhere to the health, age, fitness, intellectual and other standards of the Defence Force, and as may be appropriate to the specific corps or mustering

[4825] Focused and directed recruitment of young men and women with leadership attributes will be key to the effectiveness of the future Defence Force

[4826] To this end: a. Appropriate selection criteria and instruments will be used that focus on the candidate’s leadership abilities

[4827] A dedicated officer selection programme will be established

[4828] The priority for the recruitment of potential leaders will lie with those candidates already in possession of a tertiary qualification

[4829] A grade 12 exemption certificate will however be the minimum requirement to enter the system as an officer cadet

[4830] The post profile of the non-leader group will determine the minimum academic qualifications as this may vary between musterings

[4831] This will be augmented by the direct probationary appointment of qualified professionals into the Regular and Reserve components

[4832] To this end the University Reserve Training Programme, as part of the Reserve Training System, will be used to acquire specialist and scarce skills

[4833] Annual and separate intakes will feed the Regular and Reserve components respectively

[4834] DEFENCE CAREER MANAGEMENT Career management will be managed by the Combat Services and Staff Divisions through a standardised career management process that aligns organisational requirements with individual career development or progression

[4835] Defence will ensure clear career-pathing and development programmes per mustering and speciality

[4836] To this end, a clearly defined corps (or mustering) post profile and person profile will support the career management process, including the identification of stages for exiting the Defence Force

[4837] The quality of defence personnel will be enhanced through dedicated remunerative and non-remunerative initiatives to acquire and retain scarce skills

[4838] Academic qualifications and scarce skills in both the Regular and Reserve components will be recognised and incentivised

[4839] The following principles will be pursued to enhance defence career management: a. Career and succession planning promotes the transfer of skills and competencies

[4840] A synergetic relationship is created between individual career plans and workplace skill plans with individuals taking co-responsibility for their own career management and development

[4841] c. Career paths are effectively communicated and individual career plans are regularly updated and compiled in consultation with the member or employee

[4842] d. Succession plans are available two years in advance

[4843] e. Commanders and line managers are actively involved in the career management process

[4844] MAINTENANCE OF DEFENCE PERSONNEL The effective retention of defence personnel requires an established and comprehensive day-to-day personnel maintenance system

[4845] To this end the following principles will be pursued: a. Defence personnel processes both support and are informed by the defence regulatory framework and defence personnel policies

[4846] b. Defence members are supported by an accessible personnel maintenance system

[4847] To this end: i. E-personnel will be pursued. ii

[4848] Individual personnel transactions will be executed promptly and accurately

[4849] iii. High-volume and repetitive personnel transactions are performed against a measurable standard

[4850] Proactive personnel processes and transactions are executed where possible and applicable

[4851] A zero tolerance on negative audit findings is maintained

[4852] DEFENCE PERSONNEL SEPARATION The Defence Force will be maintained as a young, healthy and fit organisation

[4853] Due to its unique composition, the Defence Force cannot offer a life-long career to all of its members

[4854] Defence members will therefore be afforded opportunities throughout their defence career to prepare and qualify themselves for a second career as useful citizens in the mainstream economy of South Africa

[4855] Personnel separation will thus be integrally linked with a defence member’s career pathway and associated service contract

[4856] A dignified, attractive exit mechanism will be developed to provide the process of severance with members at specified career gateways

[4857] Notwithstanding, and for a variety of reasons, the services of certain defence members may be required for a period that surpasses their designated retirement age

[4858] An amendment to the Defence Act (Act No 42 of 2002) and a consequent policy system are required whereby the services of such defence members may be extended with the approval of the Minister as the Executive Authority

[4859] A government-wide mechanism must be found to exit members who no longer meet their post profile requirements due to age, health, fitness or competence standards

[4860] This may include: a. Being exited in a dignified and sensitive manner

[4861] The transfer to other government departments where such members may be more effectively utilised

[4862] Ongoing support to such members in their transition and exit

[4863] Personnel separation will be decentralised to the combat services

[4864] The following principles will be pursued in the separation of defence personnel: a. Defence maintains a system to prepare defence members for their transition to a second career (Transition Assistance Programme) through assisted labour market entry at identified exit stages

[4865] b. Placement assistance offices and other mechanisms and agencies assist defence members in finding employment opportunities

[4866] A seamless migration from the Regular component to the Reserve component must be ensured

[4867] On separation, defence members may volunteer to be retained as members of the Reserve component, in which they are available for service on a part-time basis, or move to the membership of the military veterans and are placed on the National Reserve

[4868] WIDER SPECTRUM OF DEFENCE ‘RANK AND SCALE’

[4869] In order to prevent the natural tendency of ‘rank inflation’, salary will be decoupled from rank and a far broader salary scale will be implemented in each rank

[4870] COMPREHENSIVE HEALTH PROGRAMME

[4871] In as much as government has a responsibility to maintain a healthy force, individual defence members have a corresponding responsibility to meet the health and fitness requirements of the Defence Force

[4872] To this end, the Defence Force shall institute a revised comprehensive health programme whereby biannual health assessments are conducted with all members, regardless of age or rank

[4873] Bearing in mind gender, age and matters such as disabilities, each defence member shall: a. Undergo a fitness evaluation

[4874] b. Undergo a body mass index evaluation

[4875] The standards for the above shall be set in regulations

[4876] Defence members not complying to the set standard will be given opportunity to remedy any non-compliance

[4877] Continual non-compliance will result in dismissal from the Defence Force

[4878] In addition to the above, the involvement of defence members in sport and allied activities shall be encouraged as a further mechanism toward maintaining the health of the force

[4879] a. As part of the professionalisation of the physical training, sport and recreation function, it is proposed that the Defence Force establishes a sports capability or sports regiment, which will be a high-performance, professional capability

[4880] This will be part of a retention and development strategy for athletes from disadvantaged backgrounds who have the potential to develop into Olympic-level athletes

[4881] This requires dedicated funding from National Treasury based on collaboration between the Defence Force, Sport and Recreation South Africa (SRSA) and the South African Sports Confederation and Olympic Committee (SASCOC

[4882] b. Establishment of this capability will enhance the capacity of the Defence Force to engage communities in developmental initiatives such as the promotion of youth development through leadership programmes centred on sports, physical education, adventure and recreation

[4883] The qualified services of sport officers and physical training instructors would be instrumental in presenting youth and cadet camps

[4884] This will serve to enhance social cohesion and also to "grow own wood

[4908] Personnel longer-term priorities

[4909] The inadequate and fragmented defence personnel management strategy, policy and system must be repositioned to provide adequate personnel strategic direction to the support of the defence mission, strategic goals and strategic tasks
