[4913] The Reserve component as contemplated in the Defence Act will be an integral element of the ‘one force’ and will be optimised to deliver assured capabilities for all defence goals and tasks

[4914] The Reserves will provide a cost-effective mechanism for capacitating the Defence Force for operational surges, sustainment of protracted operations and major combat operations as well as providing specialist and scarce skills not normally found in defence

[4915] Reserves will also serve at all levels of command and management

[4916] TENETS The Reserve component will harness the widest pool of societal talent for defence and will uphold a volunteer ethos

[4917] It will be sustained by formal governance mechanisms and safeguards and be appropriately and equitably resourced

[4918] The Reserve component will be integral to the design and structure of the Services as well as their development trajectories

[4919] As such, Reserves may also be constituted as fully fledged stand-alone design or structure elements under command of a higher order single Service or joint headquarters

[4920] Extensive use will be made of Reserves in all staff divisions at all levels of the Defence Force

[4921] The Reserves will provide a cost-effective specialist and scarce-skill capacity to the Defence Force

[4922] Whilst the Reserves are part of the ‘one force’, their management will be approached and tailored with an understanding of their unique and specific requirements

[4923] In the final outcome, however, the Reserves will conform in every respect to the professional military competency required of their Regular counterparts

[4924] Reserve units will be spread throughout South Africa so as to enable access to reserve service by citizens in both urban and rural areas

[4925] Reserve units will also provide a platform for the Defence Force to contribute to ordered developmental tasks

[4926] Specialist skills vested in the Reserves will be applied internally, as ordered, to the developmental needs of urban, peri-urban and rural communities, and to external post-conflict reconstruction and development operations

[4927] The Reserve component will be formally provided for within the defence programmes and sub-programmes, with funding linked to specific outcomes

[4928] These outcomes are to be quantified as measurable targets for each Service and Division and will be reflected in strategic and annual performance plans as well as in the performance agreements of commanders

[4929] The relative size of the Reserve component remains dependent on the strategic situation but, nonetheless, must be able to meet the required development trajectory capacity requirements and the capacity forecast requirements for operations and other defence tasks and activities

[4930] The Reserves will therefore be organised, staffed, equipped, trained and maintained at appropriate levels of readiness

[4931] The Reserve component will be quantified by means of an establishment table and a post structure that will be reflected on the defence structure management system, enabling costing and resource allocations in accordance with readiness requirements

[4932] Personnel acquisition for the Reserves will be provided at Service level by programmes that include the following: an initial military intake stream focused on recruitment of South African youth; focused direct recruitment of professionals and specialists; a University Reserve Training System at tertiary education institutions; and the translation of members leaving the Regulars as well as members from the former statutory and non-statutory forces that volunteer to join the Reserve component

[4933] The training outcomes required by the overarching defence education, training and development system will remain equally relevant for the Reserve and Regular components

[4934] However, the methodology used in achieving the same will be structured and delivered in a manner that caters for Reserve-unique aspects

[4935] Measures will be taken to involve business and state entities in assisting young reservists with employment opportunities

[4936] Vocational skills development in collaboration with the Sector Training Authorities (SETAs) and job placement of the members will be an ongoing activity

[4937] This will be decentralised to Service-level with outsourcing contracts awarded to reputable companies that specialise in these services

[4940] a. This requires enhanced logistics interoperability, based on the establishment of a single integrated logistic information system and a single defence logistics process

[4948] DEFENCE LOGISTICS SYSTEM A single, comprehensive and rigorous logistic system will be established that can be tailored to requirements and is capable of delivering combat service support to both internal and external operations in accordance with defence combat service support doctrine

[4950] Enable jointness and interoperability

[4951] Provide combat service support on a joint and multinational basis, yet recognising the uniqueness of systems operating on land, in the air, at sea and in the military health domain

[4953] lifecycle management and quality management perspectives

[4955] f. Create a common Defence Force logistics language

[4962] DIRECT DEFENCE LOGISTICS Strategic direction for defence logistics will be centralised, while logistics execution will be decentralised

[5180] FINANCE EXPERTISE Establishment of a Finance Corps

[5181] The defence finance management system is a core component of the defence combat service support which must be provided from the 5th line to the 1st line within the theatre of operations

[5182] This necessitates that the vast majority of defence finance officials are militarised

[5183] To this end: a. The intent is to re-establish a uniformed finance capability within the Defence Force as a deployable corps in support of successful defence operations

[5184] A Finance Corps must be established with its unique personnel management and personnel development systems

[5185] A Corps Director will be established

[5186] Further corps managers will be established at the Service level, including being the finance capability manager for the particular service

[5187] A Personnel Management Code (PMC) for finance must be established to manage finance officials

[5188] d. Finance functional training, alongside defence formative and military training, will be established whereby finance officials will be educated and trained in the functional areas identified within a finance learning path focused on defence finance management practises and processes

[5189] e. To this end, all previous military finance practitioners, irrespective of current mustering, must be offered the opportunity to militarise

[5190] This must be extended to include defence civilians with "CA" suffix currently serving in the Financial Management Division as finance functionaries

[5191] A needs-analysis must be conducted to determine the military, formative and functional training required by members militarising

[5192] Such training must be built into the established career paths of members, without prejudice to the affected individuals

[5193] The militarisation of the finance capability must be underpinned by addressing the contractual relationship of the Defence Force with such members, including, but not limited to: career-pathing, pension, group-life insurance, medical benefits and salary notches

[5194] Those that do not wish to militarise may remain in the finance management system or their otherwise current career path outside of the finance corps as defence civilian employees

[5195] i. A Finance Corps Reserve component must be established to support the Defence Force’s standing and surge capability

[5196] j. Finance practitioners providing a financial management service to the Defence Secretariat will primarily be civilian but military finance members may be seconded to the Defence Secretariat

[5197] Performance agreements for finance functionaries will follow the line of command

[5200] To this end: i. An occupation specific dispensation will be pursued to obtain and retain such specialist staff, including remunerative and non-remunerative means as well as intensive education, training and development programmes. ii

[5201] Agreements will be entered into with educational institutions to develop capable defence finance personnel into chartered accountants through specific training interventions

[5202] b. Specific measures will be taken to ensure sustained availability of finance personnel, including remunerative and non-remunerative means as well as intensive education, training and development programmes

[5203] c. Special focus will be placed on ensuring the availability of appropriate, competent finance officials through attracting, recruiting, educating, training, developing, retaining, motivating, correctly deploying and eventually redeploying sufficient competent finance personnel

[5204] The continuous staffing of the finance management system will be achieved by rotating personnel within the Services and Divisions

[5215] DEFENCE INFORMATION AND COMMUNICATION SYSTEM REQUIREMENT Defence information is a strategic resource over which the Defence Force must exert complete control, ensure inviolable security and maintain absolute autonomy, this from the 5th to the 1st line of combat service support

[5216] Appropriate defence information and communication systems will be informed by the defence mission, goals and tasks

[5217] The concept of ‘information as a strategic resource’ will drive all thinking on defence information management, hence the use of the term “information resource management”

[5218] DEFENCE INFORMATION AND COMMUNICATION SYSTEM PRINCIPLES

[5219] Common defence information and communication systems must be capable of delivering combat service support to both internal and external operations in accordance with defence combat service support doctrine

[5220] To this end the following principles will apply from the 5th to the 1st level of combat service support: a. Access to Defence Information

[5221] i. Information and communication systems must enable access to relevant defence information required for the execution of functional tasks securely and efficiently, and when and where required by acquiring, accessing and distributing information to remote locations in a secure manner

[5222] Efficient secure connectivity must be established between sensors and military, corporate and common information and communication systems

[5223] Defence must maintain autonomy in terms of providing access to its information and communications system infrastructure

[5224] Accurate, quality, non-duplicated and relevant information must be available to authorised users in the correct form and format, and when required

[5225] b. Information and Communication System Security

[5226] An aspect of modern warfare is the use of non-lethal weapon capabilities which invoke battle between adversaries for the exploitation and protection of information and communication systems

[5227] The protection of information as a strategic resource places emphasis on the requirement to develop a significant offensive and defensive capability to exploit and defend information systems

[5228] The defence information and communication systems security architecture must be aligned across all systems to consistently maintain the confidentiality, integrity and availability of information

[5229] c. Economic Optimisation. i. Defence information and communication systems must be centred on modern, technologically advanced, efficient and effective, yet affordable information and communication technology capabilities

[5230] Such capabilities are constrained by scarce financial resources and thus emphasis will be placed on overall value-for-money through administrative systems based on proven technology

[5231] The development of shared defence information and communication systems will enjoy precedence over the duplication of systems with similar functionality

[5232] The emphasis will thus fall on a common information and communication technology architecture

[5233] A balance between unique systems and COTS and MOTS must inform procurement considerations, with specific emphasis being placed on maintaining strategic capabilities and niche technology competence

[5234] A pragmatic approach based on local procurement will be applied whenever it is feasible to do so

[5235] d. Enabling Command and Control & Management Processes

[5236] i. Defence command and control and administrative information systems must provide accurate, relevant and timely information to all levels of command during force preparation, employment and support activities with respect to every sphere of military business. ii

[5237] Information processing must synchronise and replicate information between geographical operational areas to maintain self-sustaining operating environments

[5238] Services and Divisions are responsible for the lifecycle management of own unique information and communication technology service delivery, maintenance and disposal

[5239] Information Resource Management

[5240] The management of information as a strategic resource extends to the planning, policy maintenance, strategic control and research and development of integrated information management services, including the lifecycle, archiving and configuration management of information

[5241] Joint Information Systems Management

[5242] The concept of information as a strategic resource will drive future information systems management

[5243] Defence information requirements will be translated into joint information systems and infrastructure needed to meet such information requirements

[5244] Joint Information Warfare

[5245] Joint information warfare seeks to both defend own information and communication systems against attack and to adversely influence the opposing forces’ use of their information systems

[5246] Good information system security protects own information systems against unauthorised access, whilst offensive actions will adversely influence the opposing forces’ utilisation of information systems

[5247] Joint Information Communication Infrastructure Management

[5248] The management and technical support of the defence information and communication infrastructure extend to the lifecycle management of defence information product systems, technical support and interoperable, interconnected and standardised information technology infrastructure

[5249] Spectrum management at an international and a national level extends to the coordination of spectrum usage with entities such as commercial spectrum users and government institutions

[5250] This requires efficient joint management of the radio frequency spectrum within the Defence Force

[5251] Integrated Information Systems

[5252] Information system integration extends across defence enterprise information system portfolios through centralised strategic control and integration of defence enterprise information systems

[5253] DEFENCE INFORMATION SYSTEMS FRAMEWORK AND STRATEGY There are mandatory criteria and changes in the information and communication technology environment requiring an appropriate defence governance, risk and compliance regime conducive to the realisation of affordable and appropriate information and communication systems and technology

[5254] A defence information and communication system interoperability framework must be established, maintained and aligned to ensure connectivity between defence administrative and command and control systems

[5255] Defence intellectual property related to the development of information and communication systems must be maintained and managed within this framework

[5256] The defence information and communication systems strategy will address five strategic focus areas: a. Optimised value of the defence information and communication technology investment

[5257] Effective information and communication technology

[5258] Integrated information and communication technology enablement

[5259] Professional information and communication technology organisation

[5260] e. Secure and protected information and communication technology

[5261] Figure 14-4: Strategic Focus Areas of Defence Information and Communication

[5262] The five strategic focus areas are of equal importance

[5263] DIRECT COMMON DEFENCE INFORMATION AND COMMUNICATION SYSTEMS Strategic direction for common defence information and communication systems will be centralised, while the execution will be decentralised

[5264] The Chief of the Defence Force’s ICS staff are responsible to plan, orchestrate, direct and control common defence information and communication systems through, inter alia, the provision of logistic policy, doctrine, functional and competency standards and standardisation and training curricula

[5265] This will be achieved through: a. Computing and communication technology

[5266] b. Enterprise management systems

[5267] c. Network-enabled command and control systems

[5268] d. Defensive and offensive information warfare

[5269] e. Providing strategic direction for the execution of ICS

[5270] EXECUTE COMMON DEFENCE INFORMATION AND COMMUNICATION SYSTEMS Defence ICS support will be executed as follows: a. 5th line information and communication systems support from the national or international commercial sector or the defence

[5271] b. 4th line deeper level information and communication systems support from within the Defence Force

[5272] c. 3rd line deployable support from the Information and Communication Systems Command within the communication zone

[5273] Typically at combat division level.) d. 2nd line intermediate support from the Information and Communication Systems Command in the theatre

[5274] Typically at brigade level

[5275] e. 1st line organisational support from the units’ own internal support structures

[5276] Typically at battalion level

[5277] The Chief of the Defence Force’s ICS staff will provide common information and communication support transversely across the Defence Force and will be the information and communication prime systems integrator for the Defence Force across both common and universal/transverse systems

[5278] The staff will provide the operational management of defence information systems

[5279] The Chief of the Defence Force’s ICS staff will further be responsible for the management of records as prescribed by the National Archives and Records Service of South Africa Act (Act No 43 of 1996) as amended, specifically Section 13 provisions regarding efficient records management in government, as well as the National Archives and Records Service of South Africa Regulations, Part V: Management of Records, which addresses the specific parameters within which government bodies should operate regarding the management of their records

[5280] In fulfilment of its constitutional obligations, Defence utilises a large number of state facilities

[5281] This includes land for training and research purposes and fixed assets such as buildings, roads and runways for force preparation and employment

[5282] Defence is consequently one of the largest users of property in South Africa and controls land in each of the nine provinces

[5283] The defence property requirement stems from its core functions and activities

[5284] This ranges from the larger training areas, Army bases, Air Force bases and ammunition depots, to smaller properties such as communication sites, shooting ranges and even remote observation posts of only a few square metres

[5285] Government owns most facilities utilised by defence

[5286] Such land is legally owned by the South African government with defence having a reservation of use, although the deeds are held by the Department of Public Works as the national custodian of all state land and facilities

[5287] Some defence land is defence endowment property transferred from the government of the United Kingdom in 1922, which is also classified as state land

[5288] Such property is governed by an Act of Parliament (Defence Endowment Property and Account Act, Act No. 33 of

[5289] The remaining infrastructure is generally leased from the private sector

[5290] Defence leases properties for shooting ranges, for forward airfields and for sites for the countrywide communication network

[5291] Defence also has “rights of use” agreements with land owners that allow certain land to be used for military purposes

[5292] THE DEFENCE LAND REQUIREMENT Defence currently has approximately 420 000 hectares of land under its control

[5293] This includes the following general categories, each being in itself a significant consideration in determining the size of defence properties

[5294] However, it should be noted that more than one of these activities could take place on portions of defence land: Training Combat Elements

[5295] The specific combat element and role for which training is required (for example deployment of mechanised or motorised infantry in conventional, peace-support-operation or area-protection roles) will determine the area of land needed to train the force

[5296] This means that the area needed for training will be determined by the combat elements (or combination of combat elements) to be trained

[5297] b. Type of Training

[5298] The types of training to be conducted also have an effect on the area of land needed for training

[5299] Smaller areas are required for dry training, field craft training and vehicle training than are required for training with live ammunition

[5300] A variety of geographical features and veld types should be present to simulate different scenarios within which skills are to be acquired. c. Expansions in Force Design and Development of new Weapon Systems

[5301] Provision must be made for expansions in force design and the development of new weapon systems

[5302] Spatial Implications of Safety Templates

[5303] The types of weapons and the combinations in which they are deployed have a profound influence on the area of land required

[5304] The safety arc for each weapon is clearly defined and must be strictly adhered to

[5305] Such safety templates form an integral part of any military area where armed training takes place

[5306] The size of a military base where armed training is performed is to a large extent determined by the ammunition used in training and the linked safety templates

[5307] The size of a military training area usually increases with the use of higher order ammunition, which requires larger safety templates

[5308] Base Areas, Administrative Areas, Maintenance Areas and Stores Depots

[5309] The sizes of these facilities are to a large extent determined by the amount of infrastructure needed to perform these functions

[5310] f. Ammunition Depots

[5311] Ammunition depots are used to store large quantities of defence ammunition

[5312] Variables that have an influence on the size of these depots include the types of munitions to be stored and the prescribed safety margins

[5313] Different types of munitions, for instance pyrotechnics and projectiles, are stored in separate bunkers for safety reasons

[5314] Clearly defined safety distances are maintained between bunkers, as well as on the perimeter

[5315] g. Weapon Ranges

[5316] The size of weapon ranges is determined by the maximum application distance and safety arcs of weapons to be employed

[5317] h. Naval Bases

[5318] The size of these facilities is to a large extent determined by the amount of infrastructure needed to perform their function and to allow for the training of personnel

[5319] i. Air Force Bases

[5320] Apart from runways and infrastructure provision, a large number of variables, such as restricted air space, aerial approach zones, safety areas on the perimeter and radio frequency requirements, are taken into account in determining the size of an air force base

[5321] j. Telecommunication Installations

[5322] A major consideration in determining the size of telecommunication installations is the required presence of a magnetically clear spectrum around the facilities

[5323] k. Rifle Ranges

[5324] Rifle ranges are designed and established according to a set of clearly defined guidelines

[5325] Variables which might come into play include land use activities on adjacent properties and the distance from residential infrastructure

[5326] The migration towards the Defence Blueprint Force Design means that the defence infrastructure footprint will have to be realigned according to South Africa’s defence needs

[5327] The Force Design will serve as the basis for determining defence facilities and environmental support requirements

[5328] The spatial dispersion of defence land and facilities will further be influenced by the pursuit of both a landward and a maritime defence strategy

[5329] The establishment of new defence operational facilities must be pursued after a thorough assessment of both the geographical location and the security requirements of South Africa’s dispersed vital infrastructure

[5330] Any expansion or reduction in the defence footprint would have to be executed in a responsible and strategic manner so as not to impact on defence capabilities and the operational readiness of the Defence Force

[5331] Surplus and redundant facilities will be surrendered to the Department of Public Works for alternative utilisation or disposal

[5332] The number of leased defence properties must be reduced by translating the portfolio of leased properties to ownership of defence properties

[5333] This may, where possible, be pursued through alternate funding models, such as cooperation with the Public Investment Corporation (PIC) or Public Private Partnerships (PPPs) where possible within the relevant framework established by National Treasury

[5334] The Chief of the Defence Force’s logistic staff will establish a comprehensive Defence Facility Strategy that will address the defence footprint requirement

[5335] In so doing new ways may be explored to manage defence facilities in a consolidated and proactive manner, including co-use and cooperation agreements

[5336] Defence strives to achieve efficiency and effectiveness in the use of facilities and has achieved a considerable reduction in its footprint by surrendering unused land to the Department of Public Works

[5337] The Government Immovable Asset Management Act (Act No. 19 of 2007) has emphasised this matter and defence strives to comply therewith

[5338] Since 1986, defence has consequently returned approximately 311 000 hectares of land to the Department of Public Works, largely as a result of a reduced defence posture, internal rationalisation, restitution claims and urban and agricultural pressures

[5339] REPAIR AND MAINTENANCE OF DEFENCE FACILITIES

[5340] The matter of the repair and maintenance of defence facilities has gained considerable prominence in recent years

[5341] Repair and maintenance is the responsibility of the Department of Public Works

[5342] However, funding constraints have severely hindered the maintenance of essential defence infrastructure, giving rise to a significant maintenance backlog which impacts directly on the operational readiness of the Defence Force and its ability to prepare and employ forces

[5343] Defence has consequently engaged in a significant repair and maintenance programme (RAMP) in collaboration with the Department of Public Works

[5344] To a large extent this has been supported through the provision of additional funding through the annual MTEF Policy Options

[5345] These consolidated interventions will contribute to the reduction of the backlog

[5346] The Defence Works Formation is to take over the full responsibility of the Department of Public Works and manage the renewal of defence assets

[5347] The Defence Works Formation, as well as SA Army Field Engineer Regiments in each province, will focus on the reduction of the repair and maintenance backlog of defence infrastructure, as well as arresting the further deterioration of defence facilities

[5348] CO-USE OF DEFENCE FACILITIES There is great pressure to become more cost-effective in defence facility management, while at the same time ensuring that the Defence Force retains its proficiency

[5349] This necessitates the exploration of alternative ways to finance and maintain defence facilities

[5350] The private sector has lodged many requests for the co-use of defence facilities in recent years

[5351] Under-developed land and under-utilised facilities can be made available for additional uses, providing there is coherence with existing defence facilities and that core military activities are not compromised

[5352] The principal restricting factor in this regard is security and safety

[5353] In many cases, alternative use will require a portion of land or facilities to be isolated from the main defence activities

[5354] Defence may further give consideration to entering into joint ventures with developers and conservation organisations to minimise the cost of managing defence facilities and to improve defence infrastructure without drawing on additional state funds

[5355] LAND RESTITUTION Defence is committed to the equitable resolution of land restitution claims in the spirit of enhancing social justice

[5356] The Restitution of Land Rights Act was approved by Parliament in 1994 and the Commission on Restitution of Land Rights was established in

[5357] Defence is affected by restitution claims against certain defence land

[5358] The restitution process provides a framework and various options to arrive at an appropriate solution through negotiation by the parties or adjudication by the Land Claims Court

[5359] Restitution can take the following forms: restoration of the land from which claimants were dispossessed; provision of alternative land; payment of compensation; alternative relief including a package containing a combination of the above, sharing of the land, or special budgetary assistance such as services and infrastructure development where claimants presently live; or priority access to state resources in the allocation and development of housing and land in the appropriate development programme

[5360] Although defence has prioritised the restoration of the land concerned, rather than other forms of restitution, this has not always been possible

[5361] In some cases the land has been retained and compensation has been made, or alternative land provided

[5362] Certain land claims remain in the restitution process and will be finalised in collaboration with the Land Claims Commissioner or in the courts

[5363] In all instances, defence remains committed to the principle of equitable restitution

[5364] “I submit that it may be useful to open bases for private activities, in order to share costs, and to create a basis for training and experience of essential manpower

[5365] This could be done by allowing private activities on selected military airfields and harbours, with due consideration for security and control.”

[5366] Principles

[5367] Defence will apply the following principles in relation to land restitution: a. Commitment to the Constitution and the affirmation of the land reform programme

[5368] A proactive approach towards restitution is adopted

[5369] c. Preference will be given to the restoration of land rather than other forms of restoration

[5370] Commitment to the speedy resolution of restitution cases

[5371] e. Creative alternatives explored in cases where land cannot be restored

[5372] Where defence land is handed back to claimants, the acquisition of alternate land will be assessed in terms of core defence functions and activities

[5373] The acquisition of alternative land arising from settlement transfers will be determined consensually amongst all relevant government departments and ministries

[5374] h. Commitment to transparency in the restitution process

[5375] i. Commitment to the resolution of land claims through negotiations and the remedy of the Land Claims Court as a last resort

[5376] Land under claim will be made available for restitution unless the Department of Defence deems it not feasible

[5377] Non-feasibility could be due to: i. Financial cost. ii

[5378] Unique location of the facility

[5379] Unique military requirements

[5380] Strategic value of the facility

[5381] DISPOSAL OF DEFENCE FACILITIES Base closure is a complex issue requiring careful consideration of processes, role players and timeframes

[5382] The closure of defence properties presents both opportunities and serious challenges

[5383] Some of the major problems associated with defence base closure are the following: a

[5384] The loss of employment opportunities in defence and associated industries as well as within local supporting economies

[5385] Some defence properties are environmentally contaminated and often require very costly clean-up operations

[5386] c. Maintenance and protection of the bases before reuse or ultimate disposal can be costly

[5387] The development opportunities arising from the reuse of bases can be plentiful depending on the geographic location and infrastructure of the base concerned

[5388] Developmental factors will be a major consideration taken into account when evaluating the various land use and conversion options for obsolete bases

[5389] State land surplus to requirements is usually handed back to the Department of Public Works

[5390] The remediation, clean-up, closure, handing over and subsequent disposal of redundant state land must take place in a coordinated manner

[5391] ENVIRONMENTAL MANAGEMENT APPROACH The increased emphasis on the sustainable use of natural resources requires a complete review of the impact of military activities on the natural and built environments

[5392] Urban sprawl causes defence installations and facilities to compete with other local activities

[5393] Public complaints over dust and noise, demands for urban development of “prime” real estate, and increasing requirements for minerals, grazing land and water are all external forces that compete with the use of land by the military

[5394] By effectively integrating environmental considerations into the planning and execution of all military activities, defence can minimise the adverse effects of its activities as well as make a substantial social contribution towards the conservation and sustainable utilisation of environmental resources in South Africa

[5395] Defence is committed to the responsible use and management of land and facilities used for the execution of its core functions and will thus minimise and manage the impact on the environment

[5396] Defence environmental management remains complex and forms an integral part of the broader defence management system

[5397] Sustainable environmental management of defence training areas will ensure that the quality of the defence land resources is maintained for realistic training in future

[5398] Incorporating environmental practices into military procedures and operations will have financial benefits such as reducing energy costs and clean-up, disposal or litigation costs

[5399] Defence remains committed to the principles of military integrated environmental management through a corporate environmental management plan and specific operational environmental implementation plans

[5400] Accordingly, defence land and facilities will be managed sustainably in accordance with the relevant legislation, policies, norms and standards aimed at minimising the negative effects of military activities

[5401] Military Integrated Environmental Management will be dealt with as a recognised and dedicated defence support function through funded corporate programmes

[5402] Military activities will be fulfilled in accordance with environmentally sustainable best practices

[5403] This commitment applies across the scope of military activities

[5404] GLOBAL ENVIRONMENTAL CHANGE Human security is promoted and threatened by a variety of economic, cultural, political and environmental factors

[5405] Global environmental change and human security refer to efforts to link security to environmental change and therefore large-scale hazards to human security posed by global environmental change include climate change, stratospheric ozone depletion, loss of biodiversity and ecosystem functioning, changes in hydrological systems and supplies of fresh water, desertification and land degradation and the depletion of non-renewable energy resources

[5406] ENVIRONMENTAL CONTINGENT LIABILITY

[5407] The obligation to clean up unexploded ordnance (UXO) and spillages on defence training areas constitutes an environmental contingent liability that must be disclosed in the annual defence financial statements

[5408] Although defence training areas are swept for duds and misfires after training exercises, they are not entirely cleared, and UXO as well as contamination from explosive debris is left behind, which poses a threat to human life and the environment, either for new inhabitants of the area or for participants in the following training exercise

[5409] Procedures and models must be developed to identify, determine and disclose such contingent environmental liabilities

[5410] ENVIRONMENTAL COOPERATIVE GOVERNANCE Defence environmental policy and activities must be consistent with national environmental policy, and promote cooperation with environmental bodies

[5411] Defence regional environmental advisory forums will be used to enlist the support of external experts in the management of military properties

[5412] GRAVES AND BURIAL SITES Some defence areas contain burial sites

[5413] Relatives and descendants are allowed to visit these graves when training activities permit and with due regard to their safety

[5414] Defence will remain sensitive to this issue and this practice will continue

[5415] This will be properly regulated in regulations to standardise procedures and set public liability regarding access to such burial sites on military properties

[5416] An inventory of all graves on defence-controlled areas will be established

[5417] CLEAN-UP AND REMEDIATION OF DEFENCE TRAINING AREAS Defence training activities have a variety of environmental impacts

[5418] Environmentally destructive effects and by-products of military operations, such as UXO, shrapnel, targets and debris which leach explosives and heavy metals into groundwater, all forms of waste, pollution, fuel spills and other chemicals released as a result of military action, and the destruction of vegetation by military vehicles or explosives, threaten the integrity of the physical environment and natural resources

[5419] These have become central drivers for cleanup and remediation due to the inherent risk to personnel, the public and the environment

[5420] Informed by safety considerations, training areas will be regularly cleared

[5421] This entails the clearing of all UXO and other visually detected debris

[5422] To this end, an inherent military range clearance (MRC) capability will be established

[5423] This process will use an integrated seven-step process to include environmentally-friendly detection of UXO and subsurface clearance technologies, as well as models and tools for determining the costing, prioritisation and Geographic Information System (GIS) decision support for the clean-up and remediation of all live-fire military training areas

[5424] ENVIRONMENT FOR MILITARY OPERATIONS Environmental considerations will be incorporated in the planning and execution of joint, combined and multinational exercises and force employment processes

[5425] Environmental management personnel will be deployed to advise and assist on environmental best practice and ensure the implementation of the necessary remediation measures following the demobilization of forces

[5426] The relationship between human security, global environmental change and military integrated environmental management is indicated in Figure

[5427] Environmental scarcity is determined by environmental change, population size and growth, and unequal distribution (or access to) resources

[5428] Of these factors, unequal access to resources is not bound by physical limits alone

[5429] Leading examples of emerging environmental change are: depletion and pollution of fresh water supplies, depletion of fisheries, degradation and disappearance of biodiversity, degradation and loss of agriculture lands, food and health safety, stratospheric ozone depletion, and global warming

[5430] These challenges will likely be growing threats to environmental security and ultimately affect human security in future

[5431] Figure 14-5: Military Environmental Management Model

[5432] The purpose of this chapter is to provide strategic guidance to the development of policies and strategies concerning the South African defence industry, with specific emphasis on the attainment of the Defence Review and the pursuit of the Defence Strategic Trajectory

[5433] The National Defence Industry Council, as discussed hereunder, will have the responsibility to further develop these strategic guidelines into specific policies and strategies

[5434] The term defence industry in this chapter refers to companies (both public and private) that are primarily concerned with the design, development, manufacture, production or support of weapons, munitions, pyrotechnics, equipment systems and other matériel for the Defence Force or for export; divisions of companies in other sectors that are so engaged; and companies that are major sub-contractors or component suppliers to such activities

[5435] Given the strategic relevance of this industry sector to South Africa’s defence and security, its indirect but considerable importance to economic and industrial development, and further its potential as a tool of foreign policy, a National Defence Industry Council will be established as a significant policy making and coordination tool for the defence industry

[5436] The National Defence Industry Council will be charged with the tasks of: Establishing and maintaining the focus of a national vision in respect of the defence industry

[5437] Coordinating approaches between the Defence Force and the defence industry in pursuit of the Defence Strategic Trajectory

[5438] Overseeing the development and implementation of policies and strategies appropriate to the defence industry, in particular, the National Defence Industrial Strategy

[5439] Ensuring the optimal integration of the defence industry within the National Development Plan, industrial and trade policy and South Africa’s regional and wider foreign policy and strategy

[5440] e. Identifying and furthering the optimal development of the defence industry

[5441] Providing the coordination of government’s marketing support to the defence industry

[5442] This National Defence Industry Council should be chaired by the Minister of Defence or, in the unavoidable absence of the Minister, by the Deputy Minister of Defence, and should have a small permanent secretariat located within the Ministry

[5443] Its members should include: a

[5444] The Secretary for Defence

[5445] The Chief of the Defence Force

[5446] The Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of Armscor, as the defence acquisition agent

[5447] A senior representative from each of the following potential clients of the industry: i

[5448] The South African Police Service. ii

[5449] The Intelligence Services

[5450] A senior official from each of the Departments of: International Relations and Cooperation

[5451] iii. Trade and Industry; and iv

[5452] Science and Technology

[5453] The Group CEO of Denel

[5454] The Chairperson of the AMD Board and senior industry executives representing the public and private sectors and the various competency areas of this industry

[5455] h. Selected scientists and academics from the CSIR (DPSS) and those universities active in defence-related research or researching other fields of relevance to the Defence Force

[5456] In order to be effective in steering and supporting the South African defence industry, the Council will meet at least quarterly to consider the state of the South African defence industry, the challenges it faces and international developments, and to make any necessary determinations and recommendations on that basis

[5457] The National Defence Industry Council may further develop legislation and consequent regulations as may be necessary for the implementation of the policy frameworks that are developed

[5458] A possible example hereof may include the promulgation, through Parliament, of enabling legislation and regulations so as to ensure government control over identified vital technologies and wider strategic independence, and the extent of foreign ownership of South African defence industry companies

[5459] POLICY INTENT BACKGROUND South Africa is one of the top thirty economic actors in the world and is not aligned to any major power

[5460] South Africa is classified as a middle-income, emerging economy, affluent in natural resources with well-developed legal, communications, financial, energy and transport sectors

[5461] Agriculture contributes 9% to the gross domestic product, with industry and services contributing 26% and 65% respectively

[5462] South Africa has by far the largest and most sophisticated economy on the African continent

[5463] South Africa has the 25th largest gross domestic product in the world accounting for 25% of Africa’s GDP and 33% of the sub-Saharan GDP, and has been ranked as the 32nd largest importer and 37th largest exporter

[5464] More than 50% of the economy is trade-related, with mining, manufacturing, services and to a lesser degree agriculture as the mainstays of the economy

[5465] The bulk of exports and imports is transported via sea lines of communication, with the Port of Durban being one of the busiest in the Southern Hemisphere

[5466] REQUIREMENT FOR A DEFENCE INDUSTRY South Africa requires an effective defence capability, which includes, as an integral element, a defence industry to support sovereign capabilities and maintain an essential level of strategic independence

[5467] A vibrant, focused defence industry is thus a major asset to South Africa, strengthens its defence and security capabilities; supports its foreign policy initiatives – particularly within the region and on the continent – and is supportive to the national development agenda

[5468] A vibrant defence industry remains a critical component of an effective South African defence capability, providing South Africa with a defence and security industrial base that must be positioned to ensure the attainment of the Defence Review and the pursuit of the Defence Strategic Trajectory

[5469] This will in the main include, were appropriate, support in pursuit of: a. Strategic independence

[5470] Sovereign capability in selected areas

[5471] c. Optimised equipment and systems

[5472] d. Cost-effective equipment, systems and services to the Defence Force and other Security Services

[5473] e. Economic benefit derived from necessary defence expenditure

[5474] Collateral benefit ensuing from the endeavours of the defence industry

[5475] SOUTH AFRICAN DEFENCE REVIEW 2015 DEFENCE INDUSTRY POLICY AND STRATEGY

[5476] The intention of government is to not only maintain, but also further develop South Africa’s defence industry as a key national asset and as a key partner in the pursuit of the Defence Strategic Trajectory

[5477] As such this industry should be identified, recognised, supported and prioritised as a strategic manufacturing sector by the Department of Trade and Industry

[5478] It is, further, the intention of government to work closely with the public and private sectors to achieve this goal and to do so cost-effectively

[5479] This will give South Africa a defence and security industrial base that will, in addition to the characteristics described above, provide increased access for Black businesses and military veterans to a sustainable technology-intensive and competitive industry sector

[5480] The development of South Africa’s defence industry must, however, occur within the context of the wider international defence industry, taking account of general developments in that industry, as well as the evolving nature of armed conflict and the requirements that arise from it, and developments in technology

[5481] Further, while that defence industry will depend heavily on government orders, it will also: a

[5482] Bring valuable technological spin-offs for the wider economy and industry, chiefly in the form of technologies new to South Africa and localised in the course of designing, developing, manufacturing or supporting defence equipment

[5483] Play a crucial role in developing the country’s intellectual and skills capital, by virtue of its need for scientists, researchers, engineers and technicians and the effect of defence projects in attracting the right calibre of people into the relevant professions

[5484] Making a major contribution to the GDP growth

[5485] Generating foreign currency earnings from export sales and the support of exported equipment and systems

[5486] The establishment, development and retention of certain defence industrial capabilities will not be solely governed by market forces, due regard being had for strategic necessity and also for strategic advantage, and particularly in respect of defence matériel over which sovereign control is required

[5487] Government may, therefore, retain or establish state-owned enterprises in technology domains that are necessary to the attainment of the Defence Review and the pursuit of the Defence Strategic Trajectory, as developed from national security and defence policy objectives, but that are not commercially viable in South Africa

[5488] Strategic Independence Strategic independence here means the ability of the Defence Force to perform its key functions for extended periods without reliance on direct foreign support in respect of critical capabilities

[5489] This will chiefly require South Africa to retain the capability to: a. Support, maintain and repair critical equipment and systems

[5490] b. Manufacture critical munitions, batteries, components and sub-assemblies

[5491] c. Manufacture such high-rate-of-use spares and other items as cannot be either: i. Stockpiled in sufficient quantity; ii

[5492] brought into production at short notice without direct foreign assistance; or iii. acquired from multiple foreign sources via multiple channels, to negate an embargo by one or more governments

[5493] Strategic independence further means the ability to: a. Conduct operational research across the spectrum of Defence Force responsibilities

[5494] b. Comprehensively and thoroughly test and evaluate equipment, munitions, systems and other defence matériel to a standard that ensures that items acquired by the Defence Force fully comply with the requirement and the related specifications, including aspects such as reliability, availability, maintainability and durability (RAM-D

[5495] c. Ensure effective in-service testing and evaluation of combat readiness and system efficiency

[5496] d. Conduct or manage directed, focused research and development in connection with the development of Defence Force requirements and the related specifications

[5497] Such capabilities are at present managed by: a. Armscor Defence Institutes: Alkantpan, Armour Development, Defence Decision Support Institute, Eclipse, Ergotech, Flamengro, Gerotek, Hazmat, Institute for Maritime Technology (IMT), Protechnik. b. CSIR Defence, Peace, Safety and Security (DPSS): Electronic Defence Evaluation and Research Institute (DERI), Aeronautics DERI, Landward DERI, Special Operations DERI, Paardefontein Antenna Test Range, Paardefontein Blast Range

[5498] c. Denel: Overberg Test Range (air, ground-, and ship-launched weapons, evaluation of weapons/combat systems, flight test support and limited satellite support

[5499] Sovereign Capability Sovereign capability here means the ability to ensure, under full national control and without reliance on any direct foreign assistance, certain capabilities identified as vital to national security, including, but not limited to, command and control, secure communications, aspects of precision-guided munitions, elements of electronic warfare, relevant algorithms and relevant software

[5500] This will require, as far as is practicable: a

[5501] The capability to integrate and support such systems and equipment

[5502] The capability to design, develop and support relevant algorithms and software

[5503] The capability to design, develop and manufacture certain equipment locally, which does not exclude the use of imported components

[5504] The control of those capabilities under custodianship by either a public or private South African-owned company

[5505] Optimised Equipment and Systems Optimised here refers to equipment and systems specifically developed or adapted to meet the demands set by: a. A harsh and unforgiving operating environment: heat, dust, torrential rain, little infrastructure and few and poor roads

[5506] A demanding operational environment: low-force densities that require dispersed operations, no clearly defined front line or even area of operations, and insecure lines of supply

[5507] The operational style developed by the Defence Force to meet those challenges: high-mobility/high-tempo, dispersed, joint operations

[5508] The need to be interoperable with selected legacy equipment and systems, including some equipment and systems used by the Police and other agencies and departments of government

[5509] The desire to achieve increased interoperability with regional partners

[5510] Ensuring the supportability of equipment and systems

[5511] Examples of such optimised equipment include wheeled combat vehicles (good operational mobility), long-range artillery (support of dispersed force elements) and rugged logistic vehicles, as well as communications equipment suited to those operational, geographic and climatic conditions

[5512] Economic Benefit The potential to leverage wider economic and industrial opportunity on the basis of necessary expenditure on defence and security equipment and systems has been demonstrated in several developing countries: Manufacturing and supporting defence matériel creates skilled and semi-skilled jobs and develops the experience and skills of the people involved, both within the defence industry itself and in the general industry companies that form part of the defence and security supply chain, executing sub-contracts or supplying some related equipment or components

[5513] Development of defence equipment establishes, and can sometimes develop, new technologies, techniques and processes that ‘spin off’ to other sectors of industry to the benefit of the national economy, enhancing international competitiveness and supporting the national development agenda

[5514] c. Defence research and development develops new technologies that also spin off to other sectors, supporting the National System of Innovation and also further reinforcing the development agenda

[5515] People with skills and experience gained in the defence industry also spin off to other sectors, expanding the national skills and experience base

[5516] There is also the potential to align the defence acquisition strategy with the industrial development strategy of the Department of Trade and Industry, for instance by designating certain sectors for localisation where there are common technologies for military and civilian products

[5517] One possible example might be found in heavy vehicles, which could also have some export potential

[5518] The defence sector has the demonstrated potential to create indigenous technologies and bring foreign technologies into the country and establish them, from which base they and the related skills can migrate to other sectors of the economy

[5519] Internationally, much existing technology has been a result of spin-off from developments in the defence industry

[5520] The trend today is for spin-on from commercial developments into the defence field

[5521] Much of the underlying technology is, in fact, still a result of past defence research, and much fundamental and applied research around the world is still being driven by the work undertaken in the defence field

[5522] SOUTH AFRICAN DEFENCE REVIEW 2015 DEFENCE INDUSTRY POLICY AND STRATEGY

[5523] The defence industry’s range of products and services will contribute to the technology and knowledge base of the country

[5524] It will further publicly pronounce on a strategy that sets out its contribution toward addressing national strategic concerns, especially developmental drivers such as education, health and economic development

[5525] LONG-TERM RELATIONSHIPS The definition of what is critical, where sovereign control is required, and where the benefits of optimisation justify the investment and cost, will be developed and set out in the Defence Industry Strategy, and amended from time to time as the strategic situation may require

[5526] Achieving and maintaining the desired level of strategic independence, the desired sovereign capabilities, and the ability to develop optimised equipment and systems will require sufficient, ongoing, long-term investment by government in: a. Relevant education, training and skills retention programmes

[5527] A defence science, engineering and technology support capability and funding of both general and specific research and development projects and programmes

[5528] c. Maintaining and modernising or upgrading facilities

[5529] d. Export support to facilitate future research and development

[5530] The responsibility lies with the Defence Force to ensure that sufficient (and sufficiently regular) funding is directed to maintaining defence industrial capabilities or technologies that are identified as having vital importance, especially in respect of the underlying technologies, the required skills, and the required research, design, development, manufacturing and support facilities

[5531] DEFENCE FORCE/DEFENCE INDUSTRY RELATIONSHIP

[5532] The defence engagement of the defence industry is premised primarily on the Defence Review, and on the attainment of the Defence Strategic Trajectory

[5533] The focus of the defence/industry relationship is thus (in the main) in the pursuit of: firstly, the development of strategic technologies and capabilities; secondly, the ongoing matériel and services needs of the Defence Force; thirdly, the in-service support of defence systems and prime mission equipment; and fourthly, upgrades and modernisation, where appropriate

[5534] Defence matériel programmes will be specifically guided by the Military Strategy, an optimised and integrated Defence Capability Strategy and a consequent Defence Long-Term Capital Plan, which must be determined by the Chief of the Defence Force

[5535] The defence matériel requirement will be ameliorated with available resources, in order to establish long term plans and programmes

[5536] Defence matériel programmes will be executed within the frameworks established for this purpose

[5537] The objective is to develop a healthy partnership between the Defence Force and its supporting industry, with local industry in principle enjoying preference, where it can practicably and cost-effectively meet requirements

[5538] This will be a policy principle in the new acquisition policy

[5539] The strategic orientation of the defence industry will be primarily informed by South Africa’s defence and security sector priorities

[5540] Local sourcing will be primarily pursued, where possible, in the following areas: a. Manufacture of missiles and wider guided munitions technology, products and systems

[5541] b. Manufacture of critical munitions and ordnance

[5542] c. Manufacture of critical and alternate energy and propulsion sources

[5543] d. Manufacture of critical and high-rate-of-use spares and other stores

[5544] e. Support of equipment, systems and weapons, and the related training systems and facilities

[5545] f. System integration to allow optimisation of equipment, weapons and systems for specific defence requirements, and to minimise strategic risk

[5546] This will be accompanied by an additional orientation on ensuring: a

[5547] The commercial viability of South African defence products, particularly those that may be required by other regional and continental armed forces

[5548] b. Harmonising, where feasible, military-off-the-shelf (MOTS) and commercial-off-the-shelf (COTS) requirements, or aligning defence orders with export orders, with the aim of achieving larger production orders to result in longer production runs and the accompanying economies of scale

[5549] Mutual spin-on and spin-off of civilian and military capabilities

[5550] An integrated government focus, informed by the defence interest and so championed by defence, will be pursued, inter alia, in the following domains where viable products, capabilities or particular niche areas exist: SOUTH AFRICAN DEFENCE REVIEW 2015 DEFENCE INDUSTRY POLICY AND STRATEGY a

[5551] The aerospace sector

[5552] The maritime sector

[5553] The landward sector

[5554] The command and control and Information Warfare sector

[5555] e. National Defence Industry Council specified South African defence and security niche or competitive edge capabilities

[5556] f. Centres of excellence enhancing or contributing to the National System of Innovation

[5557] Potential new business in cooperation with other nations, and particularly in cooperation with South Africa’s strategic partners

[5558] The support of equipment, systems and weapons, and related training systems and facilities, may (where it is practicable and it holds no disadvantage in respect of operational readiness, the ability to deploy forces, sustainability and resilience) be considered for outsourcing

[5559] INDUSTRY FOCUS AREAS

[5560] It is not the intention to recreate the exceptional breadth and depth of capabilities that was a feature of the defence industry during the period of the arms embargo, as that: a. Is not essential to South Africa’s national security; b. Would be neither cost-effective nor practicable at a time when defence companies worldwide are having to globalise to survive; and c. Would tend to remove the industry from relevant global supply chains, making it increasingly difficult to win substantial export orders

[5561] The intention is rather to focus on those areas and sectors of defence technology and manufacturing that offer real potential to meet the policy intent set out above

[5562] It is important to ensure that the flow of national contracts for defence and security research, development, manufacturing and support is structured and phased such that: a

[5563] The Defence Force brings equipment and systems into service at a steady rate to ensure an efficient commissioning process and to avoid block obsolescence

[5564] The domestic defence and security industry has a viable base load of work to: Sustain research, design, development, industrialisation and manufacturing capabilities and capacities

[5565] enable it to continuously renew itself in terms of human capital and capital equipment; and iii. serve as a base for export ventures

[5566] It is, further, the intention that the Defence Force, like all other government entities, will contribute toward addressing national strategic concerns, especially developmental drivers such as education, health and economic development

[5567] The defence industry’s range of products and services will also contribute to the technology base of the country

[5568] AREAS OF COMPETENCE The focus of national support for the defence industry, based on military priorities, will, therefore, be on primarily local sourcing, insofar as is practicable, in the following areas: a. Support of equipment, systems and weapons and the related training systems and facilities

[5570] c. Manufacture of critical, specialised batteries and other energy sources

[5574] f. Modernisation and upgrading of equipment, platforms and systems to optimise them for their roles as conditions or requirements evolve, and to extend their service lives

[5575] g. Development of specific critical equipment and systems

[5576] h. Development of specific optimized equipment and systems

[5577] i. Sustained manufacture of equipment required in large numbers or amounts

[5579] b. Information warfare, at all levels of war

[5580] c. Secure communications

[5581] d. Information technology, including data fusion technology

[5585] h. Missile and wider guided munitions technology

[5595] It may, for instance, be possible to: a. Expand South Africa’s capabilities in the field of unmanned aerial systems on the basis of existing capabilities in that field and in related fields, and on the basis of the airframe development capability resulting from UAV projects and the light multi-role aircraft currently in development; b. develop one or both of those concept aircraft into a viable operational system with real export potential; or c. build on the Air Force’s medium- to long-term requirements for combat support and medium transport helicopters to develop a local manufacturing capability and linked maintenance, repair and overhaul capability to support other helicopters in the wider region

[5596] In addition, government will support niche capability areas in which the South African defence and security industry has a demonstrable edge or potential to gain such edge

[5597] Among them are: a. Precision-guided weapons and precision engagement systems

[5598] b. Fire direction systems

[5599] c. Products or technologies in any field in which an edge can be established
