[5714] With an eye to ensuring sovereign control over identified vital technologies and wider strategic independence, the government will control the extent of foreign ownership of South African defence industry companies

[5715] Restrictions will apply in respect of defence matériel related to capabilities that are required to be under sovereign control or are considered essential in the interests of strategic independence

[5716] The development, manufacture and support of defence matériel over which sovereign control is deemed essential will, to the extent possible, be restricted to South African defence companies or, when necessary, partly South African-owned defence companies

[5717] To this end, it will be important to make proper provision for single-source contracts

[5718] The development, manufacture and support of defence matériel related to strategic independence will, to the extent possible, be restricted to South African defence companies or partly South African-owned defence companies, but may be contracted to South African-based defence companies. c

[5719] Where it is necessary or preferable – for instance for access to technologies – for such companies to carry out such work in partnership with foreign companies, this will be permitted, provided only that suitable and agreed security measures are implemented

[5720] SOUTH AFRICAN DEFENCE COMPANY A South African defence company is one that is fully controlled by South African owners, who have at least a 51% shareholding, those being: a. South African companies with no foreign shareholding exceeding 49% and fully controlled by South African citizens; and/or b. South African citizens who do not hold any dual nationality; and c. whose executive management comprises South African citizens who do not hold any dual nationality; and which, further, d. have their relevant manufacturing and, preferably, their relevant research and development facilities in South Africa; and e. are fully compliant with all relevant South African legislation, except insofar as there may be a waiver or waivers granted in consideration of strategic issues

[5721] This requirement does not preclude a South African company participating in a joint venture project with a foreign company, even on a minority share basis, except in that there may be no direct linkage to sovereign projects other than by prior agreement with the Defence Force in such cases where cooperation with foreign companies is essential to the project, for instance in order to acquire or develop the required technologies

[5722] Where there is any significant foreign interest in a South African defence company as defined above, security of uninterrupted supply to the Defence Force and security of all South African intellectual property will be ensured by means of appropriate government-to-government agreements

[5723] South African defence companies may compete for any and all defence contracts within their field of competence, and will enjoy preference, provided that: a. Their products and/or services fully meet the requirement in all critical respects

[5724] They demonstrate the ability to support that product through its lifecycle, including such upgrades that may be necessitated or required from time to time

[5725] No foreign product demonstrates an overwhelming advantage over the local product

[5726] Their price and long-term support price structure are: i. Broadly in line with other offers; or ii. are considered acceptable given the advantages of local sourcing

[5727] A defence company will be considered to be partly South African-owned for the purposes of defence contracting if: a. At least 26% of its shares are held by South African citizens or by a South African company

[5728] Its relevant manufacturing and/or development facilities, or those relevant to any contract in question, are located in South Africa

[5729] There is security of uninterrupted supply to the Defence Force

[5730] There is an agreement with the Defence Force, if deemed necessary accompanied by a government-to-government agreement, covering the security of intellectual property owned by the Defence Force or being developed under contract from the Defence Force, including no transfer outside South African hands or foreign access to such intellectual property otherwise in terms of that agreement or a specific contract

[5731] The company demonstrates a real, tangible and enduring commitment to: i. Adding economic value to South Africa. ii

[5732] Skills development in South Africa

[5733] The company is fully compliant with all relevant South African legislation, except insofar as there may be a waiver or waivers granted in consideration of strategic issues

[5734] Partly South African-owned defence companies may compete for any and all defence contracts within their fields of competence, including items over which sovereign control is required, given that the relevant security requirements are met, and will enjoy preference over companies with no or a smaller South African shareholding, provided that: a. Their products and/or services fully meet the requirement in all critical respects

[5735] They demonstrate the ability to support that product through its lifecycle, including such upgrades that may be necessitated or required from time to time

[5736] No foreign product demonstrates an overwhelming advantage over the local product

[5737] Their price and long-term support price structure are: i. Broadly in line with other offers; or ii. are considered acceptable given the advantages of local sourcing

[5738] SOUTH AFRICAN-BASED DEFENCE COMPANY A defence company may be considered to be South African-based if

[5739] The relevant manufacturing and research and development facilities are in South Africa and are locally controlled in respect of their operation to the extent required to ensure uninterrupted supply to the Defence Force; or b. it has other major such facilities in South Africa; and c. there is security of uninterrupted supply to the Defence Force; and, further, d. there is an agreement with the Defence Force, if deemed necessary accompanied by a government-to-government agreement, covering the security of intellectual property owned by the Defence Force or being developed under contract from the Defence Force, including no transfer outside South African hands or foreign access to such intellectual property other in terms of that agreement or a specific contract; e. the company demonstrates a real, tangible and enduring commitment to: i

[5740] Adding economic value to South Africa. ii

[5741] Skills development in South Africa

[5742] the company is fully compliant with all relevant South African legislation, except insofar as there may be a waiver or waivers granted in consideration of strategic issues

[5743] South African-based companies may compete for the development, manufacture and support of defence matériel in respect of which strategic independence is required, and for the development, manufacture and support of all other equipment, systems, stores and supplies, and will enjoy preference over foreign companies, provided that: a. Their products and/or services fully meet the requirement in all critical respects

[5744] They demonstrate the ability to support that product through its lifecycle, including such upgrades that may be necessitated or required from time to time

[5745] No foreign product demonstrates an overwhelming advantage over the local product

[5746] Their price and long-term support price structure are: i. Broadly in line with other offers; or ii. are considered acceptable given the advantages of local sourcing

[5747] In exceptional circumstances South African based companies may be considered for sovereign items, but only within the framework of contract-specific controls set to ensure sovereign control of that matériel and the related technologies and intellectual property

[5748] FOREIGN-CONTROLLED DEFENCE COMPANIES IN SOUTH AFRICA Local defence companies that are not compliant with the requirements set out above are not considered to be South African, partly South African-owned or South African-based in respect of sovereign equipment or systems or those considered essential for strategic independence

[5749] Such companies: a. May compete for the development, manufacture and support of defence matériel, commodities and services not considered sovereign or required for strategic independence, and their bids will enjoy an advantage over entirely foreign companies if all else is equal

[5750] May be allowed to compete in respect of items required for strategic independence, if they can show that effective local manufacture and support can be established where that is practicable, and that such manufacture and long-term support can continue despite opposition or even prohibition by the government of the country in which they are headquartered or in which the majority of the ownership resides

[5751] All companies wishing to compete for Defence Force contracts must also have a record, or in the case of newer companies the demonstrated intent, to support the national development agenda as outlined in government policy from time to time, particularly in respect of a commitment to training and skills development and to deepening and expanding South Africa’s knowledge and technology base

[5752] Their performance and/or commitment in this respect, with due allowance for variances in what is practicable in a particular sector and in the case of smaller companies, will be a factor in evaluating bids

[5753] Local branches of foreign companies may compete for the development, manufacture and support of general defence matériel, commodities and services

[5754] Where, however, such a local branch is in effect no more than a marketing or representative office, that company will be regarded as being a foreign company with no local presence

[5755] Foreign companies with no South African branch may be allowed to compete for such contracts, but may be required to establish a local branch to manufacture, support or assist with the support of the relevant defence matériel if the contract is awarded to them, if

[5756] That is important to ensure effective support to the Defence Force; or b. there is a major economic impact; and if c. such establishment is practicable

[5757] All foreign suppliers will be required to meet the industrial participation requirements set by the Department of Defence and the Department of Trade and Industry, as stipulated by national economic and development policy, as well as other relevant legislation

[5758] Commitment to supporting South Africa’s national development agenda will, as in respect of South African-based companies, be a factor in evaluating bids

[5759] STATE-CONTROLLED OR -OWNED DEFENCE COMPANIES The establishment, development and retention of certain defence industrial capabilities will not solely be governed by market forces, due regard being had for strategic necessity and also for strategic advantage, and particularly in respect of defence matériel over which sovereign control is required

[5760] The state may, therefore, retain or establish state-owned enterprises in technology domains that are key to the intent of the defence industry policy and strategy, as developed from national security and defence policy objectives, but which are not commercially viable in South Africa

[5761] Where a commercial entity is active in such a technology domain, but finds it is no longer viable as a business, the state may: a. Acquire that entity; b. acquire control of that entity; or c. invest in that entity or the relevant portion thereof, with regard for the protection and control of that investment

[5762] Where the state chooses to acquire control or majority or full ownership of a company, the owners will be compensated to a mutually accepted market value, taking into account the demonstrated and verifiable past investment in the company’s defence capabilities and technology development made in good faith by the owners to support the Defence Force

[5763] State-owned entities that are potentially viable as commercial enterprises, and that are not engaged in areas that are either sovereign or otherwise particularly sensitive, may be sold into private ownership, in whole or in part, provided that there is assurance that this entity will continue with work deemed essential to the Defence Force

[5764] Private defence entities may not be sold, in whole or part, to foreign entities without the agreement of the Minister of Defence, which will not be unreasonably withheld

[5765] In a case where the existing owners must divest themselves of their ownership of a defence industry entity, the state may choose to acquire that entity or a portion thereof at a mutually accepted market value

[5766] Similarly, private defence entities may not close certain capabilities or exit the industry without the agreement of the Minister of Defence

[5767] Where existing owners must take such action, the state may: a. Enter into an agreement with the owners to support retention of that capability, or to ensure the survival of the entity or a part of the entity; or b. acquire the entity, in whole or part, if applicable, compensating the owners to a mutually accepted market value

[5768] In some cases where this might be a logical course of action, the state may enter into a public-private partnership arrangement with a defence industry entity, for instance a government owned/contractor operated arrangement in respect of a manufacturing facility

[5769] All such acquisitions, disposals or other such arrangements will be in accordance with the relevant legislation and regulations except where the exigencies of the defence and security environment might demand a departure, in which case a fair outcome for the other party will be ensured by negotiation or arbitration

[5770] Denel Denel is a national security asset, with the primary purpose of designing, developing, manufacturing and supporting defence matériel

[5771] In addition thereto, Denel is charged with

[5772] The custodianship of assigned sovereign or strategic defence capabilities, technologies and abilities, inclusive of those that may be at risk, the loss of which would threaten South Africa’s required defence capability

[5773] The design, development, manufacture and support of important capabilities which may not be commercially viable

[5774] The divisions of Denel are classified as follows: a. Denel Dynamics – Sovereign

[5775] b. Denel Land Systems – Strategic

[5776] c. Denel Aviation – Strategic. d

[5777] Rheinmetall-Denel Munitions – Strategic

[5778] e. Pretoria Metal Pressings (PMP) – Strategic

[5779] f. Overberg Test Range (OTR) – Strategic

[5780] Denel will, in carrying out such projects, make optimal use of private South African companies in the defence industry and in the wider industrial sector, acting as the prime contractor and, where it has the capability to do so, as the system integrator

[5781] The relationship between the Defence Force and Denel will at all times remain a normal contractual one

[5782] Denel may also be contracted by other state entities to carry out projects that are key to national strategy, suited to its capabilities and not commercially viable, provided that it can do so without detriment to its primary purpose

[5783] Denel may dispose of, wholly or partially, to private owners such divisions that are not involved in sovereign projects or deemed essential to strategic independence or key to the intent of defence industrial policy

[5784] The state may allow investors, local and foreign, to acquire minority shareholdings in those divisions in which it chooses to retain majority ownership

[5785] Any minority shareholding will be strictly monitored to ensure security and sovereignty

[5786] Due regard will be paid in this respect to economic imperatives and foreign policy objectives

[5787] Consideration should be given to establishing a maritime division within Denel to take over the management of the Naval Dockyard (and any other mutually identified facility) in terms of a properly planned division of both functions and responsibilities between itself and the Navy

[5788] The position of the Dockyard as an entity managed by Armscor has not produced the hoped for results

[5789] Simply transferring it back to the Navy may, however, restrict its ability to carry out work that could reduce the cost of ownership to the Navy; examples of such other work would include: Refit, repair, modernisation, conversion or upgrading of naval and coast guard vessels of other countries, working in conjunction with industry, in some cases as the prime contractor, in others as a sub-contractor. Support for the complex vessels of the offshore diamond and gas/oil exploration industries, working in conjunction with specialist companies in those sectors

[5790] Support for the complex vessels of the offshore diamond and gas/oil exploration industries, working in conjunction with specialist companies in those sectors

[5791] The establishment of a Denel maritime division will be an optimal approach, specifically the application of Denel's systems engineering capability and its ability to sustain better upkeep of warships and other naval vessels

[5792] Sovereign command and control technology will be established within either Denel or a selected South African-owned company

[5793] Defence acquisition will be carried out by Armscor as the defence matériel acquisition agency to ensure the necessary compliance in the acquisition of defence matériel and related stores

[5794] Armscor will also assist the Defence Force to be an intelligent buyer by, in concert with local industry as may be appropriate, conducting, contracting or overseeing: Evaluation of acquisition, procurement, research, development and manufacturing models in other countries

[5795] b. Evaluation of lifecycle management practices in other countries

[5796] c. Research and evaluation in respect of foreign weapons, equipment and systems

[5797] The planned and focused development of a science, engineering and technology support capability: i. In areas identified as key to the future capability of the Defence Force; and ii. to support the operations and management of the Defence Force

[5798] Armscor will, in principle, not develop or manufacture equipment, nor compete in any way with local industry, but will conduct, contract or coordinate: a. Background technology monitoring and research, to be able to advise the Defence Force and local industry

[5799] b. Research and development in particularly sensitive areas (such as chemical, biological and radiological defence

[5800] c. Research and development in areas in which it is already engaged (such armour technology

[5801] d. Research and development in niche areas as may be identified by the Defence Force from time to time

[5802] In the event of an urgent operational requirement that cannot be met by industry, from available resources, Armscor may, nonetheless, arrange and oversee development and manufacture, by sub-contractors or in-house

[5803] Armscor has the additional function of supporting and assisting the development of the South African defence industry and its capabilities

[5804] In this respect Armscor will work with the Defence Force and the industry to develop acquisition, procurement and logistic/technical support strategies that: a. Ensure optimal acquisition, procurement and support for the Defence Force

[5805] Support the national strategy to develop and strengthen the defence industry

[5806] c. Support South African defence industry market penetration

[5807] DEFENCE INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY Defence intellectual property may, in the main, be created or developed by: a. Investment and product development in the course of an acquisition or procurement programme; b. investment in a dedicated research and development programme in pursuit of defence science, engineering and technology objectives; or c. investment arising from the Defence Industrial programme

[5808] For the purposes of this section, defence intellectual property means: Any intellectual property that is created exclusively or partially with defence funds, and may be found in, or take the form of, books, manuscripts, reports and notes, computer software, inventions, drawings and designs, data items, data packs, specifications, models, photographs, trademarks and other graphical images

[5809] Defence intellectual property includes intellectual property that is created through indirect contracting, such as contracts made by the other party with a sub-contractor, as well as intellectual property that is obtained or created exclusively or partially through the Defence Industrial Participation (DIP) programme or other contracts or co-operations of the Defence Force with foreign entities or countries, where the Defence Force and/or the other party are legally entitled to the intellectual property

[5810] The management of defence intellectual property will be broadly guided by a Defence Force policy, through contractual arrangements undertaken to regulate acquisition and research and development projects

[5811] Intellectual property may be further regulated by means of patent registration as may be decided on a case-by-case basis

[5812] The above places the burden on the state to ensure significant rigour concerning the management of defence intellectual property in future defence matériel contracts

[5813] Such contracts may, based on the merit of each transaction, address important defence intellectual property considerations including but not limited to the following: a. Management of commercial background and foreground intellectual property

[5814] b. Ownership, use and transfer of background and foreground intellectual property

[5815] c. Ownership, use and transfer of defence intellectual property created or developed, including the co-ownership relationship

[5816] d. Management of indivisible defence intellectual property

[5817] The modification, altering, development, amendment or enhancement of defence intellectual property

[5818] The registration of patents

[5819] g. Royalties arising or payable from defence intellectual property

[5820] Right of use or licence to use defence intellectual property

[5821] i. Third party transfer of defence intellectual property; j. Loss or unlawful use of defence intellectual property; k. Sale or change of ownership of defence intellectual property

[5822] l. Management of defence intellectual property under instances of joint ventures, alliances and sale of company equity

[5823] m. Measures of protection and confidentiality

[5824] n. Safekeeping and general military security arrangements concerning defence intellectual property

[5825] o. Arms control, dual-use and non-proliferation considerations

[5826] p. Procedures to manage or dispose of redundant defence intellectual property

[5827] q. Settlement of disputes

[5828] In some instances defence intellectual property may be further regulated by binding bilateral instruments concluded on a government-to-government basis to either regulate all intellectual property exchanged between the two countries or to regulate the management of specific intellectual property related to a particular government-to-government transaction

[5829] The ownership of all and any intellectual property in respect of any defence matériel or technology developed under a direct government defence contract or indirectly as part of a direct government defence contract, will reside with defence, unless specifically ceded to another body or person, regardless of any patents that may be lodged

[5830] Where the cost of development was shared by the developing company, companies or individuals, the ownership of the resulting intellectual property will be held pro rata by defence and those companies or individuals as determined in the relevant contractual agreement(s), which will cover, inter alia, the required levels of sovereignty and secrecy, the use of background technology, the future transfer of such intellectual property and the matter of royalties

[5831] Defence intellectual property that is brought into South Africa by a company, or is created or developed by a company using its own funding, remains the property of that company

[5832] The Defence Force will not divest itself of such intellectual property except with the agreement of the Minister of Defence that so doing does not present a strategic risk

[5833] The Minister of Defence, advised by the Secretary for Defence and the CEO of Armscor, will decide on the management of intellectual property related to defence matériel deemed sovereign or critical to strategic independence

[5834] The CEO of Armscor is the responsible authority for the day-to-day management of all Defence Force-owned intellectual property

[5835] In managing its intellectual property, defence will keep foremost in mind that an excessive emphasis on royalties will hamper the ability of the South African defence industry to penetrate other defence markets

[5836] The royalties to be levied will, therefore, not exceed accepted international market trends and best practice

[5837] Where levying royalties would endanger the conclusion of export contracts, consideration will be given to waiving such royalties in favour of concluding such contracts and furthering South African penetration of the international defence market, with the resulting intrinsic benefits to the Defence Force

[5838] As a general principle the Defence Force will not patent its intellectual property, as that would: Entail considerable and ongoing cost

[5839] b. Compromise the security of the technologies, processes or products concerned

[5840] The Defence Force will, instead, ensure the protection of its intellectual property by implementing: a. Best practice in the management of trade secrets

[5841] b. National secrecy and security provisions

[5842] TECHNOLOGY SPIN-OFF The spin-off of capabilities and technologies from the defence industry and the defence research institutes into the wider South African economy and industry will be encouraged and supported

[5843] Royalty arrangements will be managed contractually by the CEO of Armscor in close consultation with defence to extract optimal value from existing technology

[5844] The preferred method of value generation will be of a non-monetary nature, seeking interested parties for reinvestment in defence industry, product enhancement, defence research or in skills development relevant to defence or aligned with emerging defence requirements

[5845] Government will also encourage the exchange of ideas between defence companies and companies in other but related fields, to make a contribution to the wider dissemination of knowledge and skills in South Africa

[5846] The only restriction in this respect will be that security considerations are taken fully into account, with the release of technologies and the exchange of personnel required to be approved by the Defence Force in any case where confidential matters are involved

[5847] DEFENCE STRATEGIC TRAJECTORY – FIVE MILESTONES The Defence Strategic Trajectory (Chapter 9 of this Defence Review) posits the following critical milestones to develop the defence capabilities that South Africa requires, namely: a. Milestone 1: Arrest the decline in critical capabilities through immediate and directed interventions

[5848] b. Milestone 2: Reorganise and rebalance the Defence Force as the foundation for future growth

[5849] c. Milestone 3: Create a sustainable Defence Force that can meet ordered defence commitments (interim end-state of the Defence Review

[5850] d. Milestone 4: Enhance the Defence Force’s capacity to respond to emerging threats (end-state of the Defence Review

[5851] e. Milestone 5: Defend the Republic against an imminent or dire threat. A defence industry sector strategy will be developed that will: meet the critical defence needs; add substance to South Africa’s deterrent posture; add substance to South Africa’s standing as a country; and provide the ability to utilise defence equipment sales in support of foreign policy

[5852] The five overlapping phases set out below, which set out the broad concept for the development of the national defence industrial strategy, and is broadly aligned to the five milestones of the Defence Strategic Trajectory

[5853] These are: a. Phase 1: Measures to retain selected capabilities and capacities at risk and the consolidation of the existing state-owned capacities

[5854] b. Phase 2: Ensure sustainment of those capabilities and capacities

[5855] c. Phase 3: Support the economic turn-around of South African and South African-based defence companies

[5856] d. Phase 4: Create conditions for further development of the South African defence industry, in cooperation, where that is relevant and practicable, with the DTI, to support the establishment and development of downstream industries

[5857] e. Phase 5: Recover, recreate or develop sovereign capabilities under South African ownership

[5858] While these milestones are essentially sequential, they will in some cases be overlapping or interlocking

[5859] The implementation of this strategy will be carried out in step with the development and implementation of the acquisition and procurement policies set out above

[5860] PHASE 1: SECURE EXISTING CAPABILITIES The first step towards achieving the desired defence industrial capability is to secure the existing capabilities and capacities as a base from which to expand

[5861] This phase will centre on placing short-term contracts locally that are focused on: a

[5862] Ensuring the immediate survival of particular companies

[5863] Ensuring the immediate retention of particular capabilities and capacities

[5864] c. Meeting identified requirements of the Defence Force

[5865] Underpinning pending and potential export orders

[5866] Such contracts will include orders for: a. Refurbishment of existing equipment that it is intended to keep in service

[5867] b. Upgrading and modernising certain defence matériel

[5868] Figure 15-1: Key Targets across the Defence Strategic Trajectory c. Replenishment of reserve ammunition stocks and spares

[5869] Continuing existing research and development projects

[5870] Defence may also assist key companies financially to ensure their immediate survival and/or to upgrade facilities

[5871] Such assistance must be provided within the regulations of the Public Finance Management Act or in terms of a waiver of those regulations

[5872] SUSTAIN EXISTING CAPABILITIES. The second milestone is to ensure the sustainability of the identified defence companies

[5873] This will be done by means of: a. Placing multi-year contracts for identified items that are required for training (eg munitions, spares) or to replenish the reserve stocks of the Defence Force

[5874] Placing multi-year contracts for the support of defence matériel in service

[5875] Placing multi-year contracts to meet immediate and near-term defence matériel needs of the Defence Force, in some cases in phased batches to enable the Defence Force to coherently rebuild certain capabilities while simultaneously providing industry with an extended order book

[5876] Adopting an acquisition strategy that makes maximum use of common systems to achieve greater interoperability and easier support in the field on the one hand and greater economies of scale on the other

[5877] This strategy will not, however, be allowed to place commonality above mission utility

[5878] Informing local companies of planned acquisitions and likely budgets, to enable them to plan ahead and invest appropriately

[5879] Expanding the present levels of research and development (R&D) funding and ensuring alignment of R&D projects with Defence Force priorities and, insofar as is practicable, with wider national R&D imperatives and goals

[5880] g. Actively supporting exports of defence matériel in production and upgrading of systems and equipment already in service with other forces; h. Establishing and supporting relevant ‘centres of excellence’

[5881] i. Supporting relevant undergraduate, post-graduate and technical courses at South African universities and other tertiary educational establishments

[5882] The third milestone is intended to support a turn-around of the industry aimed at ensuring its long-term viability

[5883] This will be achieved within identified existing capabilities and within capabilities that can be quickly and efficiently established: a. Giving the Defence Force medium-term and long-term authority to commit funds to equipment projects and programmes

[5884] Standardising on platforms in production or about to enter production to extend production and facilitate through-life support, albeit not favouring commonality at the expense of missionsuitability

[5885] Adopting a half-generation change-over policy for equipping the defence force

[5886] This will guard against block obsolescence and give both the Defence Force and the industry the benefit of predictable longer production runs

[5887] Extending orders for in-production equipment and systems and items about to go into production, to equip approximately half of the existing fleet or envisaged fleet in each case

[5888] e. Actively supporting the export of equipment that is in current production for the Defence Force

[5889] f. Making visible the Defence Force’s medium-term and long-term requirements to the industry, ideally by establishing a Capital Expenditure Statement as a public document in respect of all but specifically sensitive projects and envisaged funding levels

[5890] g. Supporting local development of equipment and systems to meet requirements that have been identified and largely defined, insofar as this is both practicable and financially sensible

[5891] h. Supporting joint ventures with foreign defence companies and countries

[5892] i. Guiding and supporting industry-funded research and development to meet future requirements and to pursue some potentially relevant ‘blue sky’ concepts

[5893] PHASE 4: SUPPORT FUTURE DEVELOPMENT

[5894] The fourth milestone is intended to establish a base from which the industry will be able to develop into the future and expand its capabilities

[5895] This will be achieved by identifying jointly with the industry those areas into which the industry can logically expand and then support that expansion

[5896] a. To meet identified sovereign and strategic independence requirements; b. where there are sufficiently substantial local requirements; c. where there is sufficient export or joint venture potential; or d. where there is substantial potential for valuable spin-offs into the economy

[5897] Export and joint venture potential, together with local requirements, exists in several fields, including guided weapons, artillery systems and areas of electronic warfare, and can be recreated in the field of tactical communications systems if that capability is restored

[5898] Areas of potentially substantial economic spin-off exist in software development and in the local manufacture of various COTS items required by the Defence Force that also have civilian applications

[5899] Where capabilities that have been identified as requiring sovereign control are in fact controlled by foreign companies, government will either: a. Acquire those capabilities from their owners at a mutually agreed market value; and in accordance with the relevant legislation and regulations, or, b. failing that, re-establish the necessary capabilities within DENEL and/or one or more South African-owned companies

[5900] In either case this will be accompanied by a focused programme to develop the skills base required for this to be done effectively and efficiently, where possible drawing back into the industry South African individuals with relevant expertise and experience to lay the foundation and to mentor their successors

[5901] KEY INDUSTRY CAPABILITY AREAS

[5902] The following sections set out in outline the minimum requirement for primary industrial capability

[5903] These capability areas apply particularly in respect of the key technology domains identified above, but are also cross-cutting in respect of all defence technology domains

[5904] EQUIPMENT AND SYSTEMS SUPPORT

[5905] This refers to a coherent system of through-life system management, from acquisition to disposal, including: a. Support during the acquisition of foreign-sourced matériel

[5906] Commissioning equipment and systems into service

[5907] c. Routine maintenance and overhaul

[5908] d. Battle damage, operational damage and accident repair

[5909] e. Controlled long-term storage and re-commissioning after extended storage

[5910] f. Decommissioning and disposal

[5911] g. Support for equipment passed on to other armed forces in the context of defence diplomacy in congruence with foreign policy and national security objectives to develop a system of closer defence ties within the SADC and the continent

[5912] SUPPORT TO MILITARY OPERATIONS An important issue is the ability of the industry to support key equipment in the field

[5913] This may require the deployment of civilian industry staff into an operational area or on operations

[5914] In such cases: a. Civilian members of defence industry companies who deploy with South African forces on an operation will be appointed to the Reserve for the duration of that deployment, in an acting rank commensurate with their posts and responsibilities

[5915] This will ensure that all South African personnel fall under a single legal system and that such industry staff enjoy the protections accorded to military personnel in the event of capture by opposing forces or arrest by neutral forces

[5916] They will be issued, on a temporary basis, with appropriate clothing and personal equipment, which may include firearms if this is considered necessary

[5917] such appointment will not in any way affect their rights and duties in terms of applicable labour legislation except insofar as required in terms of the conduct and security of operations and to ensure their safety

[5918] The Defence Force will be responsible for the transport, protection, accommodation and subsistence of such company staff to and within the operational area, with those costs being for its account, to be charged against the cost of the operation concerned

[5919] Defence industry staff deployed in an operational area will be required to adhere to all instructions issued by the local command in respect of movement and security

[5920] To cater for inherent risks of being deployed to an operational area, special measures must be developed to ensure due care and adequate compensation in the event of injury or loss of life

[5921] CRITICAL MUNITIONS AND RELATED MATTERS

[5922] This refers particularly but not exclusively to: a. All munitions likely to be used in large quantities, munitions for locally developed weapons, and specialised munitions with limited shelf-life

[5923] Specialised batteries for, among other things: communications and other electronic equipment; missiles, torpedoes and other guided weapons; and remotely operated systems

[5924] HIGH RATE-OF-USE SPARES AND CRITICAL STORES

[5925] This refers to, among other things: a. Spares for weapons, weapon systems and unmanned systems

[5926] b. Spares for communications and other electronic equipment

[5927] c. Spares for combat vehicles and tactical logistic vehicles

[5928] d. Spares for combat and transport rotary-wing and fixed-wing aircraft

[5929] e. Spares for naval vessels

[5930] Replacement filters for respiratory (individual and collective) equipment

[5931] g. Pharmaceuticals, medical stores, decontamination chemicals and stores, and spares for medical equipment

[5932] h. Field rations, uniforms and general field equipment

[5933] It is necessary to keep in mind that some of these spares and stores will be expended in the course of disaster aid and similar operations

[5934] SYSTEM INTEGRATION A system integration capability critically allows the Defence Force to acquire optimal sub-systems and equipment from different suppliers in order to: a. Develop optimised equipment and systems without the cost of developing sub-systems

[5935] b. Deploy and support equipment and systems; c. Integrate complex system environments with other systems to construct a ‘system of systems’

[5936] d. Develop system backbones or links to facilitate interoperability among forces

[5937] e. Modernise, upgrade and convert equipment and systems optimally

[5938] The system integration capability must include the ability to independently: a. Integrate precision weapons and related systems with in-service and future platforms

[5939] Modify key missile (and related system) algorithms, for example those governing guidance and control, attack profiles and electronic countercounter-measures capability

[5940] c. Integrate unmanned systems with other in-service and future systems

[5941] EQUIPMENT MODERNISATION AND UPGRADE Most modern platforms (aircraft, ships and vehicles) and systems have a service life of twenty to thirty years, thus requiring the Defence Force to modernise and upgrade such systems to ensure optimal effectiveness and to meet evolving threats

[5942] Having the ability within the country to modernise, upgrade and convert equipment and systems allows the Defence Force to optimally manage its equipment both in terms of its utility and in terms of cost-effectiveness

[5943] This capability is in many respects a combination of the ability to support equipment and of a systems integration capability

[5944] CRITICAL EQUIPMENT AND SYSTEMS Critical equipment and systems are those that are essential to the conduct of operations or those which can provide a useable tactical edge

[5945] Examples include: a. Secure communications systems

[5946] b. Information operations systems

[5947] c. Electronic warfare systems

[5948] d. Reconnaissance and intelligence collection, management and evaluation systems

[5949] e. Precision weapons, including missiles and guided and homing bombs and projectiles, and particularly low cost, man-portable and low-collateral damage weapons, and fire direction systems

[5950] Having the ability to develop, manufacture and support such systems will also provide the capability to optimise them to suit the Defence Force’s needs

[5951] OPTIMISED EQUIPMENT AND SYSTEMS The operational environment and the operational style of the Defence Force are such that there is a requirement for optimised systems and equipment in some defence capability areas, and real potential advantage to be gained in others

[5952] It will not be practicable to autonomously develop optimised equipment in all cases, but it will be possible to do so: a. Where the numbers required justify local development and industrialisation. b

[5953] Where there is significant export potential

[5954] SOUTH AFRICAN DEFENCE REVIEW 2015 DEFENCE INDUSTRY POLICY AND STRATEGY b

[5955] In partnership with original equipment manufacturers. UNMANNED SYSTEMS The strategic, operational and tactical potential of unmanned systems is advancing and expanding at a significant rate

[5956] The Defence Force must make optimal use of such systems and understand the impact on own forces operations of such systems in the hands of opposing forces

[5957] The Defence Force will draw on technical and scientific advice to: a. Evaluate and monitor developments in unmanned systems and related technologies at the strategic, operational and tactical levels

[5958] Develop service-level and joint unmanned systems doctrines and strategies

[5959] c. Work with the defence industry, the relevant research and development bodies and the relevant government departments to develop and implement a national unmanned systems strategy to cover: i

[5960] The employment of unmanned systems, including integration at relevant levels. The acquisition, integration and support of unmanned systems

[5961] The acquisition, integration and support of unmanned systems

[5962] The development and production of unmanned systems in South Africa

[5963] There is a good logic for manufacturing locally, without necessarily developing locally, normal civilian standard equipment that must be acquired or procured in large numbers or quantities

[5964] Quite apart from military advantage, this will further job creation and sustainment, reduce import expenditure and also potentially lead to export earnings

[5965] CHEMICAL, BIOLOGICAL AND RADIOLOGICAL DEFENCE South Africa does not intend to use, acquire or develop chemical, biological or radiological (or nuclear) weapons; nor is there any near-term likelihood of South Africa becoming involved in armed conflict with a country that has such weapons

[5966] It is, however, necessary for South Africa to conduct research and development work in this field in order to be able to: a. Understand the risks and dangers involved; c

[5967] develop the necessary intelligence collection and sensor technologies to guard against such attack; c. acquire or develop and manufacture protective equipment and clothing for critical facilities, emergency response teams and military personnel; d. acquire or develop and manufacture relevant inoculations, antidotes and supportive medicines for personnel who may be exposed to such agents or weapons; e. acquire or develop and manufacture decontamination equipment and materials

[5968] The responsibility for ensuring that the necessary capabilities are to hand is that of the Defence Force

[5969] It is, therefore, also the responsibility of the Defence Force to initiate, fund and support the necessary research to allow effective and efficient acquisition and/or development and manufacture of the necessary equipment, clothing and medicines

[5970] All research, development, manufacture, production and storage carried out in respect of this requirement will be carried out in strict compliance with South Africa’s relevant international treaty obligations and the related national legislation and regulations

[5971] GENERAL COMMODITIES The Defence Force requires various general commodities and civilian-standard equipment in large quantities and numbers

[5972] While there is no critical need to manufacture such items in South Africa, this can make economic sense in some cases, and particularly so when there is also a substantial civilian market for the same or an essentially similar item

[5973] There may be a particular opportunity here to support small and micro-businesses and military veterans, especially where there is logic to procuring particular commodities from businesses in the immediate area of a Defence Force base

[5974] CONCLUSION The success of the defence industry will be its integration into mainstream South African industrial policy as a distinct and supported sector in the wider industrial base

[5975] Defence thus has an onerous responsibility to work together with all stakeholders towards this end, and specifically the integration of the defence industry sector into the Industrial Policy Action Plan, and any subsequent amendment

[5976] The next iteration of the National Development Plan should include the Defence Industry as part of South Africa’s national industrial base

[5977] The future defence industry strategy will be developed by the National Defence Industry Council, drawing on the expertise within the Defence Force, the Defence Secretariat and the defence acquisition agent, and in conjunction with the industry and with inputs from the Department of Trade and Industry and the Department of Science and Technology

[5978] This strategy will be updated as required to take into account the evolving strategic situation and developments in defence technology and the international defence industrial environment

[5979] The implementation of this strategy will be carried out in step with the development and implementation of the acquisition and procurement policies

[5980] The strategy will further be aligned and interlinked with government’s wider economic and industrial development strategies, including: a. Support for small business enterprises

[5981] Furthering the general BBBEE and military veterans policies as they develop

[5982] c. Inclusion of the defence industry as a sector in its own right in the IPAP of the DTI, rather than jointly with Aerospace (IPAP 2012/13 – 2014/15, Paragraph 14.17) and specific recognition of and support for realising this sector’s potential in respect of: i. Exploiting new opportunities created by South-South cooperation (IPAP, 12.1.2). ii

[5983] Potential for development of long-term advanced capabilities (IPAP, Cluster 3) and specifically 14.15 “advanced manufacturing” and 14.16 “advanced materials”

[5984] In relation to other sectors, including: Metal fabrication and boat-building (Cluster 1), including the potential for the development of a comprehensive ship-building sector

[5985] Automotive products and components, and medium and heavy commercial vehicles (Cluster

[5986] Aerospace, electro-technical and ICT (Cluster

[5987] Inclusion of the defence industry in the DTI’s Manufacturing Competitiveness Enhancement Programme (MCEP

[5988] e. Aligning, without sacrificing strategic independence, the Defence Force acquisition strategy with: i. The Preferential Procurement Policy Framework Act. ii

[5989] The Competitive Supplier Development Programme (CSDP) of the DTI

[5990] The Technology Localisation Programme of the Department of Science and Technology

[5991] f. Inclusion of the defence industry in the Support Programme for Industrial Innovation (SPII) of the Department of Trade and Industry, reversing the present specific exclusion of the defence sector by Paragraph 5.6 of the SPII Rules Document (Version 3.0 dated 1 April

[5992] g. Alignment with the policies, strategies and efforts of other government departments and agencies insofar as is practicable and without detriment to the support provided to the Defence Force

[5993] An urgent follow-on activity will be the further determination of strategic capabilities and technologies, as well as niche capabilities and technologies, which must be driven and maintained at a corporate level

[5994] To this end, it is recommended that a Prioritisation Committee be established by the Minister for this purpose and which will report to the National Defence Industry Council

[5995] South Africa’s Defence Policy is premised on the Constitution of the Republic of South Africa (Act No 108 of 1996), the Defence Act, 2002, (Act No 42 of 2002, as amended), the White Paper on Defence and the Defence Review

[5996] The 1996 White Paper on Defence and the 1998 Defence Review require review due to changes in the strategic environment and a new Defence Policy must be established in order to ensure continued relevance and legislative compliance

[5997] The Defence Review Committee (hereafter referred to as the Committee) was established on 05 July 2010 to undertake a complete review of South Africa’s Defence Policy

[5998] The Committee was established under authority of the Minister of Defence and Military Veterans (hereafter referred to as the Minister) in her capacity as the Executive Authority for the Department of Defence, and in terms of the Treasury Regulations Chapter 20: Commissions and Committees of Inquiry: 20.1 A ‘committee’ means a committee of inquiry appointed by the executive authority and includes an interdepartmental committee of inquiry, but does not include any permanent commission, board, council, committee or similar body, whether appointed pursuant to any law or otherwise

[5999] The members of the Committee are appointed under individual contract, and are remunerated in terms of the provisions of Treasury Regulations Chapter 20: Commissions and Committees of Inquiry and on the basis of a written determination by the Accounting Officer: 20.2 Remuneration of Members

[6000] An official member may not receive additional remuneration

[6001] Subsistence and other allowances may be paid to the official member by the institution that employs the official member in accordance with his or her conditions of service

[6002] A non-official member must be remunerated according to scales approved by the National Treasury

[6003] Should the accounting officer deem it necessary, he or she can, in consultation with the executive authority, determine other remuneration, provided that - (a) the terms of reference are properly defined in terms of time and cost; and (b) if applicable, the remuneration is considered taking into account the tariffs as determined by the institute that regulates the profession that the non-official member belongs to

[6004] The remuneration of all members of a commission or committee must be disclosed as notes to the financial statements of the institution

[6005] The Committee must execute its mandate in accordance with these Terms of Reference and any other directive that may be provided by the Minister

[6006] MANDATE 3.1 With due cognisance of the 1996 White Paper on Defence and the 1998 Defence Review, the Committee is required to propose a new Defence Review for the consideration of the Minister, and through which the Minister can engage the National Executive and the Legislature on South Africa’s future defence policy direction

[6007] The proposed new Defence Review is required to: 3.1.1 Identify the high-order principles pertinent to the defence function

[6008] Ensure comprehensive alignment of South Africa’s Defence Policy with the Constitution, domestic statute and international law

[6009] Establish a long-term policy and strategy defence vision supportive of South Africa’s strategic posture and international responsibilities

[6010] Enunciate the complete spectrum of defence responsibility, through stated defence functions, high-level goals and tasks, identifying strategic concepts and doctrine and required defence capabilities

[6011] Provide a level of defence effort which must be pursued by the Defence Force

[6012] Provide a sound policy base for determining the concomitant Military Strategy and the Blueprint Defence Force 'Force Design' and 'Force Structure

[6013] Provide the long-term defence trajectory, in terms of defence organisational interventions, force generation and defence capability development

[6014] Provide a high-level, first-order discussion on the funding principles, practices and requirements of the defence organisation

[6015] Provide a strategic discussion on the role and function of South Africa’s defence industry, with all relevant ramifications thereto

[6016] In the course of drafting the proposed new Defence Review, the Committee shall take, inter alia, the following into consideration

[6017] The primary object of the Defence Force and other Constitutional and statutory imperatives

[6018] The fundamental defence challenges and concomitant interventions required

[6019] Government priorities, including the Medium-Term Strategic Framework. 3.2.4 The strategic security environment, trends and predictions, including emerging sources of insecurity

[6020] Current national security policy processes

[6021] South Africa’s national interests

[6022] South Africa’s international relations policy, international relations strategy and international obligations

[6023] International best practice on defence matters and recent international experiences in policy making, with particular reference to developments on the African continent

[6024] The nature and scope of the South African defence industry, its products and its strategic domestic and international partners

[6025] The manufacture, marketing, sale, export, import and transit of South African armament and related goods and services

[6026] South Africa’s fiscal framework and policy as it applies to the defence sector

[6027] In the course of its work the Committee is required to consult extensively in the following domains: The Defence Force

[6028] The Defence Secretariat

[6029] Relevant government departments and agencies

[6030] Relevant public entities

[6031] The defence industry

[6032] Appropriate organised labour and employee organisations

[6033] Appropriate academic institutions, research organisations and non-governmental organisations

[6034] The people of South Africa at a grass-roots level

[6035] SOUTH AFRICAN DEFENCE REVIEW 2015 DEFENCE REVIEW COMMITTEE – TERMS OF REFERENCE

[6036] The multilateral African peace and security structures

[6037] Bilateral partners, as the opportunity may arise

[6038] The work of the Committee must seek to achieve maximum consensus on the proposed Defence Review through

[6039] Enhancing public understanding of the defence mandate and public support for the Defence Force

[6040] Expanding the understanding of the defence contribution to national security, national interests and foreign policy

[6041] Deepened consensus in the Executive and the Legislature on South Africa’s defence needs and requirements

[6042] Deliverables

[6043] A public engagement process (and record thereof) on the draft Defence Review

[6044] A revised draft Defence Review following public consultation, input and submissions

[6045] A range of presentations to engage stakeholders and decision-makers, including the National Executive and the Legislature

[6046] A summary of the Defence Review

[6047] An abstract of the key policy pronouncements, interventions required and the proposed defence trajectory

[6048] A decision-support tool to estimate the level of defence capabilities required and the high-level funding requirement thereto

[6049] An updated and consolidated suite of documents and presentations for the Minister to engage Cabinet and Parliament

[6050] A final suite of approved Defence Review documents which can be submitted for printing

[6051] The Committee shall assist the Minister in any manner required and shall undertake any further work as may be directed

[6052] The Committee may, on their request, and to the extent that it is feasible, assist the Secretary for Defence and the Chief of the Defence Force with matters related to the Defence Review

[6053] A Chairperson, assisted by a Deputy Chairperson, shall preside over the Committee and will direct, control and manage the work of the Committee

[6054] specifically through: 5.1.1 Providing broad strategic direction to the Defence Review process

[6055] Managing and directing Defence Review political and consultative engagements

[6056] Providing policy and strategy direction to the drafting of the Defence Review

[6057] Providing direction to the administrative support of the Defence Review process, including the prescribing of internal controls as may be required in accordance with departmental and government policy

[6058] The Committee shall comprise three components, namely: the Defence Review Committee itself, a Resource Group and a Secretariat which supports the Committee (Figure A

[6059] The Committee deliberates on strategic issues and provides strategic direction to the Defence Review process

[6060] The Resource Group researches and drafts documents as required by the Committee and conducts other tasks as directed by the Chairperson

[6061] Researching, coordinating and drafting research documents

[6062] Preparing and delivering necessary presentations

[6063] Monitoring, evaluating, analysing and interpreting domestic, regional, continental and global developments relevant to the Defence Review

[6064] Researching, coordinating and drafting the Defence Review document

[6065] Establishing and maintaining a system to configure and manage Defence Review documents and presentations

[6066] Formulating specialist advice and inputs as required

[6067] The Secretariat, provided by the Department of Defence, provides: 5.5.1 Administrative and other support to the Committee and the Resource Group

[6068] The efficient, effective and economical use of resources, within the parameters of set policies in this regard

[6069] The capacity to acquire, manage and account for the resources availed to the Committee

[6070] A system of internal controls for the resources availed to the Committee

[6071] Secretariat services that enable the work of the Committee

[6072] Specific liaison points will be established with the Office of the Secretary for Defence and the Office of the Chief of the Defence Force for the coordination of the Committee’s engagement with the Defence Secretariat and the Defence Force

[6073] Official members serving on the Committee and any of its sub-structures are required to

[6074] Through their respective command channel, account to the Chairperson for their performance

[6075] FUNDING THE WORK OF THE COMMITTEE The work of the Committee will be funded from the vote of the Department of Defence and in particular from the Administration Programme: Sub-Programme Policy and Planning

[6076] The Chairperson shall convene the Committee according to a programme as will be agreed upon with the Minister

[6077] The Chairperson shall determine the time and place of committee meetings

[6078] The Deputy Chairperson will preside over meetings in the event of the absence of the Chairperson

[6079] The Committee may seek specific guidance or advice from the Minister before proceeding to new areas of work

[6080] A quorum shall consist of the Chairperson (or in the absence of the Chairperson, the Deputy Chairperson) plus a simple majority of the members

[6081] The Committee may still meet if a quorum is not reached, provided that all decisions taken are presented for adoption at the next quorated Committee meeting

[6082] Committee members are required to declare any possible conflict of interests arising from service on the Committee

[6083] Committee members shall conduct themselves in a manner befitting their appointment to the Committee

[6084] The deliberations and work undertaken by the Committee remain confidential and no member is authorised to disclose such information unless it is in accordance with the agreed Work Plan or any decisions of the Committee

[6085] Confidentiality and Intellectual Property Rights will be specified in the Memorandum of Understanding to be concluded between the Department and each Committee member

[6086] The Committee shall endeavour to arrive at its decision by means of consensus

[6087] In instances where consensus is not possible, the Committee shall make its decision by means of a vote

[6088] In addition to a deliberating vote, the Chairperson and Deputy Chairperson shall enjoy a casting vote

[6089] On a vote being tied, the Chairperson and Deputy Chairperson shall exercise their casting votes

[6090] The Chairperson shall use all means at his/her disposal to resolve any dispute or impasse

[6091] At his/her discretion, the Chairperson may request the Minister to resolve such dispute or impasse

[6092] The Committee may establish sub-committees as it deems fit

[6093] The Committee may, through the Chairperson, request advice, assistance or support from the Secretary for Defence and/or the Chief of the Defence Force. The Committee may, as necessary, co-opt defence experts or officials to support the Committee, provided such co-option is directed through the Secretary for Defence and/or the Chief of the Defence Force

[6094] THE SECRETARY FOR DEFENCE 8.1 The Secretary for Defence, as Accounting Officer and Head of Department, shall: 8.1.1 Provide overall administrative and technical support to the Committee

[6095] Provide appropriate resources required for the functioning of the Committee

[6096] Assign a senior official as the nodal point between the office of the Secretary for Defence and the Committee

[6097] Ensure coordinated flow of Defence Secretariat inputs into the Defence Review process

[6098] Avail technical experts to the Committee as may be required by the Committee

[6099] Liaise with the Minister on the matters pertaining to the work of the Committee, as and when required

[6100] CHIEF OF THE SOUTH AFRICAN NATIONAL DEFENCE FORCE 9.1 The Chief of the SANDF shall: 9.1.1 Assign a senior member as the nodal point between the office of the Chief of the SANDF and the Committee

[6101] Ensure coordinated flow of SANDF inputs into the Defence Review process

[6102] Avail technical experts to the Committee as may be required by the Committee

[6103] Facilitate engagement between the Chiefs of Divisions/Services and the Committee

[6104] Facilitate access to units and sight visits as may be required by the Committee

[6105] Liaise with the Minister on the matters pertaining to the work of the Committee, as and when required

[6106] RECORD KEEPING

[6107] The Committee Secretariat shall be responsible for the keeping of records for the activities of the Committee

[6108] The records of the Committee shall be subject to auditing (internal or external) as may be required from time to time

[6109] COMMUNICATION. The Head of Communication (HOC) in the Ministry shall be responsible for all communication matters related to the Defence Review

[6110] The Committee will be supported by a communication strategy which will be planned, organised and managed by the HOC and which shall, inter alia, include: Public consultation and Imbizo

[6111] Defence Review branding, primary themes and key messages

[6112] PARLIAMENTARY AND CABINET ENGAGEMENT Cabinet and Parliamentary engagement will be coordinated and conducted solely under authority of the Minister
