[6203] Developmental Agenda D-1 SOUTH AFRICAN DEFENCE REVIEW 2015 INTRODUCTION Perennial Defence Questions 1. All governments across the world face similar questions when attempting to identify their national defence requirements: a. What is the nature of the current and future security and defence environment

[6204] What international role does the country aspire to? c. What regional and continental role does the country aspire to? d

[6205] When and how should ‘hard’ and ‘soft’ power be deployed, including military power

[6206] e. What work will accordingly be required of defence

[6207] f. What must defence be able to at a stretch

[6208] g. What should defence not do? h

[6209] When required to do all things at all times, which tasks could be done in alliance with other countries and what capabilities will be required as a result? i

[6210] What risks must government be prepared to take, since government cannot insure against every imaginable risk

[6211] j. Consequently, how much is the nation prepared to pay for security and the resources defence requires? k

[6212] How should defence be structured, organised and equipped to best fulfil requirements within resource constraints

[6213] National Defence Intent

[6214] An analysis of the above questions is intended to lead to a common understanding of the level of defence required by the country, of a realistic national defence requirement and how it is to be satisfied – a National Defence Intent

[6215] The essential elements of this are an understanding of, and agreement on, what is expected of defence, how this is to be achieved and what broad capabilities this would require

[6216] These are captured, expressed and elaborated on in the Defence Review, which is government’s highest-level policy statement on defence

[6217] The Defence Review

[6218] The Defence Review must express government’s intent for defence in a way that enables lower-level defence planning

[6219] As such it must

[6220] Highlight key aspects of the environment impacting on defence – the context for defence planning. Outline South Africa’s national security policy – a vital governance factor in defence planning

[6221] Discuss the mandate, missions and roles of defence and the priorities accorded to various tasks in order to support national security policy – statutory and policy governance factors

[6222] Define the defence outcomes to be pursued in terms of national security policy – the ends of defence; e. Detail the corresponding strategic defence concept and strategic capabilities – the Ways and Means of Defence; f. Give strategic guidelines on all of the above for lower-level defence planning

[6223] It is only when defence intent has been unpacked to the level of detail where the resource and cost implications become visible, that it will become evident whether the stated level of intent is feasible, or not

[6224] If the allocated or anticipated resources are insufficient to establish and sustain the capabilities required by the stated defence intent, adjustments to the defence requirement, the defence concept or the resource allocation, or a combination of these will be required to establish a balance between intent and resources

[6225] ESTABLISHING THE LEVEL OF DEFENCE AMBITION

[6226] The level of defence ambition is an expression of national security policy and government’s foreign policy, understood within the context of the defence mandate, as derived from the statutory framework governing defence, particularly the constitutional functions of defence

[6227] All these factors form the governance framework within which defence ambition and the corresponding defence requirements must be determined

[6228] D-2 DETERMINING THE LEVEL OF DEFENCE AMBITION

[6229] In addition, the level of defence ambition and requirement is context-dependent

[6230] This comprises the geostrategic setting for defence, as derived from environmental analyses and intelligence appreciations, and scenarios at a strategic and defence level

[6231] Subject to the governance factors and within context, defence intent comprises three broad issues: a. Defence outcomes – the objectives to be pursued by defence – the ENDS of defence

[6232] b. Defence mission, strategic goals, tasks and concepts – the WAYS of defence

[6233] c. Defence capability requirements – the broad capabilities and force levels required to achieve the outcomes – the MEANS of defence

[6234] The defence mandate derived from the Constitution is a general statement of purpose, covering the full spectrum of possible defence employment

[6235] The functions listed in the Constitution stipulate the purposes for which the Defence Force may be employed

[6236] This needs to be qualified in the light of environmental circumstances and the national security policy, government priorities and the availability of resources

[6237] Defence will thus not be expected to become involved in every possible contingency

[6238] Involvement in many contingencies will be discretionary and complete categories could be eliminated as a matter of policy, based on their extreme unlikelihood, resource constraints, government priorities or other considerations

[6239] The defence outcomes are a function of the sub-set of contingencies defence will be expected to deal with and reflect the ends government wishes to achieve through defence involvement in the selected contingencies

[6240] The defence concept broadly describes the way by which the defence outcomes will be pursued

[6241] It includes the priority accorded to various contingencies or classes of contingencies, guidelines on concurrency and whether capabilities must enable an autonomous or collaborative response (either bi- or multilateral

[6242] The defence capability requirement is a statement of the level of operational capability that would be required by or committed to a particular contingency or class of contingencies, in accordance with the defence outcomes and defence concept

[6243] Since it involves broad classes of threat, within hypothetical futures, only broad statements of requirement are possible

[6244] These will nevertheless give valuable guidance to lower-level defence planning

[6245] The level of defence ambition is thus contained within the Defence Review and elaborates on the types and objectives of operations, missions and tasks envisaged in selected situations, broad guidelines concerning the conduct of such operations, including guidelines concerning concurrency, and the capabilities required for such operations

[6246] It is a vital high-level policy guideline for all defence planning and must be the subject of consensus between government and defence, and of great importance within defence itself

[6247] ‘GEO-STRATEGIC & DEFENCE SCENARIOS’ – A TOOL TO DETERMINE DEFENCE AMBITION Environmental Scan and Intelligence Appreciations

[6248] While the future is inevitably shrouded in uncertainty, it is impossible to plan defence capabilities without some idea of how the future might develop

[6249] The first stage of this work is therefore to review national and defence intelligence appreciations and environmental analyses to determine the main characteristics and trends that are observed in the environment

[6250] This work reflects on relevant environmental characteristics and trends at the global, continental, regional and domestic levels

[6251] Strategic Scenarios

[6252] The characteristics and trends identified during the environmental analysis give an indication of possible future developments but cannot accurately predict the future

[6253] The way in which trends develop and the interaction between factors inevitably introduce uncertainty

[6254] Even if the environment remains relatively stable, the future can therefore develop along a spectrum of alternative pathways

[6255] This will impact on defence requirements

[6256] Defence planning must therefore take account of alternative futures

[6257] The use of scenarios is an accepted way of accommodating and preparing for such alternative futures in a planning process

[6258] Scenarios are purpose-specific and are constructed around those drivers affecting the issue under investigation

[6259] Strategic scenarios reflecting relevant trends and possible high-level developments identified in the environmental scan were therefore written to create alternative contexts for deliberations on defence capabilities

[6260] Strategic scenarios were developed to reflect the emerging environment

[6261] These are: Status Quo – A Continuation of the Current Trajectory

[6262] b. Africa Arising – An Optimistic Future

[6263] c. Regression – A Pessimistic Future

[6264] DETERMINING THE LEVEL OF DEFENCE AMBITION

[6265] Each scenario was developed in summary and detailed format to sketch various contexts within which events requiring a defence response could occur

[6266] The scenarios are dealt with in detail in a separate report

[6267] It is important to note that the futures described in the scenarios are entirely hypothetical but were considered plausible in light of current environmental analyses and intelligence appreciations

[6268] They were not predictions, ie statements regarding what will happen within some bounds of probability, but are statements about the spectrum within which the future might develop

[6269] They also did not include extreme events that would dramatically alter the defence landscape, such as a meltdown of the global political and/or economic system, catastrophic long-term environmental disruption or widespread and hostile major power involvement in Africa

[6270] Extreme events are not impossible

[6271] The most extreme– major meteorite strikes and eruptions of mega-volcanoes that affected all life on Earth – have occurred in geological time and are possible, even probable, in the future

[6272] However, such events alter the security landscape to such an extent that the “rules of the game” are redefined

[6273] A direct major power threat to South Africa would be such an event, implying a significant strategic realignment

[6274] While it is valid to ask “what if?” regarding such events, planning that is actually implementable within available resources must proceed from more constrained visions of the future

[6275] The above scenarios represent such a vision

[6276] Consequent Defence Scenarios

[6277] Events requiring the deployment of military forces do not occur in a vacuum

[6278] The strategic scenarios provide context to such events

[6279] Levels of threat involving combinations of target and source, compatible with the strategic scenarios, are therefore identified to describe plausible manifestations of events or conflict that might occur within the particular strategic scenario

[6280] The spectrum of plausible contingencies represents a defence scenario compatible with the strategic scenario

[6281] This two-step approach, working from strategic scenarios to compatible defence scenarios, is not unique to South Africa

[6282] References to a similar approach have been found in literature regarding the Australian, Swedish and Bulgarian defence planning processes

[6283] To illustrate the relationship between scenarios at the strategic and defence levels: Given a strategic scenario of relative political stability, advancing democracy and economic development at a regional level – the Africa Arising scenario – a state-based threat against South Africa is highly unlikely but overt armed conflict might still be possible in parts of Africa

[6284] Similarly, within the same strategic scenario, an intra-state defence scenario of general civil conflict in South Africa is highly unlikely, but general threats to human security will still exist and might be a serious threat to some countries

[6285] Each contingency implies a possible level of military involvement, including SANDF involvement

[6286] Potential SANDF involvement could thus include participation in multilateral peace missions, direct defence of South Africa, an autonomous intervention, and so forth

[6287] During the process the motivations and qualifications relating to each contingency and the possible modes of SANDF involvement should therefore be noted

[6288] The collection of such plausible contingencies comprises the defence scenario for the corresponding strategic scenario

[6289] The same process of analysis is thus conducted for each strategic scenario

[6290] DEFENCE AMBITION FRAMEWORK & METHODOLOGY

[6291] The defence intent framework is a mechanism to give structure to the deliberation of defence requirements

[6292] In the absence of such a structure it is extremely difficult to coherently debate the complex relationships between all the factors that will influence a decision on defence capabilities

[6293] Deliberations can easily zoom in on a highly unlikely worst-case scenario or some pressing current concern, to the exclusion of many important but less dramatic contingencies

[6294] A framework such as this makes it possible to trace a logic in terms of the whole picture

[6295] The framework consists of two sub-frameworks, one designed to investigate the inter-state dimension, the other the intra-state dimension

[6296] Each sub-framework lists a spectrum of possible threats, from those that involve low levels of violence or threats of natural origin, to those involving extreme violence such as civil war within a country or total war between states

[6297] The second dimension of the frameworks lists the locus or focus of a threat and, in some cases, whether the source would be African or non-African

[6298] A combination of a particular level of threat and a focus/source combination describe a contingency that may require a defence response

[6299] The framework is used in the first place to identify possible defence contingencies that would be plausible within the strategic scenarios

[6300] The set of contingencies compatible with a strategic scenario represents the corresponding defence scenario

[6301] Each contingency must be considered in terms of the possible defence response, the scale of the response, the priority accorded to it, and various other factors to enable a decision on whether provision for such a contingency should be included in the Strategic Intent

[6302] These deliberations will determine where the focus of defence effort should be, what level of capability would be required and what provision should be made for future developments

[6303] DETERMINING THE LEVEL OF DEFENCE AMBITION

[6304] These conclusions, guidelines and motivations form the basis for the policy that will direct detailed defence planning

[6305] While the conceptual approach and the output of the process must inevitably be presented to defence principals and decision-makers, there is a risk in exposing the finer mechanics in a forum where conditions preclude discussion in sufficient depth to create a full understanding

[6306] People are very likely to differ on or misunderstand aspects of the structure, definition or content of a framework or model

[6307] Understanding and agreement that have taken days or weeks to achieve among staff intimately involved in developing and using such a tool, cannot be created in minutes

[6308] If the presenter is not totally au fait with the tool and the content and/or is not given sufficient time to properly explain, misconceptions will inevitably be formed

[6309] Once formed, such misconceptions are very difficult to correct and can undermine the credibility of the entire exercise

[6310] This is not just true of this framework, it is a reality that should be borne in mind when any complex analysis is presented to decision-makers

[6311] This is emphatically not a mechanistic, paint-by-numbers process

[6312] It requires high levels of judgment and important decisions on strategic guidelines for further planning, but in giving structure to deliberations on intent, it will contribute to convergence on this key issue

[6313] INTER-STATE FRAMEWORK

[6314] The inter-state framework reflects the spectrum of possible scenarios for inter-state threats and is intended to facilitate discussion on an appropriate South African defence ambition regarding such threats, whether they involve South Africa, its external interests, other African countries and/or non-African states

[6315] The levels of threat included are as follows (verbatim from Figure D-1): Political and Economic Conflict: Alliances, propaganda, economic and political cooperation/ sanctions, military cooperation and/or assistance

[6316] Conflict management through negotiation, mediation, arbitration

[6317] Sub-National Conflict: Boycotts, seizures, violations of territorial integrity, assassination, acts of terror, sabotage, hostage-taking, state-sponsored plundering of resources, training, advice and military assistance

[6318] c. Overt Armed Conflict: Sporadic armed clashes, skirmishes, raids and temporary incursions by conventional forces

[6319] Limited ends rather than major change in status quo

[6320] Examples: Libya-Egypt 1977, Mali-Burkina Faso 1985, Mauritania-Senegal

[6321] Figure D-1: Defence Intent Framework: Inter-State Dimension

[6322] The structure of the intra-state framework is conceptually identical to that of the inter-state framework

[6323] The rows in the table describe various levels of potential threat to security, from low-level threats of both natural and human origin, to full civil war

[6324] The threat spectrum is as follows (verbatim from Figure D-2): Threats to General Human Security: Natural and human disasters, crime, breakdown of essential services, plundering of resources, mass migrations, large numbers of illegal aliens, refugees, protests, civil disobedience/unrest

[6325] b. Civil Threats to Constitutional Order: Violent protests, sporadic communal violence, mass civil disorder, uncontrolled organised crime, breakdown of law and order

[6326] c. Sub-state Threats to Constitutional Order: Systematic low-key violence by non-state groupings including terrorism, assassination, hostage taking, seizures, sabotage, piracy

[6327] d. General Civil Conflict: Widespread communal inter-group violence and civil disorder

[6328] Examples: Kenya 2007-2008, Jos, Nigeria

[6329] e. Insurgency: Armed rebellion, revolt or insurrection to weaken or gain control of the state

[6330] Examples: Uganda-LRA 1987, Tuareg Rebellion

[6331] Armed intra-state conflict between civilian groups or between the state and a group motivated by identity issues, a desire for secession or for control of the state

[6332] Examples: Liberia 1989-1996, Algeria

[6333] Threats may involve South Africa, SADC and non-SADC states, South African interests in such states, and non-African states

[6334] The framework is depicted in Figure D

[6335] As before, the framework is used to map defence scenarios considered plausible within the higher-level context, and to identify the scenarios that should be included in the deliberation of South Africa’s level of defence intent

[6336] RISK ASSESSMENT

[6337] The selection of the contingencies to be addressed in the defence ambition requires the prioritisation of plausible contingencies according to a consistent set of criteria

[6338] A risk model developed for the purpose of assessing strategic niches in the defence industry was adapted for this purpose

[6339] The risk associated with an event is typically defined as the probability of the event, multiplied by some measure of the impact of the event

[6340] In essence this describes the approach used in the risk model

[6341] The probability of a contingency is related to the scenario with which it is associated

[6342] So, for instance, it seems logical that the probability of armed conflict between countries would be higher in the pessimistic scenario mentioned earlier, than in the optimistic scenario

[6343] However, a scenario is not a prediction and even if it were, it would be impossible to predict the probability of a future event with precision

[6344] The estimates of probability used in the model are therefore not only first-order judgments of absolute probability within the context of the particular strategic scenario, but should reflect a judgment of the likelihood of occurrence of each contingency relative to the other contingencies

[6345] The potential impact of each contingency is assessed using the following criteria: Impact on the South African economy

[6346] b. Impact on the economy of the region

[6347] c. Human impact in South Africa in terms of death and displacement

[6348] d. Human impact in the region in terms of death and displacement

[6349] e. Impact on South Africa’s territorial integrity

[6350] f. Impact on South Africa’s international standing

[6351] g. Impact on morale in South Africa

[6352] A scale is used to measure potential impact in terms of each criterion

[6353] This scale is also expressed as numerical scores that enable the computation of average impact across criteria

[6354] Risk is then expressed as the product of probability and impact

[6355] Risk Assessment: Illustration DETERMINING THE LEVEL OF DEFENCE AMBITION

[6356] The assessments are plotted graphically to enable a visual comparison of the relative probability, impact and risk of various contingencies

[6357] Figure D-3 is an illustration of such a graphic

[6358] According to the definition of risk as the product of probability and impact, contingencies having both a high probability and a high impact are high-risk contingencies

[6359] These would occupy the upper-right sector of the graphic, as illustrated by Contingency 1 in Figure D

[6360] Contingency 3, on the other hand, has a very high impact but such a low probability that it falls in the low risk sector

[6361] For the purpose of the illustration, high-, medium- and low-risk sectors are indicated but this illustrates the general principle

[6362] In practice the decision on exactly where the boundaries should lie, while still following the principle, is a matter of judgment

[6363] The position of a contingency represents its absolute risk

[6364] The size of the circle represents the risk of the contingency relative to Contingencies 2 and

[6365] In combination these give an indication of the absolute and relative priorities contingencies should enjoy

[6366] Since hypothetical future events are being considered, this can obviously be nothing more than a judgment of the potential order of magnitude of the impact of a type or category of contingency

[6367] The changes in the positions of the contingencies under the various scenarios give a useful indication of possible developments and priorities

[6368] This information is used to define the assessments in the defence intent framework

[6369] In any single scenario, higher risk contingencies would normally assume higher priority

[6370] However, when multiple scenarios are considered, contingencies that may constitute a low risk in most but a very high risk in one, might justify a higher priority

[6371] Interactions between contingencies should also be considered since work invested in some contingencies could have the effect of reducing the probability of occurrence of others

[6372] In yet other cases, the decision might be taken to merely monitor risk indicators related to a scenario or contingency, using a change in those indicators as a trigger for measures to deal with or contain an emerging situation

[6373] However, it cannot be over-emphasised that the scenario analysis and risk assessments are not assessments of or predictions regarding actual anticipated events

[6374] They are mental exercises that are intended to help participating staff think through the spectrum of possible futures in a structured, logical manner, so that they will better understand what the future might hold and will therefore be better prepared to make recommendations regarding future defence requirements

[6375] It is, essentially, a way of improving judgment

[6376] ANALYSIS OF SCENARIOS THE OPTIMISTIC TRAJECTORY ‘AFRICA ARISING’ STRATEGIC SCENARIO

[6377] Despite the economic and military rise of the East, it maintains healthy relations with Western countries marked by a reduction in political tension in order to maintain good trade relations

[6378] The UN Security Council has provided Africa and South America each with a de facto permanent seat, allowing the interests of developing nations to be better represented

[6379] This places reconstruction and development in Africa much higher on the UN agenda and creates more urgency and commitment in the UN, the World Bank and among EU donors and agencies to become more closely involved in assisting poor and conflict-stricken African countries

[6380] Within the AU and regional economic communities (RECs), African states unite more closely to protect and promote common continental and sub-regional political, economic and security interests given the high demand for Africa’s natural resources

[6381] The number and intensity of intra-state conflicts continue to decline as in the rest of the world

[6382] Donors also start to invest more in demobilisation, disarmament and reintegration (DDR) and security sector reform which were underfunded for a long time

[6383] Africa maintains its record economic growth rate with booming prices in commodities such as oil, gas and coal, which has enabled Africa to make significant progress in its strive towards achieving the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs

[6384] Reforms in many African countries towards building more mixed economies in sectors such as agriculture and manufacturing, reduce reliance on income from such commodities

[6385] More scientific ways of farming enable Africa to largely avoid food security crises, despite water scarcity and droughts caused by climate change

[6386] Africa’s overall economic growth reduces economic inequalities within and between countries

[6387] Most African countries have a growing middle class as social mobility is improving

[6388] Economic growth is also allowing African states to significantly improve their education and health systems

[6389] Africa maintains its general trend towards civil and political freedom

[6390] The exponential growth in cell phone use in Africa is enabling various civic groups in Africa to mobilise around common interests for elections and to hold their governments more accountable, which results in improved governance and democratisation

[6391] Large-scale infrastructure projects are improving connectivity and trade between African countries and improve the export of goods to other continents

[6392] It also enables a freer movement of skilled and unskilled labour within and between RECs

[6393] In summary, the strategic scenario is characterised by a stable international system, relatively rapid but uneven economic growth and political development and high levels of African cooperation with growing participation in global economic and political affairs

[6394] There is relative peace and stability, with sporadic but decreasing conflict in some countries

[6395] Solidarity, constructive engagement, development and participation in and through international institutions are the order of the day

[6396] There has been significant improvement in human development and progress toward African Renaissance ideals

[6443] THE MIDDLE-ROAD TRAJECTORY ‘MAINTAINING THE STATUS QUO’ STRATEGIC SCENARIO The international system is a multi-polar world with continuing diffusion of power

[6444] There is increasing pressure particularly from developing countries to reform the UN Security Council, the G8, the IMF and the World Bank to reflect current international dynamics and to better represent the interests of the developing world

[6445] The US, the EU, Russia, China, India and Japan continue to play major roles, but with other states and other types of international actors occasionally rising to importance on various international issues

[6446] Risk Assessment for the Intra-State Defence Scenario: Optimistic Trajectory Stable economic relations are considered more important than military or politicalideological concerns, but competition for access to natural resources and markets in developing regions, including sub-Saharan Africa, is creating political tension between emerging and developed economies

[6447] Prior to the international economic recession, Africa experienced relatively high rates of economic growth

[6448] African countries with valuable minerals and significant oil and gas reserves recovered well after the recession

[6449] Low-income African countries without significant infrastructure and industrial capacity, were less affected by the recession

[6450] On average, most African countries experience higher and steady economic growth rates, but on an insufficient scale to meet the demand for development on the continent

[6451] Inadequate economic growth causes slow progress with Africa’s general health status and human development compared to the rest of the developing world

[6452] There is uneven development in and between Africa’s RECs

[6453] Africa therefore made limited progress in terms of sustainable human development and achieving the MDGs

[6454] Africa’s high level of professional skills loss inhibits its potential for job creation, innovation and direct global integration

[6455] Africa continues its general trend towards democratisation and respect for human rights, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa

[6456] Drawn-out intrastate conflicts in countries such as the DRC, Somalia, Uganda and Nigeria are difficult to stop and remain a problem in terms of peace and security on the continent

[6457] Yet the number of inter- and intra-state conflicts in Africa is declining together with the number of deaths in armed conflict

[6458] In this sense Africa has made progress towards a more stable and peaceful continent, but is largely dependent on UN/multinational peace missions in the Great Lakes as well as Sudan/Darfur and its neighbouring states, to prevent these regional conflicts from escalating

[6459] The number of refugees in Africa’s conflict hotspots is increasing at an alarming rate – creating tension between neighbouring countries about the burden that refugee camps place on their economies and security forces

[6460] Food security problems due to climate change and old farming methods are worsened by the large numbers of refugees and internally displaced people, as many people are unable to grow crops on a sufficient scale and therefore become dependent on international food aid

[6461] Except for oil-producing countries such as Algeria, Angola and Nigeria, most African states invest very little in their armed forces, which creates a general decline in military capabilities and the ability of states to control their own territory

[6462] South Africa is a case in point, with a stagnant defence budget which is declining in real terms, high inflows of illegal immigrants and a low level of education among military professionals, which is eroding the SANDF’s image, credibility and standing in Africa

[6463] African militaries have become dependent on strong powers to take part in African peace missions, particularly for air transport and logistics

[6464] While the AU has ratified many policies and resolutions, it struggles to provide sufficient early-warning and political intervention to prevent conflicts, making the AU reactive instead of proactive

[6465] Due to a lack of resources and capacity, the AU also struggles to partner with foreign donors and development agencies for reconstruction and development on the continent

[6466] The lack of regional cooperation in the AU has resulted in the African Standby Force not reaching its set milestones and being largely unprepared for largescale peace enforcement

[6467] In summary, the international system is relatively stable

[6468] There is moderate to rapid but unstable economic growth in some African countries, stagnation or regression in others

[6469] Regional development is uneven

[6470] Generally there is progress toward peace, stability and democracy but some countries and regions are still afflicted by persistent conflict

[6471] Regional cooperation in support of AU ideals is limited

[6472] Human development continues to lag behind the rest of the developing world, impeding global integration

[6510] STRATEGIC SCENARIO The international system is a turbulent and competitive multi-polar system with rising economic and military tension between strong powers

[6511] Cooperation within and between RECs is declining internationally including Africa, due to competition between states for access to dwindling energy sources and minerals to maintain their economic growth

[6512] The UN, AU and SADC have become largely ineffective in international affairs as member states fend for themselves

[6513] There is a strong shift to mercantilism as countries try to protect their industries against cheap imports by means of tariff barriers and other trade restrictions particularly in the North

[6514] As strong powers try to compete for or maintain exploitation rights for fossil fuels and minerals in African countries, they increasingly turn a blind eye to unconstitutional changes of political power, human rights violations and economic mismanagement of African governments

[6515] Undeclared small arms and conventional weapons transfers to African governments often form part of contracts to obtain rights to exploit natural resources which exacerbates the proliferation of small arms on the continent

[6516] A lack of solidarity, cooperative intent and security cooperation in Africa has aggravated the situation of inter- and intra-state conflicts on the continent

[6517] Border disputes over oil-rich areas have escalated into incidents of small-scale battles between neighbouring states

[6518] As African countries try to cope with rapidly increasing populations and youth bulge, urbanisation and megacities, they spend less on maintaining and expanding their commercial and industrial infrastructure – resulting in the deterioration of much of Africa’s economic infrastructure

[6519] Most African states cannot keep up with the demand for essential services and policing in mega-cities

[6520] Organised crime syndicates and some international terrorist groups exploit this situation and expand their activities – becoming a threat to state security

[6521] There are also more incidents of inter-communal fighting between religious and ethnic groups competing for political power

[6522] The military capabilities of armed forces in most African countries have deteriorated extensively and many have been reduced to militias that mainly protect the ruling elite and their economic interests

[6523] As a result, military interventions aimed at protecting foreign economic interests have increased

[6524] Incidents of piracy around the Horn of Africa and the Gulf of Guinea are increasing due to a lack of law and order on land – raising concerns about the impact on international trade

[6525] Strong powers are making increasing use of private military and security companies (PMSCs) to protect their economic interests in Africa, without cooperating with international protocols for regulating the PMSC industry

[6526] Subsequently security sector reform is receiving less attention in Africa

[6527] Figure D-11: Risk Assessment for the Intra-State Defence Scenario: Current Trajectory SOUTH AFRICAN DEFENCE REVIEW 2015 DETERMINING THE LEVEL OF DEFENCE AMBITION African countries are unable to feed their growing populations with internal produce due to climate change and continued subsistence farming

[6528] Africa therefore faces serious food and water security challenges and many countries are dependent on international food aid

[6529] The deterioration of security in many African countries results in the withdrawal of NGOs and UN agencies from the continent – leaving few organisations behind who are able to provide aid in both urban and remote rural areas

[6530] In summary, the international system is turbulent with intense competition for global dominance and increasing economic and political instability at global and continental levels

[6531] There is widespread conflict within and sometimes between African states due to demographic pressures and competition for resources

[6532] Economic resources are severely strained

[6533] Solidarity, cooperative intent and collective security mechanisms have been eroded and have in some cases broken down

[6534] There is increasing military intervention by external powers to secure their interests, particularly access to resources

[6560] CONSOLIDATION OF ANALYSIS ACROSS ALL THREE SCENARIOS

[6561] The preceding analysis sketched three scenarios at the strategic level

[6562] These were elaborated into collections of generic contingencies representing corresponding defence scenarios

[6563] The associated risk analyses were judgments regarding the probability and impact of those contingencies in the context of the strategic scenarios

[6564] All of this is a mental exercise designed to stimulate and structure thoughts about possible futures

[6565] Those futures are hypothetical but are considered plausible in the light of current environmental analyses and intelligence appreciations

[6566] They do not include extreme events that would dramatically alter the defence landscape, such as a melt-down of the global political and/or economic system, catastrophic long-term environmental disruption or widespread and hostile major power involvement in Africa

[6567] Risk Assessment for the Intra-State Defence Scenario: Pessimistic Trajectory There can be no guarantee that the future will play out within the constraints sketched above

[6568] However, it is impossible to plan in the absence of objectives and constraints – mathematically, optimisation of an objective function is only possible within given constraints

[6569] If either changes, the solution will change

[6570] So, too, with defence planning, where expectations of the future (including the funding to be allocated to defence) are vital constraints

[6571] If those expectations change significantly, re-planning is required

[6572] The analysis as it stands thus implies certain planning assumptions and/or guidelines: Force planning within a constrained future

[6573] The management of risks outside that future by other means

[6574] c. Replanning if events indicating a departure from that constrained future should develop

[6575] The use of the force-in-being to deal with extreme events until the Defence Review can be implemented

[6576] However, defence capabilities must also support and enable the regional, continental and global role South Africa desires and is expected to play, ie defence must be configured and equipped to reflect and give expression to South Africa’s international status and its national security and foreign policies

[6577] Balance must be achieved between national ambitions, defence capabilities and defence funding

[6578] As a starting point, planning assumptions/guidelines must be set within the constrained future of the scenarios

[6579] Since neither the optimistic nor the current trajectories pose any real challenges for defence, the following general guidelines are proposed: a. Contingencies considered plausible within the pessimistic trajectory will be set as baseline

[6580] Priorities will be set as follows: i. High- or medium-risk contingencies affecting South Africa or its vital interests

[6581] High- or medium-risk contingencies affecting SADC and similar contingencies affecting the rest of Africa

[6582] iii. Low-risk, high-impact contingencies

[6583] Peacetime defence interaction and support to government departments

[6584] v. Other contingencies

[6585] The SANDF force-in-being should be capable of dealing with high- or medium-risk contingencies

[6586] Given sufficient warning and resources, the SANDF should be capable of expanding or adjusting to meet low-risk, high-impact contingencies

[6587] Early warning systems will be in place and resources will be allocated as and when required

[6588] e. South African involvement in contingencies other than threats to South Africa or its interests will be discretionary within the context of peace missions or other multinational actions

[6589] f. Force planning will make provision for concurrent activities to a specified level

[6590] Where that level is exceeded, higher risk contingencies will take priority

[6591] g. Cyber security will be a ubiquitous requirement

[6592] In addition to these general guidelines, specific guidelines will apply in determining the capability requirements for the inter- and intra-state dimensions

[6593] CONSOLIDATED INTER-STATE DIMENSION Figure D-16: The Inter-State Defence Scenario: Consolidated The consolidated inter-state scenario is presented in Figure D

[6594] Specific guidelines applying to the inter-state dimension are

[6595] As the leading state in SADC and in Africa, South Africa must be able to match the military capabilities of its peers

[6596] In terms of defensive capability, despite the absence of any military threat to South Africa from the region, this means that the SANDF must as a force in being at least be able to defend against a threat to the level of overt armed conflict from a neighbouring state

[6597] This capability should be the focus of a balanced, sustainable military force, able to meet other commitments

[6598] The SANDF force-in-being should provide the basis for expansion to a level where the SANDF will be able to defend against a threat of limited war from a contiguous state

[6599] No specific provision will be made for overt threats from non-contiguous African sources: i. There are no plausible causative factors or strategic motivations evident. ii

[6600] Globally there is no historical precedent for such action

[6601] The capability to project force over the distances involved is very limited

[6602] It implies complicity of a contiguous state or a violation of the integrity of such a state

[6603] In the first case it will be treated as a threat from a contiguous state; in the second, as a threat to that state, which will be dealt with multilaterally

[6604] A threat to South Africa from external sources beyond Africa constitutes an extreme event that implies major power involvement

[6605] Due to the asymmetry this entails, the extreme unlikelihood of such an event and the limited resources available to the SANDF, the SANDF will not specifically make provision for such a threat

[6606] The risk will be managed primarily by other means

[6607] The SANDF should be able to contribute to multinational peace missions to the level of peace enforcement in the context of inter-state limited war involving other African states

[6608] However, such involvement and the scale thereof are discretionary and will be determined by the specific situation

[6609] Criteria for such involvement and a predetermined maximum level of involvement are to be set

[6610] f. Threats to South Africa’s interests will preferentially be dealt with at a multilateral level

[6611] However, the SANDF should have the capability for limited autonomous operations in defence of vital interests

[6612] Those interests and the maximum level of autonomous action are to be defined

[6613] g. SANDF deployments beyond Africa will be exceptional, of limited scale and duration, and subject to other priorities

[6614] In general, threats to security closer to South Africa will enjoy priority

[6615] h. Contingencies at the level of general or total war are excluded from the planning baseline due to the low probability and resource implications thereof

[6616] The development of such a scenario implies a major change in the international order, requiring re-planning of defence capabilities

[6617] i. Participation in military diplomacy, assistance and other cooperative interaction will be a standing commitment in support of South Africa’s regional, continental and global role

[6618] The consolidated intra-state scenario is presented in Figure D

[6619] As before, the focus of the force-in-being is on medium- to high-risk contingencies, although in its internal role even some low-risk contingencies may involve SANDF support to the SAPS and other departments

[6620] Specific guidelines applying to this dimension are

[6621] The SANDF force-in-being should have the capability to fulfil the following short-term requirements: i. Assistance to the SAPS and civil authorities in dealing with general threats to security. ii

[6622] Assistance to the SAPS and civil authorities in countering low-level threats to security including civil threats to the constitutional order and sub-state threats such as terrorism and piracy

[6623] The protection of South Africa’s external interests against direct or indirect threats

[6624] Threats to South Africa’s interests will preferentially be dealt with at a multilateral level

[6625] However, the SANDF should have the capability for limited autonomous operations in defence of vital interests

[6626] Those interests and the maximum level of autonomous action are to be defined (including maritime interests

[6627] Participation in multinational regional/continental peace missions occurring in the context of general civil conflict in a SADC state or elsewhere in Africa

[6628] Such participation shall be discretionary to a predetermined maximum scale and shall be subject to other priorities

[6629] In the longer term the SANDF shall have the ability to scale up to the following requirements: i. Assistance to the SAPS and civil authorities in countering a significant internal threat, including low-level insurgency. ii

[6630] Participation in multinational regional/continental peace missions to the level of peace enforcement in a civil war situation

[6631] Such participation shall be discretionary to a predetermined maximum scale and shall be subject to other priorities
